parole.significato: belonging to a domain or territory
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch -dom, from Old Dutch -duom, from Proto-West Germanic *-dōm, from Proto-Germanic *-dōmaz. Cognate with English -dom, German -tum.

parole.significato: Forms nouns for the female counterpart of something.
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch -egge, -igge, from Old Dutch *-igga, from Proto-West Germanic *-ggjā, from Proto-Germanic *-gjǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *-ikyeh₂.
From Old Dutch *-el, from Proto-West Germanic *-il, from Proto-Germanic *-ilaz.

parole.significato: Forms verbs from nouns and adjectives. The stem of the word itself does not change.
parole.testo: Primarily from weak class 2, from Middle Dutch -en, from Old Dutch -on, from Proto-West Germanic *-ōn, from Proto-Germanic *-ōną, from Proto-Indo-European *-eh₂yéti (denominative) and *-h₂ti (factitive). Also partially from weak class 1 (Old Dutch -en, from Proto-West Germanic *-jan) and strong verb

parole.significato: A suffix present on certain adverbs.
parole.testo: From Old Dutch -ana, from Proto-West Germanic *-anā, from Proto-Germanic *-anē.

parole.significato: Used to form the (strong) feminine singular genitive.
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch -er, from Old Dutch -ro, from Proto-West Germanic *-eʀā, from Proto-Germanic *-aizōz.

parole.significato: -ness, -ity, -hood; forms nouns from adjectives, denoting the abstract quality of the adjective.
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch -heit, from Old Dutch -heit, from Proto-West Germanic *-haidu, from Proto-Germanic *haiduz. Cognate with German -heit, English -hood.
From Middle Dutch -ich, from Old Dutch -ag, -ig, from Proto-West Germanic *-g, from Proto-Germanic *-agaz, *-īgaz, *-ugaz, each a variant of a common suffix *-gaz, from Proto-Indo-European *-kos.

parole.significato: Creates action nouns referring to the performance of a verb, or the result thereof.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle Dutch -inge, from Old Dutch -inga, -unga, -onga, from Proto-West Germanic *-ingu, *-ungu, from Proto-Germanic *-ungō.

parole.significato: Forms nouns for a person originating from a place or family.
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch -inc, from Old Dutch -ing, from Proto-West Germanic *-ing, from Proto-Germanic *-ingaz.

From earlier -ken, from Middle Dutch -ken, -kin, -kijn, from Old Dutch *-kīn, apparently representing Proto-West Germanic *-ukīn, a double diminutive, from *-uk + *-īn. The standard Dutch -tje and its variants are derived from -ke(n) through palatalization. Cognate with German -chen, Low German -ken
From Middle Dutch -lijc, from Old Dutch -līk, from Proto-West Germanic *-līk, from Proto-Germanic *-līkaz. Cognate with German -lich, English -ly, Old Norse -līkʀ.
A suffixed variant of loos, from Middle Dutch -loos, from Old Dutch -lōs, from Proto-West Germanic *laus, from Proto-Germanic *lausaz.
From Old Dutch -nissi, -nussi, from Proto-West Germanic *-nassī.

parole.significato: Used to form adjectives of characteristic from nouns or verbs.
parole.testo: From earlier -sch, from Middle Dutch -sch, from Old Dutch -isc, from Proto-West Germanic *-isk, from Proto-Germanic *-iskaz (from which also -isch via German), from Proto-Indo-European *-iskos.

From Middle Dutch -schap, from Old Dutch -skap, from Proto-West Germanic *-skapi, from Proto-Germanic *-skapiz. Cognates Cognate with German -schaft, Swedish -skap, West Frisian -skip, English -ship, Danish -skab, Norwegian -skap See English -ship and Old English -sciepe.

parole.significato: -age, -ion; Creates neuter nouns indicating something which performs or has undergone an action, or something which res…
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch -sel, from Old Dutch -isli, from Proto-West Germanic *-islī. Cognate with German -sel, Old English -else, Swedish -else.

parole.significato: forms certain verb forms of the second person singular, second person plural, and third person singular:
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch -t, -et from Old Dutch -it, -et, -ot a merger of the following historical inflectional suffixes: # second person singular (originaly second person plural) present tense: Proto-West Germanic *-id, *-iþ, *-ōþ *-ēþ, from Proto-Germanic *-id, *-iþ, *-ōþ, *-aiþ # second person singular

parole.significato: forms certain verbal nouns, mostly of strong verbs
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch -t a merger of a variety of verbal noun forming suffixes: # Old Dutch -t, -thi, from Proto-West Germanic *-þi, from Proto-Germanic *-þiz # Old Dutch -t, -thu, Proto-West Germanic *-þu, from Proto-Germanic *-þuz # Old Dutch ot, Proto-West Germanic *-ōþu, from Proto-Germanic *-ōþuz

parole.significato: appended to an adjective, making a feminine noun which refers to the size or quality referred to by the adjective, cogn…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle Dutch -ede, from Old Dutch -itha, from Proto-West Germanic *-iþu, from Proto-Germanic *-iþō, from Proto-Indo-European *-teh₂. Middle Dutch -ede was shortened to -de in late Middle Dutch, and the suffix was devoiced to -te according to the 't kofschip rule. This voiceless variet

parole.significato: Appended to a noun (or occasionally another part of speech), making it diminutive.
parole.testo: From earlier -tjen, from Middle Dutch -kijn, from Old Dutch -kīn, which is the ancestor of the suffixes -ke, -ken, -tje (and its subvarieties: -je, -etje, -pje, -kje) and Afrikaans -tjie ([ci]). All forms descend from the Proto-West Germanic *-ikīn, *-ukīn, itself a double diminutive produced by com

parole.significato: barge (type of ship that sails on rivers)
parole.testo: Rebracketing of naak, a now-obsolete form which was still used in early modern Dutch (compare adder, from earlier nadder), from Middle Dutch aecke and non-rebracketed naecke; the latter derives from Old Dutch *nako, from Proto-West Germanic *nakwō, from Proto-Germanic *nakwô (“boat, ship”).
From Middle Dutch âel, from Old Dutch *āl, from Proto-West Germanic *āl, from Proto-Germanic *ēlaz.
From Middle Dutch āle, from Old Dutch *alo, from Proto-West Germanic *alu, from Proto-Germanic *alu, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂elut-. Doublet of ale.
From Middle Dutch aelmoesene, from Old Dutch [Term?], from Proto-West Germanic *alemōsinā, from Vulgar Latin *alemosyna, from Latin eleēmosyna, from Ancient Greek ἐλεημοσύνη (eleēmosúnē).

parole.significato: liquid excrements of animals, liquid manure, slurry
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch ael, adel, from Old Dutch *adal, from Proto-West Germanic *adal, from Proto-Germanic *adalaz (“liquid manure”). Cognate with Old English adel, adela (“liquid manure; filth”). More at addle.
From Middle Dutch āenbilt, from Old Dutch *anafelt, from Proto-West Germanic *anafalt. The second component has been modified by influence of Dutch beeld.

parole.significato: on (positioned at the outer surface of; attached to)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch āne, from Old Dutch ana, from Proto-West Germanic *ana, from Proto-Germanic *ana.
From Middle Dutch aencomen, from Old Dutch *anakuman, from Proto-West Germanic *anakweman. Equivalent to aan + komen.
From Middle Dutch aenvanc, from Old Dutch *anafang, from Proto-West Germanic *anafangi. Deverbal from aanvangen. Compare German Anfang.

parole.significato: monkey, ape, simian; any member of the infraorder Simiiformes
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch āpe, from Old Dutch *apo, from Proto-West Germanic *apō, from Proto-Germanic *apô.
Inherited from Middle Dutch âer, from Old Dutch *ār, from Proto-West Germanic *ahaʀ, from Proto-Germanic *ahaz.
From Middle Dutch āert, from Old Dutch *ard, from Proto-West Germanic *ardi, from Proto-Germanic *ardiz.

From Middle Dutch erdappel (“hog's bread”), equivalent to aarde (“soil, earth, ground”) + appel (“apple”), cognate with Middle Low German erdappel (modern Low German Erdappel), Old High German erdapful (“pumpkin, squash, melon”) (modern German Erdapfel (“potato”)), West Frisian ierappel (“potato”),

parole.significato: strawberry (berry of various plants of genus Fragaria)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch erdbēre, erdbēsie, from Old Dutch *erthberi, from Proto-West Germanic *erþubaʀi, from Proto-Germanic *erþōbazją (literally “earth-berry”). The latter part of the compound was replaced in modern Dutch with bei, from Middle Dutch baye, from Old French baie, from Latin bacca. Cognate
From Middle Dutch aertbēvinge, erdbēvinge, from Old Dutch *erthbivunga, from Proto-West Germanic *erþubibungu. Equivalent to aarde + beving.
From Middle Dutch āerde, from Old Dutch ertha, from Proto-West Germanic *erþu, from Proto-Germanic *erþō. False cognate of Arabic أَرْض (ʔarḍ).

From Middle Dutch erdijn, from Old Dutch *irthīn, from Proto-West Germanic *irþīn, from Proto-Germanic *irþīnaz, equivalent to aarde + -en. Reformed by analogy with aarde, undoing the effects of umlaut.
From Middle Dutch āers, from Old Dutch *ars, from Proto-West Germanic *ars, from Proto-Germanic *arsaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁órsos.

parole.significato: an abbey, monastery under a prelate styled abbot
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch abedîe, abdîe, from Old Dutch *abbadea, from Proto-West Germanic *abbadejā. Equivalent to abt (“abbot”) + -ij.
From Middle Dutch achte, acht, from Old Dutch ahto, from Proto-West Germanic *ahtō, from Proto-Germanic *ahtōu, from Proto-Indo-European *oḱtṓw.
From Middle Dutch achte, from Old Dutch *ahta, from Proto-West Germanic *ahtu.
From Middle Dutch achten, from Old Dutch ahton, from Proto-West Germanic *ahtōn. By surface analysis, acht (“attention, heed, consideration”) + -en.
From Middle Dutch achter, from Old Dutch after, from Proto-West Germanic *aftar, from Proto-Germanic *after.

parole.significato: regard, esteem, estimation (opinion or judgment of something, negative or positive)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch achtinge, from Old Dutch ahtinga, from Proto-West Germanic *ahtungu. By surface analysis, achten (“to regard, consider”) + -ing (“-ing, -ation”). Cognate with German Achtung.

parole.significato: viper, adder (snake of the family Viperidae)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch adder, adre, rebracketing of nadder, nadre, from Old Dutch *nadra, from Proto-West Germanic *nadrā.
From Middle Dutch adel, from Old Dutch *athal, from Proto-West Germanic *aþal, from Proto-Germanic *aþalą.
From Middle Dutch âdem, from Old Dutch *āthom, from Proto-West Germanic *āþm, from Proto-Germanic *ēþmaz.
From Middle Dutch âdemen, from Old Dutch *āthamon, from Proto-West Germanic *āþmōn. Equivalent to adem + -en.
From Middle Dutch ādere, from Old Dutch *āthera, from Proto-West Germanic *ādrā.
From Middle Dutch afgrisen, from grisen (whence also modern griezelen), from Old Dutch *grīsan, from Proto-West Germanic *grīsan, from Proto-Germanic *grīsaną.
From Middle Dutch afscheden, from Old Dutch *afskeithan, from Proto-West Germanic *abaskaiþan, from Proto-Germanic *abaskaiþaną. Equivalent to af + scheiden.
From Middle Dutch akelich, which comes from akel (“suffering”) + -ich, derived from Proto-West Germanic *akan. Related to German eklig.

From Middle Dutch aker, eker, haker, from Old Dutch *aker, from Proto-West Germanic [Term?], Latin aquarium. The loan from Latin is likely very early, as evidenced by the shifted consonants in Old High German ahhāri, ahari, agari. Doublet of aquarium.

parole.significato: agricultural field (field on which crops are grown)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch acker, from Old Dutch akker, from Proto-West Germanic *akr.
From Middle Dutch al, from Old Dutch al, from Proto-West Germanic *all.

parole.significato: a type of folkloristic humanoid or spirit; an elf
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch alf, from Old Dutch *alf, from Proto-Germanic *albiz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *albʰós. Doublet with Dutch elf (“elf”), a modern borrowing from English.

parole.significato: all (every individual of the given class)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch alle.

parole.significato: artemisia (any herb of the genus Artemisia)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch alsene, from Old Dutch *alasina, from Proto-West Germanic *alahsinā.
From Middle Dutch alsô, from Old Dutch alsō, from Proto-West Germanic *allswā. Equivalent to al + zo. Doublet of als.
From Middle Dutch ambacht, from Old Dutch ambaht, from Proto-Germanic *ambahtaz, from Gaulish ambaxtos, from Proto-Celtic *ambaxtos. The same source has led to the form ambt. Cognate with German Amt.
From Middle Dutch ander, from Old Dutch ander, from Proto-West Germanic *anþar, from Proto-Germanic *anþeraz.
From Middle Dutch appel, from Old Dutch appel, from Proto-West Germanic *applu, from Proto-Germanic *aplaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ébōl.
From Proto-West Germanic *appluwīn. Equivalent to appel (“apple”) + wijn (“wine”).

From Middle Dutch arbeit, from Old Dutch arbeit, arbeith alongside arvit, arvith, from Proto-West Germanic *arbaidi ~ *arbaiþi, from Proto-Germanic *arbaidiz. Some commentators think that the form with -b- must be due to influence by Old High German arbeit, but this is not certain. The stop could al

parole.significato: eagle, large bird of prey of the family Accipitridae
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch aernt, from earlier aren, from Old Dutch *aro, from Proto-West Germanic *arō, from Proto-Germanic *arô.

From Middle Dutch arm, from Old Dutch arm, from Proto-West Germanic *arm, from Proto-Germanic *armaz (“arm”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂(e)rmos (“a fitting, joint”), a suffixed form of *h₂er- (“to join, fit together”). Cognate to Avestan 𐬀𐬭𐬨𐬀 (arma) and Old Persian [script needed] (arma).
From Middle Dutch arm, from Old Dutch arm, from Proto-West Germanic *arm, from Proto-Germanic *armaz, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *h₂erH- (“to be sparse”).
From Middle Dutch armoede, from earlier armode by analogy with moed, from Old Dutch *armodi, from Proto-West Germanic *armōdī, from Proto-Germanic *armōdiją.

From Middle Dutch ersetere, arseter, arsete, from Old Dutch ercetere, from Proto-West Germanic *arcijātārī. The modern form is based on or influenced by German Arzt. All borrowed from Medieval Latin arcīāter, from Late Latin archīāter, from Ancient Greek ἀρχιατρός (arkhiatrós).

From Middle Dutch asche, from Old Dutch *aska, from Proto-West Germanic *askā, from Proto-Germanic *askǭ. Cognate with Low German Asch, German Asche, English ash, West Frisian jiske, Danish aske, Swedish aska.
From Middle Dutch navegheer, avegaer, from Old Dutch *navugēr, from Proto-West Germanic *nabugaiʀ, from Proto-Germanic *nabōgaizaz. Cognate with English auger, Old Norse nafarr.
From Middle Dutch averute, from Old Dutch *avarūta, from Proto-West Germanic *abrūtā, from Latin abrotonum, from Ancient Greek ἀβρότονον (abrótonon). Doublet of averoon.
From Middle Dutch âvont, from Old Dutch āvont, from Proto-West Germanic *ābanþ, from Proto-Germanic *ēbanþs.

parole.significato: evening star; the planet Venus as seen in the western sky in the evening
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch âvontsterre, from Old Dutch *āvontsterro, *āvontsterno, from Proto-West Germanic *ābanþsternō, from Proto-Germanic *ēbanþsternǭ. Equivalent to avond + ster.
From Middle Dutch bake, from Old Dutch *baco, from Proto-West Germanic *bakō.
From Middle Dutch bāne, from Old Dutch *bana, from Proto-West Germanic *banu, from Proto-Germanic *banō. Compare German Bahn.

parole.significato: a bier, a stretcher, a litter; a device used to carry someone or something, especially wounded or dead people
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch bâre, from Old Dutch bier, from Proto-West Germanic *bērō, from Proto-Germanic *bērō, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer- (“to carry, bear”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian Beere (“stretcher, bier”), English bier, German Bahre (“bier, stretcher”).

From Middle Dutch bare, from Old Dutch *bāra, from Proto-West Germanic *bārā, from Proto-Germanic *bērǭ (“wave, billow”). Cognate with West Frisian baar, Middle Low German bâre (“wave”), Old Norse bára (“wave, undulation, uneven surface”) (whence Middle English bare (“wave, billow”), English bore (“

parole.significato: beard (mass of facial hair that includes chin hair)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch baert, from Old Dutch *bart, from Proto-West Germanic *bard, from Proto-Germanic *bardaz, Proto-Indo-European *bʰardʰ-eh₂.
From Middle Dutch bars, baers, from Old Dutch *bars, from Proto-West Germanic *bars.

Inherited from Middle Dutch baes (“master of a household, friend”), from Old Dutch *baso (“uncle, kinsman”), from Proto-West Germanic *baswō, from Proto-Germanic *baswô. Cognates include Middle Low German bās (“supervisor, foreman”), Old Frisian bas (“master”); possibly also Old High German basa, wh

parole.significato: to chatter, to chit-chat, to talk casually
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch babbelen, from Old Dutch *babbalon, from Proto-West Germanic *babalōn, from Proto-Germanic *babalōną.
From Middle Dutch bat, from Old Dutch *bath, from Proto-West Germanic *baþ, from Proto-Germanic *baþą.
From Middle Dutch bāden, from Old Dutch bathon, from Proto-West Germanic *baþōn, from Proto-Germanic *baþōną. By surface analysis, bad + -en.
From Middle Dutch backen, baken, from Old Dutch *bakkan, *bakan, from Proto-West Germanic *bakan, from Proto-Germanic *bakaną, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₃g-.

parole.significato: a ball or any object with such a shape
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch bal, from Old Dutch *bal, from Proto-West Germanic *ballu, from Proto-Germanic *balluz. Doublet of baal.
From Middle Dutch balch, from Old Dutch balg, from Proto-West Germanic *balgi, from Proto-Germanic *balgiz.
From Middle Dutch balke, from Old Dutch *balco, from Proto-West Germanic *balkō, from Proto-Germanic *balkô.
From Middle Dutch banc, from Old Dutch *banc, from Proto-West Germanic *banki, from Proto-Germanic *bankiz.
From Middle Dutch bannen, from Old Dutch *bannan, from Proto-West Germanic *bannan, from Proto-Germanic *bannaną.

From Middle Dutch barch, barech, from Old Dutch barcho, *barug, from Proto-West Germanic *barug, from Proto-Germanic *barugaz. Cognate to English barrow (Old English bearg), West Frisian baarch (Old Frisian barch), Old Saxon barug, dialectal German Barch (Old High German barug), and Old Norse bǫrgr.

From Middle Dutch bersten, barsten, from metathesis of Old Dutch brestan, from Proto-West Germanic *brestan, from Proto-Germanic *brestaną, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰres- (“to burst, break, crack, split, separate”).
From Middle Dutch bast, from Old Dutch *bast, from Proto-West Germanic *bast.
From Middle Dutch baten, from Old Dutch *baton, from Proto-West Germanic *batēn, from Proto-Germanic *batāną, from the same root as beter.
From Middle Dutch basen, from Old Dutch *bason, from Proto-West Germanic *basōn.
From Middle Dutch bebinden, from Old Dutch *bibindan, from Proto-West Germanic *bibindan, from Proto-Germanic *bibindaną. Equivalent to be- + binden.
From Middle Dutch bedde, from Old Dutch bedde, from Proto-West Germanic *badi, from Proto-Germanic *badją.

parole.significato: to become calm, to calm down
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch bedaren, from Old Dutch *bidarēn, from Proto-West Germanic *bidaʀēn, from *bi- + *daʀēn.

From Middle Dutch bedecken, from Old Dutch bithekken, from Proto-West Germanic *biþakkjan, equivalent to be- + dekken. Cognate with English bethatch and English bedeck, German bedecken, Swedish betäcka.
From Middle Dutch bedenken, from Old Dutch *bithenkan, *bithenkon, from Proto-West Germanic *biþankijan, from Proto-Germanic *biþankijaną. Equivalent to be- + denken.

A merger of two earlier verbs: * bedodden (“deceive”), from Middle Dutch dodden, from Proto-West Germanic *dudiʀōn or *dudirōn, frequentative form derived from Proto-Germanic *dud- (“to move, be moved”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰew- (“to move, advance, move away, pass away”). * bedotten (“confuse
From Middle Dutch bedriegen, from Old Dutch bidriegan, from Proto-West Germanic *bidreugan.
From Middle Dutch bēelde, from Old Dutch bilithe, bilithi, from Proto-West Germanic *biliþi (“picture, image”).

parole.significato: a kind of good female spirit
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle Dutch belewitte (“elf, good spirit”), from Old Dutch *biliwitti, from Proto-West Germanic *biliwiti (“elf, kobold”). Compare German Bilwis (“a kind of demon”) and Old English bilewit (“innocent, calm”).

parole.significato: leg, limb of a person, horse (other animals would have poten) and certain objects (again many have poten)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch bêen, from Old Dutch bēn, from Proto-West Germanic *bain, from Proto-Germanic *bainą.

parole.significato: a bear, any member of the family Ursidae
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch bēre, from Old Dutch *bero, from Proto-West Germanic *berō, from Proto-Germanic *berô.
From Middle Dutch bêer, from Old Dutch *bēr, from Proto-West Germanic *bair.

parole.significato: liquid, notably human manure (excrement gathered in a pit to fertilize)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch bere, from Old Dutch [Term?], from a derivative of Proto-West Germanic *bermō (“yeast”), related to Old English beorma, Albanian burmë.

From Middle Dutch begin, from Old Dutch *bigin, from Proto-West Germanic [Term?], from the verb *biginnan (“to begin”) (whence beginnen). Cognate with Old High German bigin and Old Frisian biginn. Compare with different prefix Old Dutch anagen, anagenni (“beginning”).
From Middle Dutch beginnen, from Old Dutch biginnan, from Proto-West Germanic *biginnan, from Proto-Germanic *biginnaną. Compare English begin.

parole.significato: to understand (concepts, ideas), to comprehend, to grasp
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch begripen, from Old Dutch bigrīpan, from Proto-West Germanic *bigrīpan. Equivalent to be- + grijpen.
From Middle Dutch behouden, from Old Dutch *bihaldan, from Proto-West Germanic *bihaldan (“to keep”). Equivalent to be- + houden.

parole.significato: a chisel, tool consisting of a slim oblong block of metal
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch beitel, betel, from Old Dutch *bētil, from Proto-West Germanic *baitil, from Proto-Germanic *baitilaz, equivalent to *beiten (the causative of bijten) + -el.
From Middle Dutch bejēgenen, prefixed variant of jēgenen, from Old Dutch *jegenen, *gegenen, from Proto-West Germanic *gaginijan, from Proto-Germanic *gaginjaną. Cognate with German begegnen.
From Middle Dutch bekennen, from Old Dutch bikennen, from Proto-West Germanic *bikannijan. Equivalent to be- + kennen. Cognates include German bekennen, and English and Scots beken.
From Middle Dutch becoren, from Old Dutch *bikoron, from Proto-West Germanic *bikoʀōn, from *bi- + *koʀōn.
From Middle Dutch belgen, from Old Dutch belgan, from Proto-West Germanic *belgan, from Proto-Germanic *belganą.
From Middle Dutch bellen, from Old Dutch *bellan, from Proto-West Germanic *bellan, from Proto-Germanic *bellaną. Cognate with English bellow, German bellen and Russian блеять (blejatʹ, “to bleat”).
From Middle Dutch belûken, from Old Dutch bilūkan, from Proto-West Germanic *bilūkan (“to enclose, lock in”), equivalent to be- + luiken (“to close, to shut”).

parole.significato: to notice; to take notice of
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch bemerken, from Old Dutch *bimerken, from Proto-West Germanic *bimarkijan. Equivalent to be- + merken. Cognate with German bemerken, also related to Middle Dutch and Middle High German bemarken, and English bemark.
From Middle Dutch bemeten, from Old Dutch *bemetan, from Proto-West Germanic *bimetan. Equivalent to be- + meten. Cognate with German bemessen and obsolete English bemete.

parole.significato: a young rascal, a naughty to mischievous kid, usually a tomboy
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch bengel, from Old Dutch *bengil, from Proto-West Germanic *bangil, from Proto-Germanic *bangilaz (“club, stick”). Similar sense development is found in German Bengel (“rascal”). Related to English bang.
From Middle Dutch berch, from Old Dutch berg, from Proto-West Germanic *berg, from Proto-Germanic *bergaz, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerǵʰ-.
From Middle Dutch bergen, from Old Dutch bergan, from Proto-West Germanic *bergan, from Proto-Germanic *berganą.
From Middle Dutch berispen, also berespen, from Old Dutch *birespen, from *respen, from Proto-West Germanic *rafsijan.

parole.significato: birch, tree of the genus Betula
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch berke, from Old Dutch *berca, from Proto-West Germanic *berku, from Proto-Germanic *berkō, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerHǵós.
From Middle Dutch bes, bese, from Old Dutch besi, from Proto-West Germanic *basi, from Proto-Germanic *basją. Compare English berry, Gothic 𐍅𐌴𐌹𐌽𐌰𐌱𐌰𐍃𐌹 (weinabasi, “grape”).

From Middle Dutch besniden, from Old Dutch bisnīthan, from Proto-West Germanic *bisnīþan. Equivalent to be- + snijden. Cognate with German beschneiden.
From Middle Dutch bestriken, from Old Dutch *bistrīcan, from Proto-West Germanic *bistrīkan. Equivalent to be- + strijken. Cognate with German bestreichen.
From Middle Dutch bet, bat, from Old Dutch *bat, *bet, from Proto-West Germanic [Term?], from Proto-Germanic *batiz.

parole.significato: to enclose, to fence, to hedge

parole.significato: an executioner, torturer, one who carries out executions and other judicial corporal punishments
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch buel, earlier buedel, from Old Dutch *budil, from Proto-West Germanic *budil, from Proto-Germanic *budilaz. Doublet of pedel.
From Middle Dutch bueren, from Old Dutch *burien, from Proto-West Germanic *burjan, from Proto-Germanic *burjaną.
From Middle Dutch bevallen, from Old Dutch *bifallan, from Proto-West Germanic *bifallan. Equivalent to be- + vallen. Cognate with German befallen (“to affect, seize, infest”).
From Middle Dutch bevēlen, from Old Dutch bifelan, from Proto-West Germanic *bifelhan.

parole.significato: to shake, to shiver, to tremble

From Middle Dutch bēver, from Old Dutch *bevar, from Proto-West Germanic *bebru, from Proto-Germanic *bebruz, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰébʰrus.
From Middle Dutch bewaren, from Old Dutch biwaron, from Proto-West Germanic *biwarōn, equivalent to be- + waren. Cognate with English beware.

parole.significato: broom (utensil consisting of fibers and a long handle, used for sweeping)

From Middle Dutch besorgen, from Old Dutch *bisorgon, from Proto-West Germanic *bisorgōn. Equivalent to be- + zorgen.
From Middle Dutch beswāren, from Old Dutch biswāren, from Proto-West Germanic *biswārijan. Cognate with German beschweren.
From Middle Dutch beswiken (“to leave, travel, faint”), from Old Dutch biswīcan (“to deceive, seduce”), from Proto-West Germanic *biswīkwan. Equivalent to be- + zwijken.
From Middle Dutch bidden, from Old Dutch bidden, from Proto-West Germanic *biddjan, from Proto-Germanic *bidjaną (“to ask”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰédʰyeti.
From Middle Dutch bieden, from Old Dutch biedan, from Proto-West Germanic *beudan (“to offer”), from Proto-Germanic *beudaną (“to offer”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewdʰ- (“be awake, aware”).

parole.significato: beer (alcoholic drink brewed from grains or other starch material)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch bier, from Old Dutch bier, from Proto-West Germanic *beuʀ, from Proto-Germanic *beuzą (“beer”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰews- (“dross”).

From Middle Dutch bitter, from Old Dutch bitter, from Proto-West Germanic *bitr.

From Middle Dutch blanc, from Old Dutch *blanc, from Proto-West Germanic *blank, from Proto-Germanic *blankaz.

parole.significato: to bleat, produce the typical baa sound of sheep

From Middle Dutch blau, blauwe, from Old Dutch *blāo, from Proto-West Germanic *blāu, from Proto-Germanic *blēwaz. Doublet of bleu.
From Middle Dutch blâsen, from Old Dutch *blāsan, from Proto-West Germanic *blāsan, from Proto-Germanic *blēsaną.
From Middle Dutch blêec, from Old Dutch *blēk, from Proto-West Germanic *blaik, from Proto-Germanic *blaikaz.

parole.significato: blaze (light-coloured spot on a horse's face)

From Middle Dutch bli (“lead (metal)”), from Old Dutch *blī, from Proto-West Germanic *blīwī, from Proto-Germanic *blīwiją.

From Middle Dutch bliden, from a merger of Old Dutch blīthen and blīthon, from Proto-West Germanic *blīþijan and *blīþēn, respectively.
From Middle Dutch bliken, from Old Dutch *blīcan, from Proto-West Germanic *blīkan, from Proto-Germanic *blīkaną (“to shine, gleam”), *blīkijaną.

From Middle Dutch bocht, becht, bacht (“garbage, dung, shit”), possibly from Proto-West Germanic *buggjan (“to buy”), though this is at odds with the last two forms.

From Middle Dutch boedel, Old Dutch *buothal, from Proto-West Germanic *bōþl, from Proto-Germanic *bōþlą. Cognate with English bottle, Icelandic ból, Swedish bol. More at build.

From Middle Dutch boc, from Old Dutch buc, from Proto-West Germanic *bukk, from Proto-Germanic *bukkaz.

From Middle Dutch bodescap, from Old Dutch *bodaskap, from Proto-West Germanic *bodaskapi. Equivalent to bode + -schap.
From Middle Dutch bōge, from Old Dutch bogo, from Proto-West Germanic *bogō, from Proto-Germanic *bugô.

From Middle Dutch broeder, from Old Dutch bruother, from Proto-West Germanic *brōþer, from Proto-Germanic *brōþēr, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰréh₂tēr.

From Middle Dutch bruun, from Old Dutch *brūn, from Proto-West Germanic *brūn, from Proto-Germanic *brūnaz.

From Middle Dutch bugen, from Old Dutch *būgan, from Proto-West Germanic *beugan, from Proto-Germanic *būganą, a variant form of *beuganą.
From Middle Dutch buuc, from Old Dutch būc, from Proto-West Germanic *būk, from Proto-Germanic *būkaz.

From Middle Dutch buse, of uncertain origin, plausibly representing an umlauted byform *beusju of Proto-West Germanic *beusu (“rush, bentgrass”) which gives Dutch bies. For the "television" sense, compare English tube.

From Middle Dutch buten, from Old Dutch *būtan, from Proto-West Germanic *biūtan (“outside of, around, without, except”), equivalent to be- + uit + -en. Cognate to English but, Luxembourgish baussen, West Frisian bûten, Saterland Frisian buute (“without”), Dutch Low Saxon buten.

parole.significato: bump (on an otherwise flat or even surface)

From Middle Dutch dierne, from Old Dutch thiorna, from Proto-West Germanic *þewernā.

From Middle Dutch degen, deghen, from Old Dutch *thegen, from Proto-West Germanic *þegn, from Proto-Germanic *þegnaz, from Proto-Indo-European *tek-. Cognate with German Degen, English thane, Icelandic þegn, Ancient Greek τέκνον (téknon).
From Middle Dutch dec, from decken, from Old Dutch thecken, from Proto-West Germanic *þakkjan, from Proto-Germanic *þakjaną. Equivalent to a deverbal from dekken.

From Middle Dutch dēken, from Old Dutch and Proto-West Germanic *dekan, from Latin decānus (“dean, chief of ten”). Compare Old High German tehhan(t) (Modern German Dechant). Doublet of decaan, a later borrowing.

From Middle Dutch decken, from Old Dutch thecken, from Proto-West Germanic *þakkjan, from Proto-Germanic *þakjaną. Equivalent to dak (“roof”) + -en (“denominative”) and shows the effect of historical umlaut.

From Middle Dutch dêelre, from Old Dutch [Term?], from Proto-West Germanic [Term?]; compare Old English dælere (English dealer), Old High German teilāri (German Teiler). By surface analysis, delen + -er. Doublet of dealer.
From Middle Dutch delven, from Old Dutch *delvan, from Proto-West Germanic *delban, from Proto-Germanic *delbaną.
From Middle Dutch dan, danne, denne (“pine tree”), from Old Dutch *danna, from Proto-West Germanic *dannā (“pine tree”). Related to German Tanne.
From Middle Dutch denken, from Old Dutch thenken, from Proto-West Germanic *þankijan, from Proto-Germanic *þankijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *teng-.
From Middle Dutch dēren, from Old Dutch deren, from Proto-West Germanic *darjan.
From Middle Dutch darven, derven, from Old Dutch tharvon, from Proto-West Germanic *þarbēn, from Proto-Germanic *þarbāną. Unrelated to bederven and verderven.

From Middle Dutch dêsem, from Old Dutch *thēsimo, from Proto-West Germanic *þaisimō, from Proto-Indo-European *teh₂-. Cognate with Old Saxon *thēsimo, Middle Low German dêsem, Old English þǣsma, Old High German deismo, Middle High German deisme, German Deisam.

parole.significato: to be good, well-behaved, moral, etc.
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch dōgen, from Old Dutch dugan, from Proto-West Germanic *dugan, from Proto-Germanic *duganą.
From Middle Dutch duene, from Old Dutch *duni, from Proto-West Germanic *duni, from Proto-Germanic *duniz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰwen-.
From Middle Dutch dōre, duere, from Old Dutch duri, from Proto-West Germanic *dur, from Proto-Germanic *durz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰwer- (“doorway, door, gate”).
From Middle Dutch dichte, from Old Dutch *thīhti, from Proto-West Germanic *þį̄ht(ī), from Proto-Germanic *þinhtaz. Cognate with English tight and German dicht (“dense”).
From Middle Dutch dief, from Old Dutch *thiof, from Proto-West Germanic *þeub, from Proto-Germanic *þeubaz.

From Middle Dutch diep, from Old Dutch diep, from Proto-West Germanic *deup, from Proto-Germanic *deupaz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewb-. Compare Low German diep, deep, West Frisian djip, English deep, German tief, Danish dyb, Norwegian dyp.

parole.significato: animal (any member of the kingdom Animalia)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch dier, from Old Dutch dier, from Proto-West Germanic *deuʀ, from Proto-Germanic *deuzą, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewsóm.
Revival by Flemish nationalists of Middle Dutch diet (“people, folk”), from Proto-West Germanic *þeudu, from Proto-Germanic *þeudō, from Proto-Indo-European *tewtéh₂. Compare Diets (“Dutch, German”).

From Middle Dutch dietsch, from Old Dutch *thiudisc, from Proto-West Germanic *þiudisk, from Proto-Germanic *þiudiskaz, from *þeudō (“people, nation”), from Proto-Indo-European *tewtéh₂ (“people”). Doublet of Duits.

From Middle Dutch die, from Old Dutch *thio, from Proto-West Germanic *þeuh, from Proto-Germanic *þeuhą. Compare West Frisian tsjea, English thigh, Icelandic þjó. The expected modern form would be *die. The diphthongised form may have originated in the plural, where Middle Dutch dien could easily be

From Middle Dutch dijc, from Old Dutch dīc, from Proto-West Germanic *dīk, from Proto-Germanic *dīkaz (compare German Teich and Deich, West Frisian dyk, English ditch, Icelandic díki), from Proto-Indo-European *dheigʷ.
From Middle Dutch dicke, from Old Dutch *thicki, from Proto-West Germanic *þikkwī, from Proto-Germanic *þekuz, from Proto-Indo-European *tégus.
From Middle Dutch dickede, from Old Dutch [Term?], from Proto-West Germanic *þikkwīþu; compare Old High German dikkida. By surface analysis, dik + -te.
From Middle Dutch dille, from Old Dutch *dilli, from Proto-West Germanic *dili.
From Middle Dutch dinc, from Old Dutch thinc, from Proto-West Germanic *þing, from Proto-Germanic *þingą.

From Middle Dutch dingen (“to convene, to plead”), from Old Dutch *thingon, from Proto-West Germanic *þingōn, from Proto-Germanic *þingōną. The verb was originally weak, but became strong by analogy with other verbs.
From Middle Dutch dissel, diessel, dessel, from Old Dutch *thehsala, from Proto-West Germanic *þehsulā, from Proto-Germanic *þehsulǭ (“axe, adze”).

parole.significato: A thistle (plant of the tribe Cynareae syn. Cardueae).
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch distel, from Old Dutch *thistil, from Proto-West Germanic *þistil, from Proto-Germanic *þistilaz.

parole.significato: yet, but, still, on the contrary, no, yes
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch doch, from Old Dutch thoh, from Proto-West Germanic *þauh, from Proto-Germanic *þauh.
From Middle Dutch dochter, from Old Dutch dohter, from Proto-West Germanic *dohter, from Proto-Germanic *duhtēr, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰugh₂tḗr.
From Middle Dutch dôden, from Old Dutch *dōden, from Proto-West Germanic *daudijan, from Proto-Germanic *daudijaną. By surface analysis, dood (“dead”) + -en. Compare German töten and English deaden.
From Middle Dutch doec, from Old Dutch *duok, from Proto-West Germanic *dōk, from Proto-Germanic *dōkaz.

parole.significato: to wrap in sheets or blankets
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch doeken, from Old Dutch *dōken, from Proto-West Germanic *dōkijan, equivalent to doek + -en.

From Middle Dutch doem, from Old Dutch *duom, from Proto-West Germanic *dōm, from Proto-Germanic *dōmaz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰóh₁mos. Compare West Frisian doem, English doom, Danish and Swedish dom.
From Middle Dutch doemen, from Old Dutch duomen, from Proto-West Germanic *dōmijan, from Proto-Germanic *dōmijaną.
From Middle Dutch doen, from Old Dutch duon, from Proto-West Germanic *dōn, from Proto-Germanic *dōną, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰéh₁t.

Vowel shortening of doof (“deaf”), from Middle Dutch dôof, from Old Dutch *dōf, from Proto-West Germanic *daub, from Proto-Germanic *daubaz (“stunned, deaf”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewbʰ- (“to whisk, be obscured”). Compare Swedish dov (“matt, muted”), English dowf.
From Middle Dutch dogen, from Old Dutch *dōgen, from Proto-West Germanic *daugijan, from Proto-Germanic *daugijaną.
From Middle Dutch dul, from Old Dutch *dol, from Proto-West Germanic *dol, from Proto-Germanic *dulaz.
From Middle Dutch dolle, from Old Dutch *tholl, from Proto-West Germanic *þoll, from Proto-Germanic *þullaz.
From Middle Dutch dom, domp, from Old Dutch dump, from Proto-West Germanic *dumb, from Proto-Germanic *dumbaz.
From Middle Dutch donre, from Old Dutch *thunar, from Proto-West Germanic *þunr. Compare German Donner, West Frisian tonger, English thunder.

From Middle Dutch donresdach, donredach, from Old Dutch *thonaresdag, from Proto-West Germanic *Þunras dag (“day of the thunder god”). Equivalent to Donar or donder + dag. Donar (North Germanic: Thor) was the Germanic god of thunder.

parole.significato: a sandy hill, typically of glacial origin, protruding above a silty area
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch *donke, Middle Dutch *donge, from Old Dutch *dunga, from Proto-West Germanic *dungu (“hill, dunghill”).
From Middle Dutch dôot, doet, from Old Dutch dōt, from Proto-West Germanic *daud, from Proto-Germanic *daudaz. Compare West Frisian dead, German tot, English dead, Danish død.
From Middle Dutch dôot, doet, from Old Dutch dōth, dōt, from Proto-West Germanic *dauþu, from Proto-Germanic *dauþuz. Compare West Frisian dead, German Tod, English death, Danish død.
From Middle Dutch dôof, from Old Dutch dōf, from Proto-West Germanic *daub, from Proto-Germanic *daubaz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewbʰ- (“to whisk, be obscured”).
From Middle Dutch dôyen, from Old Dutch *thōien, from Proto-West Germanic *þauwjan, from Proto-Germanic *þawjaną.
From Middle Dutch doder, from Old Dutch *dodro, from Proto-West Germanic *dodrō.
From Middle Dutch dôre, from Old Dutch *dōro, Proto-West Germanic *dauʀō.

parole.significato: thorn, sharp extremity of a plant
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch dorn, dōorn, from Old Dutch thorn, from Proto-West Germanic *þornu, from Proto-Germanic *þurnuz.

parole.significato: a shell (of an egg or a fruit for example)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch doppe, dup, from Old Dutch *dopp, *dupp, from Proto-West Germanic *dopp, *dupp, from Proto-Germanic *duppaz (“hollow, well, bowl”). Cognate with German Topf (“pot”).
From Middle Dutch dôpen, from Old Dutch dōpen, from Proto-West Germanic *daupijan, from Proto-Germanic *daupijaną.

parole.significato: dry, wilted (having a relatively low or no liquid content)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch dorre, from Old Dutch *thurri, from Proto-West Germanic *þurʀī, from Proto-Germanic *þursuz, from Proto-Indo-European *ters-.
Inherited from Middle Dutch dorp, from Old Dutch thorp, from Proto-West Germanic *þorp, from Proto-Germanic *þurpą, from Proto-Indo-European *treb- or *trab-. Doublet of terp.
From Middle Dutch dorst, from Old Dutch thurst, from Proto-West Germanic *þurstu, from Proto-Germanic *þurstuz, from Proto-Indo-European *ters-.
From Middle Dutch dôven, from Old Dutch *dōven, from Proto-West Germanic *daubijan, from Proto-Germanic *daubijaną. Equivalent to doof (“deaf”) + -en.
From Middle Dutch dôven, from Old Dutch *dōvon, from Proto-West Germanic *dobēn, from the same ultimate source as *daub (“deaf, stunned”).

From Middle Dutch drade, from Old Dutch [Term?], from Proto-West Germanic [Term?]. cognates include Old High German drāto (“quickly, suddenly, violently, intensely”) and its adjectival counterpart drāti; ultimately all derive from the same root to which draaien (“to turn”) (English throw, German dre
From Middle Dutch drâyen, from Old Dutch thrāien, from Proto-West Germanic *þrāan, from Proto-Germanic *þrēaną, from Proto-Indo-European *terh₁-.
From Middle Dutch andrake, from Old Dutch *anadrako, from Proto-West Germanic *anadrekō (“duck leader”).

parole.significato: wide rural lane with trees planted on both sides
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch dreve, from Old Dutch *drēva, from Proto-West Germanic *draibu, from Proto-Germanic *draibō, from *drībaną (“to drive”).

From Middle Dutch drec, from Old Dutch *threkk, from Proto-West Germanic *þraki, from Proto-Germanic *þrakjaz. Compare English dreck, German Dreck (“dirt; filth”), Old Norse þrekkr, Swedish träck. Wider Indo-European cognates include Latin stercus (“dung, manure”). Attested since 1285 in the sense "
From Middle Dutch drenken, from Old Dutch drenken, from Proto-West Germanic *drankijan, from Proto-Germanic *drankijaną, causative of *drinkaną (modern drinken).
From Middle Dutch drie, from Old Dutch thrie, from Proto-West Germanic *þrīʀ, from Proto-Germanic *þrīz, from Proto-Indo-European *tréyes.
From Middle Dutch drift, also dricht, from Old Dutch *drift, from Proto-West Germanic *drifti, from Proto-Germanic *driftiz. Equivalent to drijven (“to drive”) + -t (“verbal noun”).
From Middle Dutch driten, from Old Dutch *drītan, from Proto-West Germanic *drītan, from Proto-Germanic *drītaną.
From Middle Dutch driven, from Old Dutch drīvan, from Proto-West Germanic *drīban, from Proto-Germanic *drībaną, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰreybʰ- (“to drive, push”).

parole.significato: to press, push (into a tight space, a crowd etc)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch dringen, from Old Dutch *thringan, from Proto-West Germanic *þringwan, from Proto-Germanic *þrinhwaną.
From Middle Dutch drinken, from Old Dutch drincan, from Proto-West Germanic *drinkan, from Proto-Germanic *drinkaną.
From Middle Dutch droeve, droue, from Old Dutch *drōvi, *druovi, from Proto-West Germanic *drōbī, from Proto-Germanic *drōbuz (“turbid”). Compare English droff and German trüb.

parole.significato: sediment in a liquid, particularly in wine, dregs
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch droesene, from Old Dutch *druosana, from Proto-West Germanic *drōsnu, from Proto-Germanic *drōhsnō (“sediment”).
From Middle Dutch droeven, from Old Dutch druoven, from Proto-West Germanic *drōbijan, from Proto-Germanic *drōbijaną. Equivalent to droef (“sad”) + -en.
From Middle Dutch drômen, from Old Dutch *drōmen, from Proto-West Germanic *draumijan, from Proto-Germanic *draumijaną.
From Middle Dutch drôge, from Old Dutch *drōgi, from Proto-West Germanic *draugī, from Proto-Germanic *draugiz.
From Middle Dutch drôom, from Old Dutch drōm, from Proto-West Germanic *draum, from Proto-Germanic *draumaz.
From Middle Dutch druve, from Old Dutch thrūva, from Proto-West Germanic *þrūbō (“grape”).
From Middle Dutch drupen, from Old Dutch driepan, *drūpan, from Proto-West Germanic *dreupan, from Proto-Germanic *dreupaną.

From Middle Dutch druyschen, from Old Dutch *driosan, from Proto-West Germanic *dreusan, from Proto-Germanic *dreusaną. The form with -s(ch)- instead of expected *druizen is due to confluence with the verb at hand in ruisen (“to rustle”).
From Middle Dutch drucken, from Old Dutch *thrucken, from Proto-West Germanic *þrukkijan, from Proto-Germanic *þrukkijaną. Cognate with German drücken (“press”) and drucken (“print”).
From Middle Dutch droppen, from Old Dutch droppon, from Proto-West Germanic *droppōn, from Proto-Germanic *druppōną.
From Middle Dutch du, from Old Dutch thū, from Proto-West Germanic *þū, from Proto-Germanic *þū, from Proto-Indo-European *túh₂.

From Middle Dutch duchtich, from Old Dutch *duhtig, from Proto-West Germanic *duhtīg. Equivalent to modern deugen (“to be virtuous”) + -ig. Originally an adjective, but chiefly used as an adverb in modern Dutch. Cognate with German tüchtig (“efficient, capable, hard, competent, big”), English dought

parole.significato: to point to, refer to, suggest
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch dieden, duden, from Old Dutch *thiuden, from Proto-West Germanic *þiudijan, from Proto-Germanic *þiudijaną.

parole.significato: a pigeon, dove, bird of the family Columbidae
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch duve, from Old Dutch dūva, from Proto-West Germanic *dūbā, from Proto-Germanic *dūbǭ.
From Middle Dutch duken, from Old Dutch *dūcan, from Proto-West Germanic *dūkan, from Proto-Germanic *dūkaną. Cognate with English (to) duck.

From Middle Dutch dume, from Old Dutch *thūmo, from Proto-West Germanic *þūmō, from Proto-Germanic *þūmô. Compare West Frisian tomme, Low German Dumen, German Daumen, English thumb, Danish tomme, Swedish tumme.

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; perhaps; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch dûne, from Old Dutch dūn, dūno, from Proto-West Germanic *dūnā, of uncertain origin, perhaps from Proto-Celtic *dūnom (“stronghold, rampart”).
From Middle Dutch duuster, from Old Dutch *thiustri, from Proto-West Germanic *þiustrī.

From Middle Dutch duutsch, a Northern variant of dietsch, both from Old Dutch *thiudisc, from Proto-West Germanic *þiudisk, from Proto-Germanic *þiudiskaz, from *þeudō (“people, nation”), from Proto-Indo-European *tewtéh₂ (“people”). Doublet of Diets.
From Middle Dutch duvel, from Old Dutch diuval, from Proto-West Germanic *diubul, from Latin diabolus, from Ancient Greek διάβολος (diábolos).
From Middle Dutch dūsent, from Old Dutch thūsunt, from Proto-West Germanic *þūsundi, from Proto-Germanic *þūsundī.
From Middle Dutch dunne, from Old Dutch *thunni, from Proto-West Germanic *þunnī, from Proto-Germanic *þunnuz. Cognate with English thin (Compare West-Flemish thinne).
From Middle Dutch dunken, from Old Dutch thunken, from Proto-West Germanic *þunkijan, from Proto-Germanic *þunkijaną.

parole.significato: to dare (do), to not be afraid (to do)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch durven. This verb originated from two Middle Dutch verbs: * durven (“to need”), from Old Dutch thurvan, from Proto-West Germanic *þurban, from Proto-Germanic *þurbaną. * durren (“to dare”), from Old Dutch durran, from Proto-West Germanic *durʀan, from Proto-Germanic *durzaną.
From Middle Dutch dos, dus, from Old Dutch thus, from Proto-West Germanic *þus.

parole.significato: dearth, scarcity; a period in which basic necessities such as food are scarce and therefore overly expensive
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch duurte, dierte, from Old Dutch *diuritha, from Proto-West Germanic *diuriþu, from Proto-Germanic *diuriþō. Equivalent to duur + -te.
From Middle Dutch duwen, douwen, from Old Dutch thuwen, from Proto-West Germanic *þų̄hijan, from Proto-Germanic *þunhijaną.
From Middle Dutch dwaes, from Old Dutch *dwās, from Proto-West Germanic *dwās. Compare German quasseln.
From Middle Dutch dwalen, from Old Dutch *dwalon, from Proto-West Germanic *dwalōn, from Proto-Germanic *dwalōną. Cognate with English dwale.
From Middle Dutch dwanc, from Old Dutch *thwang, from Proto-West Germanic *þwangi, from Proto-Germanic *þwangiz.

parole.significato: in a crosswise direction, transverse, at right angles
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch dwers, from Old Dutch *thweres, genitive form of Proto-West Germanic *þwerh, from Proto-Germanic *þwerhaz (“cross, adverse”). Cognates include English thwart and queer, Swedish tvär, Danish tvært, German quer, Gothic 𐌸𐍅𐌰𐌹𐍂𐌷𐍃 (þwairhs).
From Middle Dutch dwâle, *dweile, from Old Dutch *thwāla, *thweila, from Proto-West Germanic *þwahilu. Doublet of dwaal.

parole.significato: dwarf (small human; small specimen, breed or species of animal)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch dwerch, from Old Dutch *dwerg, from Proto-West Germanic *dwerg, from Proto-Germanic *dwergaz. Compare West Frisian dwerch, German Zwerg, English dwarf, Danish dværg.

parole.significato: to dwindle, to decline in number or size
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch dwinen, from Old Dutch *dwīnan, from Proto-West Germanic *dwīnan, from Proto-Germanic *dwīnaną.
From Middle Dutch dwingen, from Old Dutch *thwingan, from Proto-West Germanic *þwingan, from Proto-Germanic *þwinhaną, *þwinganą.
From Middle Dutch ebbe, from Old Dutch *ebba, from Proto-West Germanic *abbjā, from Proto-Germanic *abjô, *abjǭ.

parole.significato: to ebb, to recede (especially of tides)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch ebben, from Old Dutch *ebbon, from Proto-West Germanic *abbjōn.

parole.significato: leech, in particular one species used in bloodletting, the European medical leech, Hirudo officinalis
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch echel, ēgele, from Old Dutch *egela, from Proto-West Germanic *egulā (“leech”). Related with egel (“hedgehog”). Cognate with German Egel (“leech”).
From Middle Dutch echt, from Old Dutch *ēhaft, from Proto-West Germanic *aiwahaft.

parole.significato: to recognize a child as one's own
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch echten, from Old Dutch *ēhaften, from Proto-West Germanic *aiwahaftijan. By surface analysis, echt + -en.
From Middle Dutch ēdel, from Old Dutch edel, edele, from Proto-West Germanic *aþuli, from Proto-Germanic *aþulijaz.

parole.significato: vinegar, especially dilute vinegar used as a drink
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch edic, from Old Dutch etig, from Proto-West Germanic *atek, metathesized variant of *aket, from Latin acētum. Cognate with Old Saxon edik, Middle Low German etik, West Frisian jittik, Old High German eȥȥih, German Essig, Old Norse edik. More distantly related to Old Saxon ekid, Old
From Middle Dutch êe, from Old Dutch ēwa, from Proto-West Germanic *aiw.
From Middle Dutch eet, from Old Dutch *ēth, from Proto-West Germanic *aiþ, from Proto-Germanic *aiþaz, from Proto-Indo-European *oyt-. Compare West Frisian eed, German Eid, English oath, Danish ed.
From Middle Dutch ecorn, eencoren, from Old Dutch *ēkorno, from Proto-West Germanic *aikwernō, from Proto-Germanic *aikwernô.

parole.significato: a, an; indefinite article, placed before a singular noun, indicating a general case of a person or thing
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch êen, from Old Dutch ēn, ein, from Proto-West Germanic *ain, from Proto-Germanic *ainaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁óynos.

parole.significato: A duck, waterfowl of the family Anatidae excluding the subfamily Anserinae; in non-scientific usage the term may be res…
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch ent, eent, from Old Dutch ened, from Proto-West Germanic *anad, from Proto-Germanic *anadz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂énh₂ts. Cognate with German Ente. The sense “Citroën 2CV” is shared with German Ente.
From Middle Dutch êre, from Old Dutch ēra, from Proto-West Germanic *aiʀu, from Proto-Germanic *aizō.
From Middle Dutch êer, from Old Dutch ēr, from Proto-West Germanic *airi, from Proto-Germanic *airiz.
From Middle Dutch êer, from Old Dutch *ēr, from Proto-West Germanic *aiʀ, from Proto-Germanic *aiz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éyos.
From Middle Dutch êerlijc, from Old Dutch ērlīk, from Proto-West Germanic *aiʀulīk. Equivalent to eer (“honour”) + -lijk.

parole.significato: first, at first, before something else
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch êerst, from Old Dutch *ērist, from Proto-West Germanic *airist(ō).
From Middle Dutch eerste, from Old Dutch *ēristo, from Proto-West Germanic *airist.
From Middle Dutch êwe, from Old Dutch ēwa, from Proto-West Germanic *aiw, from Proto-Germanic *aiwaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eyu- (“vital force”).
From Middle Dutch effen, from Old Dutch *evan, from Proto-West Germanic *ebn, from Proto-Germanic *ebnaz. Doublet of even.

From Middle Dutch eghel, from Old Dutch *igil, from Proto-West Germanic *igil, from Proto-Germanic *igilaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eǵʰis (“hedgehog”). Compare German Igel. Echel (“leech”) is commonly thought to be related to this term.
From Middle Dutch egge, from Old Dutch *egga, from Proto-West Germanic *aggju. Cognate to English edge.
From Middle Dutch ei, from Old Dutch *ei, from Proto-West Germanic *aij, from Proto-Germanic *ajją, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ōwyóm.
From Middle Dutch eigen, from Old Dutch *eigan, past participle of *eigan (“to own”), from Proto-West Germanic *aigan, from Proto-Germanic *aiganą.

parole.significato: oak tree (tree of the genus Quercus)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch eike, êke, from Old Dutch *eik, *ēk, from Proto-West Germanic *aik, from Proto-Germanic *aiks, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eyǵ- (“oak”). The form in ei- is regular in south-eastern dialects, but may also have developed elsewhere after the adjective *eikīn (“oaken”, modern eiken), w
From Middle Dutch ecle, ekele, from Old Dutch *ēkila, *eikila, from Proto-West Germanic *aikilā. Equivalent to eik (“oak”) + -el. For the derogatory sense, compare English dickhead.

From earlier einde with apocope of the final -e, from Middle Dutch ende, einde, from Old Dutch endi, einde, from Proto-West Germanic *andī, from Proto-Germanic *andijaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂entíos.
From Middle Dutch eischen, from Old Dutch *eiskon, from Proto-West Germanic *aiskōn.
From Middle Dutch egestre, exter, from Old Dutch *agastra, from Proto-West Germanic *agastrijā.

parole.significato: a unit of length corresponding to about 69 cm: ell, cubit
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch elne, elle, from Old Dutch *elina, from Proto-West Germanic *alinu. Cognate with English ell, German Low German Ell, German Elle.

From Middle Dutch elft, possibly from an Old Dutch *alvit, from Proto-West Germanic *albut (“swan”). The semantic link to swans would be the fish's white color; the Germanic term ultimately derives from Proto-Indo-European *albʰós (“white”). This Indo-European word is generally accepted to be the mo
From Middle Dutch elc. Compare English each, West Frisian elk, from Proto-West Germanic *aiwgahwalīk (“each, every”), analyzed as *aiw (“ever, always”) + *ga- + *hwilīkaz.
From Middle Dutch ellende (“abroad, exile”), from Old Dutch elilendi (“exile”), from Proto-West Germanic *alljas (“other”) + *land (“land”), compare German Elend (“misery”).
From Middle Dutch elpenbeen, from Old Dutch elpantbēn, from Proto-West Germanic *elpandabain (“ivory”).
From Middle Dutch elpenbenen, from Old Dutch elpantbēnin, from Proto-West Germanic *elpandabainīn, equivalent to elpenbeen + -en.
From Middle Dutch elpendier, from Old Dutch *elpandier, from Proto-West Germanic *elpandadeuʀ.

parole.significato: larva of a crane fly, juvenile member of the Tipulidae
parole.testo: From Proto-West Germanic *āmā (“larva”).
From Middle Dutch ēmer, emmer, emere, from Old Dutch *embar, from Proto-West Germanic *ambrī. Possible doublet of amfoor.
From Middle Dutch ende, from Old Dutch ande, inde, from Proto-Germanic *andi, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂entí.
From Middle Dutch enge, from Old Dutch *engi, from Proto-West Germanic *angī, from Proto-Germanic *anguz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂énǵʰus. Cognate with German eng, from Old High German engi.
From Middle Dutch ênich, from Old Dutch ēnig, from Proto-West Germanic *ainag, from Proto-Germanic *ainagaz. Equivalent to een (“one”) + -ig.

From Middle Dutch enkel, possibly from Old Dutch *ēnkal, from Proto-West Germanic *ainakul, from Proto-Germanic *ainakulaz (“only, sole”), related to Proto-Germanic *ainahô (“only, sole”). Cognate with West Frisian inkel (“single”), Middle Low German enkel, enkelt (“simple, single”), German Low Germ

From Middle Dutch entegen, from Old Dutch [Term?], from Proto-West Germanic [Term?]. Compare Old English onġean (English again), Old High German ingegin (German entgegen), Old Saxon angegin. Equivalent to aan + tegen.
From Middle Dutch eppe (“celery or similar plant”), from Old Dutch *eppi, from Proto-West Germanic *api, from Latin apium.

parole.significato: yard (open area adjoining and belonging to a house)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch erve, from Old Dutch ervi, from Proto-West Germanic *arbī, from Proto-Germanic *arbiją.

From Middle Dutch [Term?], from Old Dutch ervidēl, from Proto-West Germanic [Term?]; compare Middle High German erbeteil (German Erbteil), Middle Low German ervedēl. By surface analysis, erven (“to inherit”) or erf (“inheritance”) + deel (“part”).
From Middle Dutch arch, erch, from Old Dutch arg, from Proto-West Germanic *arg, from Proto-Germanic *argaz.

From Middle Dutch erven, from Proto-West Germanic *arbijan, from Proto-Germanic *arbijaną, denominative from *arbiją, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃erbʰ- (“change allegiance or status or ownership”). Equivalent to erf + -en.
From Middle Dutch erwete, from Old Dutch *erwit, from Proto-West Germanic *arwīt, from Proto-Germanic *arwīts. Cognate with German Erbse.

From Middle Dutch essche, from Old Dutch *aska, from Proto-West Germanic *ask, from Proto-Germanic *askaz, *askiz. Compare West Frisian esk, English ash, German Esche, Danish ask, compare Welsh onnen, Latin ornus (“wild mountain ash”), Lithuanian úosis, Russian ясень (jasenʹ), Albanian ah (“beech”),

parole.significato: synonym of sjalot (“shallot (Allium cepa var. aggregatum)”)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch *aschlook, from Old Dutch *asklōk, Proto-West Germanic *askalauk (“shallot”).
From Middle Dutch espe, from Old Dutch *aspa, from Proto-West Germanic *aspu, from Proto-Germanic *aspō.
From Middle Dutch et-, at-, ad-, from Old Dutch *ed-, *id-, from Proto-West Germanic *id-, from Proto-Germanic *idi-. Cognate with English ed-.
From Middle Dutch ēten, from Old Dutch etan, from Proto-West Germanic *etan, from Proto-Germanic *etaną, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁édti.
From Middle Dutch etten, from Old Dutch *etten, from Proto-West Germanic *attjan, from Proto-Germanic *atjaną. Doublet of etsen.
From Middle Dutch etter, from Old Dutch *ēttar, from Proto-West Germanic *aitr.
From Middle Dutch etteren, from Old Dutch *eittaron, *eitaron, from Proto-West Germanic *aittrōn. Equivalent to etter + -en.
From Middle Dutch evel, ovel, oevel, from Old Dutch uvil, from Proto-West Germanic *ubil, from Proto-Germanic *ubilaz. Cognate with English evil, West Frisian evel, and German übel.
From Middle Dutch even, effen, from Old Dutch *evan, from Proto-West Germanic *ebn, from Proto-Germanic *ebnaz.
From Middle Dutch ēver, from Old Dutch *evur, from Proto-West Germanic *ebur. Cognate with Latin aper, Proto-Slavic *veprь (“wild boar”).

parole.significato: donkey, ass (Equus asinus or Equus asinus asinus)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch ēsel, from Old Dutch esil, from Proto-West Germanic *asil, from Late Latin asellus.
From Middle Dutch flassche, flessche, from Old Dutch *flaska, from Proto-West Germanic *flaskā, from Proto-Germanic *flaskǭ. Doublet of fiasco and flacon.

parole.significato: to go, to move from one place to another
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch gâen, from Old Dutch gān, from a fusion of Proto-West Germanic *gān and *gangan, from Proto-Germanic *gāną and *ganganą, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰeh₁-, *ǵʰengʰ-.
From Middle Dutch gaer (“ready”), from Old Dutch garo (“ready”), from Proto-West Germanic *garu, from Proto-Germanic *garwaz (“ready”). More at yare.

From Middle Dutch gaert, from Old Dutch *gart, from Proto-West Germanic *gard, from Proto-Germanic *gardaz, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰórdʰos or *gʰerdʰ-. Cognate with English yard (compare also garden), obsolete German Gart, German Garten, Danish gård. Also, cognate with Proto-Slavic *gard or *gor

From Middle Dutch gaerde, from Old Dutch gardo, from Proto-West Germanic *gardō, from Proto-Germanic *gardô, an n-stem form derived from Proto-Indo-European *gʰórdʰos, from *gʰerdʰ-. Related to gaard. Cognate to English garden and German Garten.
From Middle Dutch gerne, gaerne, from Old Dutch *gerno, from Proto-West Germanic *gernō, from Proto-Germanic *gernô (“willingly, gladly”), an adverbial form of *gernaz (“willing”).
From Middle Dutch gaden, from Old Dutch *gadon, from Proto-West Germanic *gadōn.
From Middle Dutch ganc, from Old Dutch gang, from Proto-West Germanic *gang, from Proto-Germanic *gangaz.

parole.significato: a goose, a waterfowl of the family Anatidae, especially of the subfamily Anserinae excepting the genera Cygnus and Cosc…
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch gans (alongside gōs, gās), from Proto-West Germanic *gans, from Proto-Germanic *gans.

From Middle Dutch gapen, from Old Dutch *gapon, from Proto-West Germanic *gapōn, from Proto-Germanic *gapōną, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰeh₁y- (“to gape, be wide open”), related to Ancient Greek χάσκω (kháskō), Russian зия́ть (zijátʹ), Sanskrit विजिहीते (vijihīte), and Proto-Germanic *gīnaną, *ganō
From Middle Dutch garen, from Old Dutch *garn, from Proto-West Germanic *garn.
Syncopic form of earlier gaderen, from Middle Dutch gāderen, from Old Dutch *gadaron, from Proto-West Germanic *gadurōn.
From Middle Dutch garve, from Old Dutch garva, from Proto-West Germanic *garbā (“sheaf”).

parole.significato: to bind grain in sheaves, to sheave
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch garve, from Old Dutch garva, from Proto-West Germanic *garbā (“sheaf”). See garf.
From Middle Dutch gast, from Old Dutch *gast, from Proto-West Germanic *gasti, from Proto-Germanic *gastiz.
From Middle Dutch gat, from Old Dutch *gat, from Proto-West Germanic *gat, from Proto-Germanic *gatą. Doublet of gate.
From Middle Dutch gave, from Old Dutch gāva, from Proto-West Germanic *gābā, from Proto-Germanic *gēbǭ, ablaut variant of *gebō.

parole.significato: Used for forming the past participle.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle Dutch ge-, ghe-, from Old Dutch gi-, ge-, from Proto-West Germanic *ga-, from Proto-Germanic *ga-, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱóm. Cognate with German Low German ge-, Dutch Low Saxon ge-, German ge-, Old English ġe- (obsolete English y-, i-, a-), Gothic 𐌲𐌰- (ga-).

parole.significato: to gesture, to point, to gesticulate
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch gebâren, from Proto-West Germanic *gabārijan or *gabārijōn. By surface analysis, ge- + baren.
From Middle Dutch gebet, from Old Dutch gebet, from Proto-West Germanic *gabed.

From Middle Dutch geburen, from Old Dutch geburien (“to happen, occur”), from Proto-West Germanic *gaburjan, from Proto-Germanic *gaburjaną. Equivalent to ge- + beuren. Cognate with West Frisian barre (“to happen”) and German gebühren (“to be due, owed”); further with Low German geböhren and Old Eng
From Middle Dutch gedenken, from Old Dutch *gethenken, from Proto-West Germanic *gaþankijan. Equivalent to ge- + denken.

parole.significato: to thrive, prosper (to grow or be successful)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch gediën, from Old Dutch githīan, from Proto-West Germanic *gaþį̄han, from Proto-Germanic *gaþinhaną. Cognates include German gedeihen, Gothic 𐌲𐌰𐌸𐌴𐌹𐌷𐌰𐌽 (gaþeihan).
From Middle Dutch geve, from Old Dutch geva, from Proto-West Germanic *gebu, from Proto-Germanic *gebō.
From Middle Dutch gelu, from Old Dutch *gelo, from Proto-West Germanic *gelu, from Proto-Germanic *gelwaz.
From Middle Dutch gene, from Old Dutch *gēn, from Proto-West Germanic *jain, from Proto-Germanic *jainaz. Compare German jener.
From Middle Dutch gêer, from Old Dutch *gēr, from Proto-West Germanic *gaiʀ, from Proto-Germanic *gaizaz.
From Middle Dutch geer, gere, from Old Dutch gero, from Proto-West Germanic *gerō, from Proto-Germanic *gerô, related to *gernaz (“willing, eager”). Also related to the verb geren (“to covet”).

From Middle Dutch gêest, from Old Dutch gēst, from Proto-West Germanic *gaist, from Proto-Germanic *gaistaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰeysd-, *ǵʰisd- (“anger, agitation”). Cognates Cognate with German Geist, West Frisian geast, English ghost, Swedish gast.
From Middle Dutch geeuwen, geuwen, ghewen, gewen, from Old Dutch *gewon, *giwon, from Proto-West Germanic *giwōn, from Proto-Germanic *giwōną.

parole.significato: the roof of the mouth, palate
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch gehemelte, from Old Dutch *gihimiliti, from Proto-West Germanic *gahimiliti, *himiliti. Cognate Middle High German gehimelze, archaic German Gehimmelze, Middle Low German hemelte, Middle Dutch hemelte. Equivalent to hemel + ge- -te.
From Middle Dutch gehoorsaem, from Old Dutch *gihōrsam, from Proto-West Germanic *gahauʀisam. Equivalent to gehoor + -zaam.

From Middle Dutch gheil, from Old Dutch *geil, from Proto-West Germanic *gail, from Proto-Germanic *gailaz, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰoylos (“frothing, tempestuous, wanton”). Cognate to English gole, German geil. The slang meaning of "cool" was likely borrowed from German geil.

parole.significato: goat, any member of the genus Capra
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch geit, from Old Dutch *geit, from Proto-West Germanic *gait, from Proto-Germanic *gaits, from a substrate language.
From Middle Dutch gelt, gheld, ghelt, from Old Dutch geld, from Proto-West Germanic *geld, from Proto-Germanic *geldą (“reward, gift, money”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰeldʰ- (“to pay”).

parole.significato: to apply, to be applicable, to be in effect
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch gelden, from Old Dutch *geldan, from Proto-West Germanic *geldan, from Proto-Germanic *geldaną, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰeldʰ- (“to pay”).
Inherited from Middle Dutch gelike, from Old Dutch *gilīko, from Proto-West Germanic *galīkō, from Proto-Germanic *galīkô.
From Middle Dutch gelike, gelijc, from Old Dutch *gilīki, from Proto-West Germanic *galīkī, from Proto-Germanic *galīkiją.
From Middle Dutch gelîkenisse, from Old Dutch gilīcnussi, from Proto-West Germanic *galīkanassī (“likeness”). Equivalent to gelijken + -nis.

From Middle Dutch gingebare, from Old Dutch *gingibero, from Proto-West Germanic *gingiberō, from Late Latin gingiber, from Latin zingiber, from Ancient Greek ζιγγίβερις (zingíberis), from Sauraseni Prakrit सिङ्गबेर (siṅgabera).
From Middle Dutch gemêen, from Old Dutch *gimēni, from Proto-West Germanic *gamainī, from Proto-Germanic *gamainiz.
From Middle Dutch gemeende, from Old Dutch *gimēnitha, from Proto-West Germanic *gamainī + *-iþu. Corresponds to gemeen (“common”) + -te.

From Middle Dutch gemelijc, ghemelijc, a derivative of Middle Dutch gāme (“joke, prank”), from Old Dutch *gamen, *gaman, from Proto-West Germanic *gaman, from Proto-Germanic *gamaną. Cognate with English game.

parole.significato: a measure of land roughly the size of an acre
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch ghemet, from Old Dutch [Term?], from Proto-West Germanic *gametan, equivalent to ge- + meten. Cognates include Old English ġemet, Old Saxon gimet, Old High German gimez.

From Middle Dutch genēren, prefixed form of nēren (which also yielded modern nering), from Old Dutch neren, from Proto-West Germanic *naʀjan, from Proto-Germanic *nazjaną; from Proto-Indo-European *nes-. From this root the verb genezen is also ultimately derived.

parole.significato: to enjoy oneself, to have a pleasant experience
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch genieten, from Old Dutch *giniotan, from Proto-West Germanic *ganeutan, from Proto-Germanic *ganeutaną. Equivalent to ge- + nieten.
From Middle Dutch genoot, from Old Dutch genōt, from Proto-West Germanic *ganaut, from Proto-Germanic *ganautaz.
From Middle Dutch gent, from Old Dutch *genit, variant of *ganut, from Proto-West Germanic *ganut, from Proto-Germanic *ganutaz.
From Middle Dutch geren, from Old Dutch geron, from Proto-West Germanic *gerēn, from Proto-Germanic *gerōną, related to *gernaz (“to eager, willing”). See also Dutch gaarne and German gern.

From Middle Dutch gerste, from Old Dutch *gersta, from Proto-West Germanic *gerstu, from Proto-Germanic *gerstō, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰersd-. Cognate with Limburgish gaes, gaers, West Flemish gerst, Zealandic gêêste, gaste, Old Saxon gersta, Middle Low German gerste, German Low German Garste,

parole.significato: synonym of duizendblad (“common yarrow, Achillea millefolium”)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch garwe, from Old Dutch *garwa, from Proto-West Germanic *garwu, perhaps a variant of *garu (“prepared, ready (of food”)), as the plant was used medicinally for digestion. Cognate with English yarrow and German (Schaf)garbe.
From Middle Dutch geschien, from Old Dutch *giskian, from Proto-West Germanic *skehan (“to spring, come up, emerge, happen”).

parole.significato: one or more guns or cannons, generally of heavy calibre
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch geschutte, possibly from Proto-West Germanic *gaskuti. Compare German Geschütz. Related to schieten.

parole.significato: a tide of the sea, either flood or ebb
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch getide, from Old Dutch *gitīdi, from Proto-West Germanic [Term?]; cognates include Old High German gizīt, Old Saxon gitīd. By surface analysis, ge- + tijd.
From Middle Dutch gevādere, from Old Dutch *gefadero, from Proto-West Germanic *gafadurjō (literally “co-father”). Equivalent to ge- (“co-”) + vader (“father”).
From Proto-West Germanic *gafangan, past participle of *fą̄han, equivalent to ge- + vangen. Comparable to Middle Low German gevangen.

From Middle Dutch gevecht, from Old Dutch [Term?], from Proto-West Germanic [Term?]. By surface analysis, ge- + vechten. Cognate to Old High German gifeht, Middle High German gevechte, German Gefecht, Old English gefeoht and West Frisian gefjocht.
Inherited from Middle Dutch gēven, from Old Dutch gevan, from Proto-West Germanic *geban, from Proto-Germanic *gebaną, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰebʰ-.
From Middle Dutch ghewaer, from Old Dutch *giwar, from Proto-West Germanic *gawar.
From Middle Dutch gewāgen, from earlier unattested *gewâen, from Old Dutch *giwān, from Proto-West Germanic *gawahwan.

From Middle Dutch gewelt, influenced by umlauted geweldich (modern geweldig), from Old Dutch giwalt, ultimately pertaining to Proto-West Germanic *ga- and *waldōn (“to govern, rule”). Cognate with English wald, German Gewalt.
From Middle Dutch gewichte, from Old Dutch *giwihti, from Proto-West Germanic *gawihtī. See also wegen, wicht.
From Middle Dutch gewin, from Old Dutch giwin, from Proto-West Germanic *gawinn; compare Old English ġewinn. Synchronically a deverbal from gewinnen.
From Middle Dutch gewinnen, from Old Dutch giwinnan, from Proto-West Germanic *gawinnan, from Proto-Germanic *gawinnaną.
From Middle Dutch gesont, from Old Dutch gisunt, from Proto-West Germanic *gasund, cognate with German gesund, Old English ġesund, and Old High German gisunt.
From Middle Dutch gireg, from Old Dutch gireg, from Proto-West Germanic *gerag, *girīg, from Proto-Germanic *gerugaz, equivalent to gier (“eager”) + -ig.
From Middle Dutch gieten, from Old Dutch gietan, from Proto-West Germanic *geutan, from Proto-Germanic *geutaną, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰewd- (“to pour”).

From Middle Dutch gift, earlier also gicht, from Old Dutch *gift, from Proto-West Germanic *gifti, from Proto-Germanic *giftiz. The word gift derives from the same source, and the words were not formally distinguished until early modern Dutch.

From Middle Dutch gifte, from Old Dutch *gift, from Proto-West Germanic *gifti, from Proto-Germanic *giftiz. Equivalent to geven (“to give”) + -t (“verbal noun”). The words gif and vergif, both meaning “poison”, derive from the same source as gift. The sense “poison” may have originated as a shorten

From Middle Dutch gī, ghi, from Old Dutch gī, from Proto-West Germanic *jiʀ, from Proto-Germanic *jīz, Northwest Germanic variant of *jūz, from Proto-Indo-European *yúHs. Doublet of jij. Compare also Low German ji, jie, English ye, German ihr.
From Middle Dutch gisel, from Old Dutch *gīsal, from Proto-West Germanic *gīsl, from Proto-Germanic *gīslaz, from Proto-Celtic *geistlos (“hostage, pledge”).

parole.significato: a guild, professional corporation with a legal status and privileges during the Ancien Regime
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch gilde, ghilde, gulde, from Old Dutch *gilda, from Proto-West Germanic *geldan (“to pay”), from Proto-Germanic *geldaną (“to pay”).

Compound of ginnen + gappen. The first part is from Middle Dutch ginnen (“to laugh”), from Old Dutch ginnan, from Proto-West Germanic *ginnan, from Proto-Germanic *ginnaną. The second part is from Middle Dutch gabben (“to mock, laugh”), from Old Dutch *gabbon (“to mock, jest”), from Proto-Germanic *

parole.significato: to make a guess, estimate, have a go
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch gissen, further etymology unclear; perhaps from a derivative of Proto-West Germanic *getan (“to get”). Cognate with English guess, West Frisian gissen, Swedish gissa, Danish gisse.
From Middle Dutch gest, gist, from Old Dutch *gest, *gist, from Proto-West Germanic *jestu, from Proto-Germanic *jestuz.

Inherited from Middle Dutch glas, from Old Dutch glas, from Proto-West Germanic *glas, from Proto-Germanic *glasą, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰel- (“to shine, shimmer, glow”). Compare Low German Glas, German Glas, English glass, West Frisian glês, Icelandic gler.
From Middle Dutch glāsen, glāsijn, from Old Dutch *glasin, *glasīn, from Proto-West Germanic *glasīn. Equivalent to glas + -en.
From Middle Dutch gliden, from Old Dutch *glīdan, from Proto-West Germanic *glīdan, from Proto-Germanic *glīdaną, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰleydʰ-.
From Middle Dutch *glippen, from Old Dutch *glippon, from Proto-West Germanic *glippōn.
Inherited from Middle Dutch gloeyen, inherited from Old Dutch *gluoien, inherited from Proto-West Germanic *glōan, inherited from Proto-Germanic *glōaną.

parole.significato: to stare, to squint, to look in a deceitful manner
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch glupen, from Old Dutch glūpan, from Proto-West Germanic *glūpan, from Proto-Germanic *gleupaną.
Inherited from Middle Dutch god, from Old Dutch got, from Proto-West Germanic *god, from Proto-Germanic *gudą. Compare English and West Frisian god, German Gott, Danish gud.

From Middle Dutch godinne, from Old Dutch *gudinna, *gudin, from Proto-West Germanic *gudini, from Proto-Germanic *gudinī (“goddess”); cognates include Old English gyden, Old High German gutin (German Göttin). By surface analysis, god + -in.
From Middle Dutch goet, from Old Dutch guot, from Proto-West Germanic *gōd, from Proto-Germanic *gōdaz, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰedʰ-.

parole.significato: to supply with material goods, to make prosperous
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch goeden, from Old Dutch *guodon, from Proto-West Germanic *gōdōn.
From older goedelijk, from Middle Dutch goedelijc, from Old Dutch *guodlīk, from Proto-West Germanic *gōdalīk, from Proto-Germanic *gōdalīkaz.
From Middle Dutch gokelare, from Old Dutch *gokalari, from Proto-West Germanic *kaukulārī, from Latin caucleārius. Equivalent to goochelen + -aar.

parole.significato: belt, a (typically leather) band worn around the waist
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch gordel, from Old Dutch gurdel, from Proto-West Germanic *gurdil, from Proto-Germanic *gurdilaz. Equivalent to gorden + -el.
From Middle Dutch gorgel, from Old Dutch *gurgula, from Proto-West Germanic *gurgulā (“throat”).

parole.significato: Gothic, pertaining to Gothic art and architecture
parole.testo: From Gotisch, from earlier Gotsch, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *gotō (which derived from Proto-Germanic *gutô) + -isch. Equivalent to Goten + -isch.
From Middle Dutch gout, from Old Dutch golt, from Proto-West Germanic *golþ, from Proto-Germanic *gulþą.

From Middle Dutch gou, gau, gō (genitive gooy), from Old Dutch gō, from Proto-West Germanic *gawi, from Proto-Germanic *gawją, a collective form equivalent to ge- (“a prefix that indicates a single collective whole”) + ouwe (“land near water or drenched with water”). Cognate of West Frisian gea, goa
From Middle Dutch grâve, from Old Dutch grāvo, from Proto-West Germanic *garāfijō.

parole.significato: willingly, gladly (meaning that the subject enjoys doing the action of the verb)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch gradig (“desirous, willing”), from Old Dutch *grādag (“desirous, hungry”), from Proto-West Germanic *grādag, from Proto-Germanic *grēdagaz (“hungry”).
From Middle Dutch gras, from Old Dutch *gras, from Proto-West Germanic *gras, from Proto-Germanic *grasą, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰreh₁- (“to grow”). Doublet of gors.
From Middle Dutch grasgroene, from Old Dutch *grasagruoni, from Proto-West Germanic *grasagrōnī, from Proto-Germanic *grasagrōniz, equivalent to gras + groen.

parole.significato: grey, not brightly colored, ashen, grubby, grimy
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch grau, from Old Dutch grāo, from Proto-West Germanic *grāu, from Proto-Germanic *grēwaz.
From Middle Dutch grāven, from Old Dutch gravan, from Proto-West Germanic *graban, from Proto-Germanic *grabaną.
From Middle Dutch grendel, grindel, from Old Dutch grindel, from Proto-West Germanic *grindil.
From Middle Dutch griec, from Old Dutch *Krēka(s), from Proto-West Germanic *Krēkō (“Greeks”).
From Middle Dutch gripen, from Old Dutch grīpan, from Proto-West Germanic *grīpan, from Proto-Germanic *grīpaną, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰreyb- (“to grasp, grab”).
From Middle Dutch grijs, from Old Dutch *grīs, from Proto-West Germanic *grīs, from Proto-Germanic *grīsaz.
From Middle Dutch grim, from Old Dutch grim, from Proto-West Germanic *grimm, from Proto-Germanic *grimmaz. Very uncommon in modern Dutch; recent usage may be influenced by English grim.
From Middle Dutch grimmen, from Old Dutch *grimman, from Proto-West Germanic *grimman, from Proto-Germanic *grimmaną.
From Middle Dutch grinden, from Old Dutch *grindan, from Proto-West Germanic *grindan, from Proto-Germanic *grindaną.

Inherited from Middle Dutch groene, from Old Dutch *gruoni, from Proto-West Germanic *grōnī, from Proto-Germanic *grōniz, from Proto-Indo-European *gróh₁nis, from *gʰreh₁-. Compare Low German grön, gröön, German grün, West Frisian grien, English green, Danish grøn.
From Middle Dutch groeten, from Old Dutch *gruoten, from Proto-West Germanic *grōtijan, from Proto-Germanic *grōtijaną.
From Middle Dutch grof, from Old Dutch *grof, from Proto-West Germanic *grob, from Proto-Germanic *grubaz.
From Middle Dutch *grolle, from Old Dutch *grollo, from Proto-West Germanic *grulljō.
From Middle Dutch gront, from Old Dutch grunt, from Proto-West Germanic *grundu, from Proto-Germanic *grunduz.
From Middle Dutch grôot, from Old Dutch grōt, from Proto-West Germanic *graut, from Proto-Germanic *grautaz.
From Middle Dutch grutte, gurte, from Old Dutch *grutti, from Proto-West Germanic *gruti, related to *greut (“grit”).

parole.significato: an old or worn-down horse, a nag
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch guul, gûle, from Proto-West Germanic *gūl- (stem form uncertain), of uncertain origin but possibly related to *geutan (“to pour”). The original sense could have been "powerful horse, male animal," in which case the "pouring" would refer to insemination. Similar sense development is

From Middle Dutch guldijn, guldin, gulden, from Old Dutch *guldīn, from Proto-West Germanic *gulþīn, from Proto-Germanic *gulþīnaz. Equivalent to goud + -en, replaced in modern Dutch with gouden in most contexts (see there for more).
From Middle Dutch gunst, gonst, prefixed from ge- + onst, onste, the latter from Old Dutch anst, from Proto-West Germanic *unsti, from Proto-Germanic *unstiz. Equivalent to gunnen + -st.

parole.significato: a hedge, thicket of woody bushes planted in a row
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch hāge, haghe, from Old Dutch *hago, from Proto-West Germanic *hagō, from Proto-Germanic *hagô (“hedge”), from Proto-Indo-European *kágʰō ~ *kagʰnós. Cognate with English haw.

parole.significato: synonym of meidoorn (“plant of species Crataegus, including hawthorn and mayblossom”)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch hāgedorn, from Old Dutch *haguthorn, from Proto-West Germanic *haguþorn. Equivalent to haag + doorn.
From Middle Dutch hāke, from Old Dutch *hako, from Proto-West Germanic *hakō, from Proto-Germanic *hakô.

parole.significato: horsecollar, collar for draught animals; made of wood or leather
