parole.testo: From Middle Dutch hame, from Old Dutch *hamo, from Proto-West Germanic *hamō, from Proto-Germanic *hamô (“horse collar”).
From Middle Dutch hâer, from Old Dutch hār, from Proto-West Germanic *hār, from Proto-Germanic *hērą.
From Middle Dutch hert, hāert, from Old Dutch *herth, from Proto-West Germanic *herþ.

parole.significato: hare, lagomorph of the genus Lepus
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch hāse, from Old Dutch *haso, Proto-West Germanic *hasō ~ *haʀ-, from Proto-Germanic *hesô.

From Middle Dutch haessen, from Old Dutch *hāssena, *hāhsena, from Proto-West Germanic *hą̄hasinu, from Proto-Germanic *hanhasinwō (“heel tendon, Achilles tendon”), from *hanhaz (“heel”) + *senawō (“sinew”).
From Middle Dutch hat, from Old Dutch *hat, from Proto-West Germanic *hati, from Proto-Germanic *hataz. Compare West Frisian haat, German Hass, English hate, Danish had.

parole.significato: lizard, non-snake reptilian of the subclass Squamata, especially of the Lacertilia
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch hagetisse, from Old Dutch *egithassa, from Proto-West Germanic *agiþahsijā (“lizard”).
From Middle Dutch hac, from Proto-West Germanic *hakkōn.

From Middle Dutch halle, from Old Dutch *halla, from Proto-West Germanic *hallu, from Proto-Germanic *hallō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱel- (“to hide, cover, conceal”). Cognate with Low German Hall, German Halle, English hall, Danish hall.
From Middle Dutch halen, from Old Dutch *halon, from Proto-West Germanic *halōn, from Proto-Germanic *halōną.
From Middle Dutch half, from Old Dutch half, from Proto-West Germanic *halb, from Proto-Germanic *halbaz. Cognate with English half, German halb, West Frisian heal, Danish halv.

parole.significato: haulm, stalk, stem of grasses (including grain and reed)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch halm, from Old Dutch *halm, from Proto-West Germanic *halm, from Proto-Germanic *halmaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱolh₂mos. Doublet of kalmoes.
From Middle Dutch hals, from Old Dutch hals, from Proto-West Germanic *hals, from Proto-Germanic *halsaz.
From Middle Dutch hāmer, from Old Dutch *hamar, from Proto-West Germanic *hamar, from Proto-Germanic *hamaraz.

parole.significato: a hand of a human, other simian or other animal with fingers
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch hant, from Old Dutch hant, from Proto-West Germanic *handu, from Proto-Germanic *handuz.

From Middle Dutch handelen, from Old Dutch handalon, from Proto-West Germanic *handulōn, from Proto-Germanic *handlōną. By surface analysis, hand + elen. Ultimately of the same origin as the English borrowing at Etymology 2 below (thus, a doublet of the same).
From Middle Dutch handelinge, from Old Dutch *handalunga, from Proto-West Germanic *handulungu. By surface analysis, handelen + -ing.
From Middle Dutch handgrepe, from Old Dutch *hantgripi, from Proto-West Germanic *handugripi, equivalent to hand + greep.
From Middle Dutch antscoen, hantscoe, from Old Dutch *hantscuoh, from Proto-West Germanic *handuskōh. Equivalent to hand + schoen (“shoe, cover”). Cognate with German Handschuh.

From a merger of two closely related but distinct verbs: * Middle Dutch haen, from Old Dutch hān, from Proto-West Germanic *hą̄han, from Proto-Germanic *hanhaną (transitive, strong class 7). * Middle Dutch hangen, from Old Dutch hangon, from Proto-West Germanic *hangēn, from Proto-Germanic *hangāną

parole.significato: a mediaeval merchants' guild or association of traders, especially among the northern continental West Germanic languag…
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch hanse, from Old Dutch hansa, from Proto-West Germanic *hansu, from Proto-Germanic *hansō.
From Middle Dutch herre, from Old Dutch *herro, from Proto-West Germanic *herʀō, from Proto-Germanic *herzô.
From Middle Dutch hart, from Old Dutch hart, from Proto-West Germanic *hard(ī), from Proto-Germanic *harduz.

parole.significato: to render hard(er), more resistant etc.; to temper metal; to steel nerves
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch harden, herden, from Old Dutch *herden, from Proto-West Germanic *hardijan, from Proto-Germanic *hardijaną.
From Middle Dutch harijn, from Proto-West Germanic *hārīn. By surface analysis, haar + -en.
From Middle Dutch hârinc, from Old Dutch *hārinc, from Proto-West Germanic *hāring.
From Middle Dutch hersten, harsten (“to scorch”), from Old Dutch *hersten, from Proto-West Germanic *harstijan.

parole.significato: heart, main muscle pumping blood through the body
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch herte, harte, from Old Dutch herta, from Proto-West Germanic *hertā, from Proto-Germanic *hertô, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱḗr.

parole.significato: reel (a machine on which wire, cable, hose etc. is wound)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch haspel, from Old Dutch *haspil, from Proto-West Germanic *haspil, from a diminutive of Proto-Germanic *haspijǭ.
From Middle Dutch haten, from Old Dutch haton, from Proto-West Germanic *hatēn, from Proto-Germanic *hatāną.
From Middle Dutch havene, from Old Dutch *havana, from Proto-West Germanic *habanu, from Proto-Germanic *habnō, *habanō.

parole.significato: any wild species or cultivar of the genus Avena
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch havere, from Old Dutch *havara, from Proto-West Germanic *habrō, from Proto-Germanic *habrô. Cognate with Old Norse hafri, Old English haver, Old High German habaro.

parole.significato: A hawk, a small bird of the family Accipitridae, especially of the genus Accipiter.
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch havic, from Old Dutch *havuk, from Proto-West Germanic *habuk. Compare Low German Haavk, German Habicht, West Frisian hauk, English hawk, Swedish hök, Norwegian hauk. The political sense derived from English hawk.
From Middle Dutch hasel, from Old Dutch *hasal, from Proto-West Germanic *hasl.

parole.significato: to have, to possess, own, hold
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch hebben, from Old Dutch hebben, from Proto-West Germanic *habbjan, from Proto-Germanic *habjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *kap- (“to grasp”).
From Middle Dutch hechten, from Old Dutch heften, from Proto-West Germanic *haftijan, from Proto-Germanic *haftijaną.
From Middle Dutch hēde, eastern variant of herde, heerde, from Proto-West Germanic *heʀdā.

From Middle Dutch heden, also hude, huden, from Old Dutch hiudo, a contraction of the instrumental phrase *hiu dago (“on this day”), from Proto-West Germanic *hiu dagu, from Proto-Germanic *hinō dagō (*hiz + *dagaz). The appearance of the vowel -e- is unusual, the expected form in modern Dutch would
From Middle Dutch hêel, from Old Dutch hēl, from Proto-West Germanic *hail, from Proto-Germanic *hailaz.
From Middle Dutch hêem, from Old Dutch hēm, from Proto-West Germanic *haim, from Proto-Germanic *haimaz.
From Middle Dutch henen (“away from here, hence”), from a Proto-West Germanic *hin-, from Proto-Germanic *hiz, and Proto-Germanic *-anē. Cognate with German hin, English hence.
From Middle Dutch here, from Old Dutch heri, from Proto-West Germanic *hari, from Proto-Germanic *harjaz, from Proto-Indo-European *kóryos.

Uncertain. The first element may derive from Proto-West Germanic *haru (“bitter, sharp”); the second may be moes, but in a sense more comparable to that found in German Gemüse (“vegetable”); the compound might then originally have meant "bitter vegetable".
From Middle Dutch heester, from Old Dutch *hēster, *heister, from Proto-West Germanic *haistr.
From Middle Dutch hêet, from Old Dutch hēt, from Proto-West Germanic *hait, from Proto-Germanic *haitaz.

From Middle Dutch heffen, from Old Dutch heffen, from Proto-West Germanic *habbjan, from Proto-Germanic *habjaną, a class 6 strong verb with j-present, from Proto-Indo-European *kh₂pyéti, from the root *kap- (“to seize”).

parole.significato: handle of a knife or other tool, haft, hilt
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch hefte, from Old Dutch *hefti, from Proto-West Germanic *haftī, from Proto-Germanic *haftiją. Forms with -cht- were dominant in Middle Dutch.

From Middle Dutch hegge, from Old Dutch *hegga, from Proto-West Germanic *haggju, from Proto-Germanic *hagjō, [Term?], from Proto-Indo-European *kagʰyo-, *kagʰyóm (“enclosure”). Related to English hedge, German Hecke; also Latin cohum, Welsh cae.
From Middle Dutch heide, hede, from Old Dutch *heitha, *hētha, from Proto-West Germanic *haiþi, from Proto-Germanic *haiþī.
From Middle Dutch heidensc, heidijnsc, from Old Dutch *hēthinisk, from Proto-West Germanic *haiþinisk, equivalent to heiden + -s.
From Middle Dutch heilich, from Old Dutch heilig, from Proto-West Germanic *hailag, from Proto-Germanic *hailagaz. Equivalent to heil (“salvation”) + -ig (“-y”).

From Middle Dutch heilsāem, from Old Dutch heilsam, from Proto-West Germanic *hailasam, from Proto-Germanic *hailasamaz. By surface analysis, heil + -zaam. Cognate with West Frisian heilsum, German heilsam, and English wholesome.
From Middle Dutch heimelijc, fro Proto-West Germanic *haimalīk. Equivalent to heim + -lijk.
From Middle Dutch hecke, from Old Dutch *hekka, from Proto-West Germanic *hakkju.

parole.significato: to heckle, to comb with a hackle (heckling comb)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch hēkelen, from Old Dutch *hekilon, from Proto-West Germanic *hakilōn.
From Middle Dutch helle, from Old Dutch hella, from Proto-West Germanic *hallju, from Proto-Germanic *haljō, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱel- (“to cover, hide, conceal”).

From Middle Dutch helt, helet (“hero, man, warrior”), from Old Dutch helt (“man”), from Proto-West Germanic *haliþ, from Proto-Germanic *haliþaz (“man, hero”). Cognate with Old English hæleþ (English health), Old High German helid (German Held), West Frisian held, Old Norse halr, hǫlðr (Norwegian Ny
From Middle Dutch hêlen, from Old Dutch *hēlen, from Proto-West Germanic *hailijan, from Proto-Germanic *hailijaną. Doublet of healen.

From Middle Dutch hēlen, from Old Dutch *helan, from Proto-West Germanic *helan, from Proto-Germanic *helaną (“hide, conceal”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱéleti. The modern sense is probably a semantic loan from German hehlen.
From Middle Dutch helm, from Old Dutch *helm, from Proto-West Germanic *helm, from Proto-Germanic *helmaz. Compare West Frisian helm, Low German Helm, German Helm, Danish hjelm.
From Proto-West Germanic *helm; cognate with Low German helm, English helm (“bentgrass, straw”). Further related to halm (“haulm”); compare English haulm, halm.
From Middle Dutch helpen, from Old Dutch helpan, from Proto-West Germanic *helpan, from Proto-Germanic *helpaną.

parole.significato: to embrace, to wrap the arms around the neck of
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch helsen, from Old Dutch *helsen, from Proto-West Germanic *halsijan. Equivalent to hals (“neck”) + -en (denominative) and shows the effect of historical umlaut.
From Middle Dutch hemde, hemede, from Old Dutch *hemithi, from Proto-West Germanic *hamiþi (“shirt”). Doublet of chemise and kamisa.
From Middle Dutch hēmel, from Old Dutch himil, from Proto-West Germanic *himil.

parole.significato: hen, female chicken; female of a related species
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch henne, from Old Dutch *henna, from Proto-West Germanic *hannju, from Proto-Germanic *hanjō, from Proto-Indo-European *keh₂n- (“to sing”).
From Middle Dutch henxt, from Old Dutch *hengist, from Proto-West Germanic *hangist, from Proto-Germanic *hangistaz.

From Middle Dutch hannep, hennep, from Old Dutch *hanap, *henip, from Proto-West Germanic *hanapi, from Proto-Germanic *hanapiz. Compare German Hanf, English hemp, Danish hamp. Doublet of cannabis and canvas.
From Middle Dutch herberghe, from Old Dutch *heribergo, from Proto-West Germanic *harjabergu.

parole.significato: to lodge (to supply with a room or place to sleep in for a time)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch herbergen, from Old Dutch *heribergon, from Proto-West Germanic *harjabergōn. By surface analysis, herberg + -en.

From Middle Dutch herfst, from Old Dutch *hervist, from Proto-West Germanic *harbist, from Proto-Germanic *harbistaz, from Proto-Indo-European *kerp-. The original meaning was “harvest time”, as is seen in herfstmaand. Cognate with German Herbst, Low German Harvst, West Frisian hjerst, English harve
From Middle Dutch hersene, from Old Dutch *hirsna, from Proto-West Germanic *hersnō, from Proto-Germanic *hersô. *hersnō

parole.significato: a deer, a ruminant of the family Cervidae; sometimes used of members of the families Moschidae and Tragulidae in non-sc…
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch hert, from Old Dutch hirut, from Proto-West Germanic *herut, from Proto-Germanic *herutaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱerh₂-.
From Middle Dutch hertōge, from Old Dutch *heritogo, from Proto-West Germanic *harjatogō.

parole.significato: to be named; to have as name; to be called
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch hêten, from Old Dutch hētan, from Proto-West Germanic *haitan, from Proto-Germanic *haitaną.
From Middle Dutch huege, from Old Dutch *hugi, from Proto-West Germanic *hugi, from Proto-Germanic *hugiz.
From Middle Dutch heuchenesse, hogenesse, hoochnesse, from Old Dutch *huganissi, from Proto-West Germanic *huganassī, equivalent to heugen + -nis.
From Middle Dutch heup, hoep, from Old Dutch *hupi, from Proto-West Germanic *hupi, from Proto-Germanic *hupiz.

From Middle Dutch hevich, from Old Dutch hevig, from Proto-West Germanic *habīg, from Proto-Germanic *habīgaz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kap-. Equivalent to heffen (“to heave”) + -ig (“-y”). Compare German hebig, English heavy. Doublet of hebi.

parole.significato: he; third-person singular masculine subjective personal pronoun
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch hi, from Old Dutch hie, hē, from Proto-West Germanic *hiʀ, from Proto-Germanic *hiz. Doublet of ie.

parole.significato: to pant, to gasp for breath
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch higen, from Old Dutch *hīgon, from Proto-West Germanic *hīgōn.

From Middle Dutch hil, hille, from Old Dutch *hul, hil, from Proto-West Germanic *hulli (“hill”). Cognate with English hill, Middle Dutch hulle (“hill”), Low German hull (“hill”), Icelandic hóll (“hill”). Related to holm.

parole.significato: a doe or hind; a female deer
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch hinde, from Old Dutch *hind, from Proto-West Germanic *hindi, from Proto-Germanic *hindiz.

parole.significato: to limp, to hobble (walk with difficulty due to injury)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch hinken, from Old Dutch *hinkan, from Proto-West Germanic *hinkan, from Proto-Germanic *hinkaną.

parole.significato: to toil, struggle, to be worn out
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch *hobben (attested only in the iterative hobbelen (“to move gently up and down, bob”)), from Old Dutch *hobbon, from Proto-West Germanic *hobbōn (“to move, stir, jump”), from or related to Proto-Germanic *huppōną (“to bob, hop”).
From Middle Dutch hōde, from Old Dutch *hotho, from Proto-West Germanic [Term?], from Proto-Germanic *huþô.

parole.significato: a hat, worn on the head
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch hoet, from Old Dutch *huot, from Proto-West Germanic *hōd, from Proto-Germanic *hōdaz. Cognate to German Hut, English hood.
From Middle Dutch hoede, from Old Dutch *huoda (attested as hôde), from Proto-West Germanic *hōdu. Cognate with German Hut. Also related with English heed.

parole.significato: to tend, to look after, to take care of
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch hoeden, from Old Dutch huoden, from Proto-West Germanic *hōdijan.
From Middle Dutch hoec, huoc, from Old Dutch *huoc, from Proto-West Germanic *hōk, from Proto-Germanic *hōkaz (“hook”), from Proto-Indo-European *kog-, *keg-, *keng- (“peg, hook, claw”).
From Middle Dutch hoen, from Old Dutch *huon, from Proto-West Germanic *hōn, from Proto-Germanic *hōną. Cognate with German Huhn, Low German Hohn.
From Middle Dutch hoeste, from Old Dutch [Term?], from Proto-West Germanic *hwōstō, from Proto-Germanic *hwōstô.

parole.significato: court, residence of a monarch or other high-placed person
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch hof, from Old Dutch *hof, from Proto-West Germanic *hof, from Proto-Germanic *hufą.
From Middle Dutch hol, from Old Dutch *hol, from Proto-West Germanic *hol, from Proto-Germanic *hulą.
From Middle Dutch hont, from Old Dutch hunt, from Proto-West Germanic *hund, from Proto-Germanic *hundaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱwn̥tós, from *ḱwṓ. Cognate to German Hund, English hound.
From Middle Dutch hônen, from Old Dutch *hōnen, from Proto-West Germanic *haunijan, from Proto-Germanic *haunijaną.
From Middle Dutch honger, from Old Dutch hunger, from Proto-West Germanic *hungr, from Proto-Germanic *hungruz.
From Middle Dutch hôvet, hôoft, from Old Dutch hōvit, from Proto-West Germanic *haubud, from Proto-Germanic *haubudą. The sense “oral sex” is a semantic loan from English head.

From Middle Dutch hôvet-, from Old Dutch hōvit-, from Proto-West Germanic *haubida- (“main”), derived from the noun *haubid (“head”) (whence Dutch hoofd). Cognate with German haupt- and Old English hēafod-.
From Middle Dutch hovetkussen, from Old Dutch *hōvitkussīn, from Proto-West Germanic *haubidakussīn. By surface analysis, hoofd (“head”) + kussen (“pillow, cushion”).

From Middle Dutch hôvetman, from Old Dutch hōvitman, from Proto-West Germanic *haubidamann (“leader; captain, head of a group,” literally “head or main person”). Cognate with German Hauptmann, Low German Hööftmann, and Old English hēafodmann. Equivalent to hoofd- + man.

From Middle Dutch hooch, the original inflected stem hō- reanalysed by analogy with the uninflected form because of word-final devoicing. From Old Dutch hōh, from Proto-West Germanic *hauh, from Proto-Germanic *hauhaz. Doublet of high. Cognate with German hoch, West Frisian heech, Saterland Frisian

From Middle Dutch hôgede, from Old Dutch *hōgitha, from Proto-West Germanic *hauhiþu, from Proto-Germanic *hauhiþō, equivalent to hoog + -te. Cognates Compare English height, Norwegian høyde, Swedish höjd, Icelandic hæð, Old High German hohida, Gothic hauhiþa.

parole.significato: a horn (sound device) or a bugle
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch horn, from Old Dutch *horn, from Proto-West Germanic *horn, from Proto-Germanic *hurną, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱer-.
By surface analysis, hoorn + -aar (perhaps referring to its antennae), but likely actually derived from Proto-West Germanic *hurnutu, whence English hornet.

parole.significato: to hope for, to wish for
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch hōpen, from Old Dutch hopon, from Proto-West Germanic *hopōn.

From Middle Dutch hôpen, from Old Dutch hōpon, from Proto-West Germanic *haupōn, from Proto-Germanic *haupōną (“to heap, heap up”), equivalent to hoop + -en. Cognate with Old High German houfōn, Middle Low German hôpen, hȫpen, Old English hēapian.

From Middle Dutch horde, hurde, from Old Dutch *hurd, from Proto-West Germanic *hurdi, from Proto-Germanic *hurdiz; cognate with German Hürde, and closely related to English hurdle (which is a diminutive of the same root). The sense "hurdle" is a semantic loan from English hurdle.
From Middle Dutch horen, from Old Dutch *hōren, from Proto-West Germanic *hauʀijan, from Proto-Germanic *hauzijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ḱh₂owsyéti.

Inherited from Middle Dutch hoorken, huerken, hurken, horken, from Old Dutch *hōrken, from Proto-West Germanic *hauʀikōn, *hauʀukōn, Derived from Proto-Germanic *hauzijaną (“to hear”) + *-ukōną, *-ikōną; cognate with West Frisian harkje (“to listen”), Middle Low German horken (“to hark”), German hor
From Middle Dutch hors, from Old Dutch hors, from Proto-West Germanic *hross, from Proto-Germanic *hrussą. Doublet of ros.

parole.significato: an area of the earth's surface which is raised relative to surrounding land; a horst
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch horst, from Old Dutch *hurst, from Proto-West Germanic *hursti. Cognate with English horst and German Horst (“horst; eyrie”).
From Middle Dutch houden, from Old Dutch haldan, from Proto-West Germanic *haldan, from Proto-Germanic *haldaną.
From Middle Dutch hout, from Old Dutch holt, from Proto-West Germanic *holt, from Proto-Germanic *hultą.
From Middle Dutch houwen, from Old Dutch houwan, from Proto-West Germanic *hauwan, from Proto-Germanic *hawwaną (“to hew, forge”).
From Middle Dutch hoey, from Proto-West Germanic *hwaij (“whey”).
From Middle Dutch huut, from Old Dutch hūd, from Proto-West Germanic *hūdi, from Proto-Germanic *hūdiz.
From Middle Dutch huden, from Old Dutch *hūden, from Proto-West Germanic *huzdijan, from Proto-Germanic *huzdijaną.
From Middle Dutch huve, from Old Dutch *hūfa, a conflation of Proto-West Germanic *hūbā (“hood, cowl”) (from Proto-Germanic *hūbǭ) and *hūfi (“hive”). Cognate with English houve and hive.
From Middle Dutch hulen, from Old Dutch *huwilon, *hūlon, from Proto-West Germanic *hūilōn.
From Middle Dutch huus, from Old Dutch hūs, from Proto-West Germanic *hūs, from Proto-Germanic *hūsą. Doublet of house and osso.

parole.significato: a houseleek, sempervivum; any plant of genus Sempervivum
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch huuslook, from Old Dutch *hūslōk, from Proto-West Germanic *hūsalauk. By surface analysis, huis (“house”) + look (“leek”), referring to their usage on the roofs of houses (compare the taxonomic name Sempervivum tectorum of the common houseleek; tectorum meaning "of roofs").
From Middle Dutch husen, from Old Dutch *hūson, from Proto-West Germanic *hūsōn, from Proto-Germanic *hūsōną, equivalent to huis + -en.

From Middle Dutch hulde (“mercy, goodwill, loyalty”), from Old Dutch huldi (“favour”), from Proto-West Germanic *hulþī, from Proto-Germanic *hulþį̄. Derivative of the rare hou (“favourable”) + -e (abstract noun suffix) preserving the original i-mutation. The Middle Dutch variant houde addopted the v
From Middle Dutch hullen, from Old Dutch *hullen, from Proto-West Germanic *hulljan, from Proto-Germanic *huljaną.
From Middle Dutch huls, from Old Dutch *hulis, from Proto-West Germanic *hulis.
From Middle Dutch huppen, from Old Dutch *huppen, from Proto-West Germanic *huppijan, from Proto-Germanic *huppijaną (“to hop”). Cognate with German hüpfen. Also related with English hop.
From Middle Dutch huren, from Old Dutch *hūren, from Proto-West Germanic *hūʀijan.
From Middle Dutch hûre, from Old Dutch *hūra, from Proto-West Germanic *hūʀiju.
From Middle Dutch hûrlink, from Old Dutch *hūrling, from Proto-West Germanic *hūʀijuling. Equivalent to huur + -ling. Compare German Heuerling, English hireling.
From Middle Dutch iegelijc, from Old Dutch iegilīk, from Proto-West Germanic [Term?]. Contains the word gelijk. Cognate with German jeglicher.

From Middle Dutch ieman, iemant, from Old Dutch ieman, *ioman. A compound of io (“always, ever”) + man (“man, person”), from Proto-West Germanic *aiw + *mann. Compare German jemand, Old English ǣġhwā.

parole.significato: an elm, tree of the genus Ulmus
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch *iep, *ijp, from Old Dutch *īp, from Proto-West Germanic *īp (“field elm”).

parole.significato: vain, overly proud (of one's appearance, status etc.)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch idel, from Old Dutch īdil, from Proto-West Germanic *īdl. Cognate with German eitel, English idle. The common Dutch loss of medial -d- led to the by-forms ijl and iel, which eventually acquired different meanings.
From Middle Dutch ilen, from Old Dutch īlen, from Proto-West Germanic *īlijan (“to make haste, hasten”).
From Middle Dutch ijs, from Old Dutch *īs, from Proto-West Germanic *īs, from Proto-Germanic *īsą.
From Middle Dutch isele, hisel, isel, from Old Dutch *īsichel, from Proto-West Germanic *īsajikil. Equivalent to ijs (“ice”) + -el.
From Middle Dutch iser, from Old Dutch *īsarn, from Proto-West Germanic *īsarn, from Proto-Germanic *īsarną, from Proto-Celtic *īsarnom, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ésh₂r̥ (“blood”).

parole.significato: I; first-person singular subjective personal pronoun
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch ic, from Old Dutch ik, from Proto-West Germanic *ik, from Proto-Germanic *ek, from Proto-Indo-European *eǵh₂óm. Compare German ich, Low German ik, West Frisian ik, English I, Danish jeg. See I (English, etymology 3).
From Middle Dutch immecare, from Old Dutch *imbikaro, from Proto-West Germanic *imbjakaʀjō, from *imbī (“bee”) + *kaʀjō (“vessel-maker”).

From Middle Dutch imme, from Old Dutch *imbi, from Proto-West Germanic *imbī. Cognate with Old Saxon *imbi, Middle Low German imme, German Low German Imm, Old High German imbi, impi, Middle High German imbe, German Imme, Bavarian Imp, Old Frisian *em, *eme, Saterland Frisian Ieme, West Frisian ime.
From Middle Dutch in, from Old Dutch in, from Proto-West Germanic *in, from Proto-Germanic *in.

From Middle Dutch invoeren, invueren, from Old Dutch *infuoren, from Proto-West Germanic *infōrijan, equivalent to in + voeren. Cognate with German Low German inföhren, German einführen, West Frisian ynfiere, Old English infēran (“to enter”).
Surface analysis yields in + zetten. From Middle Dutch insetten, from Old Dutch insetten, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *insattjan. Compare German einsetzen and English inset.

parole.significato: year (the time it takes the Earth to circle the Sun; its equivalent on other planets)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch jâer, from Old Dutch jār, from Proto-Germanic *jērą, from Proto-Indo-European *yeh₁-.
From Middle Dutch jaerdach, from Old Dutch *jārdag, from Proto-West Germanic *jāradag, from Proto-Germanic *jēradagaz, equivalent to jaar + dag.

From Middle Dutch jacht, jaecht, jaget, from Old Dutch *jagot, from Proto-West Germanic *jagōþu (“hunt, hunting”). Equivalent to jagen (“to hunt”) + -t (“verbal noun”). Cognate with German Jagd. The form jaecht is due to contraction and jacht to subsequent pre-cluster shortening. (Compare maagd, in
From Middle Dutch jāgen, from Old Dutch *jagon, from Proto-West Germanic *jagōn.

From Middle Dutch *jammeren, iammeren, from Old Dutch *jāmaron, from Proto-West Germanic *jāmarōn, from Proto-Germanic *jēmarōną, equivalent to jammer + -en. Cognate with English yammer, German jammern.
From Middle Dutch jegen, jegens, with unetymological -s from Old Dutch gegin, from Proto-West Germanic *gagin, from Proto-Germanic *gagin. See also tegen. Cognate with Middle Low German jegen.

From Middle Dutch joken, juecken, long-vowel variants of jocken, jucken, from Old Dutch *jukken, from Proto-West Germanic *jukkjan. The long vowels developed before the single consonants in the 2nd and 3rd person singular forms, e.g. Old Dutch 3rd person singular *jukit. Cognate with German jucken,

From Middle Dutch jonc, from Old Dutch junc, from Proto-West Germanic *jung, from Proto-Germanic *jungaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂yuh₁n̥ḱós. Compare German jung, English young, Danish ung, Icelandic ungur.

Cognate with German jauchzen. The further etymology is not entirely clear. If the Dutch and German words are inherited from a common source, the word would be of Proto-West Germanic origin at the very latest, although it has been suggested that the Dutch word could represent a borrowing from German.

From Middle Dutch cale, from Old Dutch *kalo, from Proto-West Germanic *kalu, from Proto-Germanic *kalwaz (“naked, bald”), from Proto-Indo-European *gelH- (“naked, bald”). Compare German kahl, West Frisian keal, English callow.

parole.significato: synonym of kaardenbol (“teasel, plant of genus Dipsacus”)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch caerde, from Old Dutch *carda, from Proto-West Germanic *kardā, ultimately from Latin carduus.
From Middle Dutch câse, from Old Dutch *kāsi, from late Proto-West Germanic *kāsī, borrowed from Latin cāseus.
From Middle Dutch caf, from Old Dutch *kaf, from Proto-West Germanic *kaf.

parole.significato: a calf (young cow or bull; young bovine)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch calf, from Old Dutch calf, from Proto-West Germanic *kalb, from Proto-Germanic *kalbaz.
From Middle Dutch calc, from Old Dutch *kalk, from Proto-West Germanic *kalk.
From Middle Dutch callen, from Old Dutch *kallon, from Proto-West Germanic *kalʀōn, from Proto-Germanic *kalzōną.

parole.significato: a comb, utensil to groom hair, fur etc.
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch kamp, from Old Dutch *kamb, from Proto-West Germanic *kamb, from Proto-Germanic *kambaz (“comb”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵómbʰos (“tooth; row of teeth”).
From Old Dutch *karag, from Proto-West Germanic *karag.

parole.significato: to churn (agitate milk rapidly to obtain butter)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch carnen, kernen, from Old Dutch [Term?], from Proto-West Germanic [Term?], from Proto-Germanic *kirnijaną.
From Middle Dutch caste (“chest”), from Old Dutch *casto, from Proto-West Germanic *kastō (“chest, reservoir”).

parole.significato: domestic cat, pussy, Felis silvestris catus
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle Dutch catte, from Old Dutch katta, *catta, from Proto-West Germanic *kattā, from Latin catta, feminine of cattus.
From Middle Dutch cāter, from Old Dutch *kataro, from Proto-West Germanic *kataʀō.

parole.significato: a jackdaw, the bird species Coloeus monedula, closely related to the crow, magpie and raven
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch cauwe, from Old Dutch *kāwa, from Proto-West Germanic *kahu (compare West Frisian ka), from Proto-Indo-European *gewH- (“to call, cry”) (compare Lithuanian giedóti, Tocharian A kāk (“he calls upon”), Sanskrit गायति (gāyati)).

From Middle Dutch cauwen, variant of couwen, cuwen, from Old Dutch *kiuwan, from Proto-West Germanic *keuwan, from Proto-Germanic *kewwaną. Though auw and ouw are now homophonous, they were formerly distinguished. The origin of the unexpected auw-vocalism is uncertain, but has been compared to Engli

parole.significato: a plot, a lot, a tract of land
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch cavele, from Old Dutch *cavela, from Proto-West Germanic *kabl, from Proto-Germanic *kablaz. Cognate with dialectal German Kabel.
From Middle Dutch kēle, from Old Dutch kela, from Proto-West Germanic *kelā, from Proto-Germanic *kelǭ.

From Middle Dutch *kēp, *kip, from Old Dutch *kip (compare Old Dutch kip (“fetter”)), from Proto-West Germanic *kipp- (“to cut, split”), from Proto-Germanic *kipp- (“to split”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵey- (“to split, divide, geminate, sprout”). Cognate with Middle Low German kēp ("notch, incisio
From Middle Dutch kēgel, from Old Dutch *kegil, from Proto-West Germanic *kagil.
From Middle Dutch key, keye, from Old Dutch *kei (in toponym keidīk (“Keidijk”)), perhaps from Proto-West Germanic *kagi (compare kegel (“cone”)), from Proto-Germanic *kagiz.

From Middle Dutch kemmen, from Old Dutch *kemben, from Proto-West Germanic *kambijan, from Proto-Germanic *kambijaną, from *kambaz (“comb”). Still used up to the 17th century, but replaced by kammen, which was re-formed from the noun.

From Middle Dutch kerel, carel, caerl, kerl, from Old Dutch *karl, *karal, *keril, from Proto-West Germanic *karil, from Proto-Germanic *karilaz. Cognate with German Kerl, Dutch Low Saxon keerl, West Frisian tsjirl, English churl, Danish karl.
From Middle Dutch kerke, from Old Dutch kirica, from Proto-West Germanic *kirikā, an early borrowing from Ancient Greek κυριακόν (kuriakón).

parole.significato: cress: a term used of various plants, chiefly but not solely of the family Brassicaceae (crucifers), particularly of th…
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch kerse, kersse, from Old Dutch *kersa, *kressa, from Proto-West Germanic *karsjā, *krassjā, from Proto-Germanic *krasjǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *gras-. Cognates include Sanskrit ग्रसति (grasati); related to English cress, German Kresse.
From Middle Dutch kerven, from Old Dutch *kervan, from Proto-West Germanic *kerban, from Proto-Germanic *kerbaną.

From Middle Dutch *kitte, from Old Dutch kitto (“fawn, kid”), from Proto-West Germanic *kittō (“fawn, chit”). Compare English chit. Compare also West Frisian kedde (“pony”), English, Swedish and Danish kid, German Kitz and Kitze, Albanian kedh and kec.

parole.significato: chain (a series of interconnected rings or links)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch kettinc, from the more common form ketene, from Old Dutch *ketinna, from ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *katinnjā, from Vulgar Latin *catenia, from Latin catēna.
From Middle Dutch cuekene, from Old Dutch *cukina, from Proto-West Germanic *kukinā, from Late Latin cocīna, from earlier coquīna.
From Middle Dutch core, cuere, from Old Dutch kuri, from Proto-West Germanic *kuʀi.

From a merger of: * Middle Dutch coren (“to test, to assess”), from Old Dutch coron, from Proto-West Germanic *koʀōn. Still found in the derived form bekoren. * Middle Dutch cueren (“to determine”), from Old Dutch *curien, from Proto-West Germanic *kuʀjan.
From Middle Dutch kever, from Old Dutch kevero, from Proto-West Germanic *kefrō. Akin to English chafer, German Käfer.
From Proto-West Germanic *kiukīn. Doublet with kuiken.

From Middle Dutch kietelen, ketelen, kittelen, kitelen, from Old Dutch *kitilon, from Proto-West Germanic *kitilōn, from Proto-Germanic *kitilōną, frequentative form of Proto-Germanic *kitōną (“to tickle”), from Proto-Indo-European *geyd- (“to stick, jab, tickle”). Cognate with Middle English kitele
From Middle Dutch kieuwe, from Old Dutch *kiowa, from Proto-West Germanic *keuwā.
From Middle Dutch kiesen, from Old Dutch *kiesan, from Proto-West Germanic *keusan, from Proto-Germanic *keusaną, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵews-.
From Middle Dutch kiken, from Old Dutch *kīkan, from Proto-West Germanic *kīkan, from Proto-Germanic *kīkaną.

parole.significato: to altercate, to dispute, to wrangle
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch kiven, from Old Dutch *kīvan, from Proto-West Germanic *kīban, from Proto-Germanic *kībaną.

From Middle Dutch kille, from Proto-Germanic *kaliz, related to Middle Dutch killen (“to be (ice) cold”). Related also to German Low German Köle, German kühl, Danish køle, Swedish kyla, Icelandic kylur, and English chill.

parole.significato: kill, waterway on sandflats or mud flats
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch kille, from Old Dutch *killa, from Proto-Germanic *kiljǭ, ultimately related to *kīnaną (“to crack, split”).

From Middle Dutch kimme (“rim of a barrel; curved sides of a ship”), from Old Dutch *kimba, from Proto-West Germanic *kimbu, related to Middle Low German kimme (“notch, outermost edge, horizon”), Middle English chimbe (“rim of a barrel”), West Frisian kym (“rim of a barrel, edge”), Swedish kim (“rod
From Middle Dutch kinne, from Old Dutch kinni, from Proto-West Germanic *kinnu, from Proto-Germanic *kinnuz, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵénus.

From Middle Dutch kint, from Old Dutch kint, from Proto-West Germanic *kind (“offspring”), from Proto-Germanic *kindą (“offspring”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵenh₁tóm (“that which is produced, that which is given birth to”), related to *ǵn̥h₁tós (“produced, given birth”), from *ǵenh₁- (“to produce,

parole.significato: lower jaw, jawbone, chin (now particularly of large or pronounced ones)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch kinnebacke, from Old Dutch kinnebaco; first element from the root of modern kin (“chin”), second element from Proto-West Germanic *bakka, a substrate word of unknown affiliation; compare Latin bucca (“cheek”) and Ancient Greek φαγών (phagṓn, “jaw”); if related to the latter, they c
From Middle Dutch kiste, from Old Dutch *kista, from Proto-West Germanic *kistu, from Latin cista, from Ancient Greek κίστη (kístē), from Proto-Indo-European *kisteh₂.
From Middle Dutch clagen, from Old Dutch clagon, from Proto-West Germanic *klagōn (“to lament, complain”).

parole.significato: clammy, damp, dank, moist and cool
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch clam, ultimately from or related to Proto-West Germanic *klaimijan (“to smear with clay”).

parole.significato: to clap (make sound or music with the hands)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch clappen, from Old Dutch *klappon, from Proto-West Germanic *klappōn.

parole.significato: A clover, trefoil; a plant of the tribe Trifolieae, particularly of the genus Trifolium
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch clavere, from Old Dutch *klēvara, from Proto-West Germanic *klaibrā.
From Middle Dutch cledinge, from Old Dutch *clēthunga, from Proto-West Germanic *klaiþungu, equivalent to kleden + -ing.

From Middle Dutch cleie, from Old Dutch *klei, from Proto-West Germanic *klaij, from Proto-Germanic *klajjaz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gley- (“to glue, stick together”). Compare German Klei, English clay.
Inherited from Middle Dutch cleine, from Old Dutch cleini, from Proto-West Germanic *klainī.
From Middle Dutch clemmen, from Old Dutch *klemmen, from Proto-West Germanic *klammjan.
From Middle Dutch cleppen, from Old Dutch *cleppen, from Proto-West Germanic *klappijan. Equivalent to klap (“clap”) + -en (“denominative”) and shows the effect of historical umlaut.

parole.significato: to stick, to be attached glue-like
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch clēven, from Old Dutch clivon, from Proto-West Germanic *klibēn, from Proto-Germanic *klibāną, from Proto-Indo-European *gleybʰ- (“to stick”).
From Middle Dutch clef, clif, from Old Dutch *klif, from Proto-West Germanic *klib, from Proto-Germanic *klibą.
From Middle Dutch climmen, from Old Dutch *climban, from Proto-West Germanic *klimban, from Proto-Germanic *klimbaną.

From early modern klokke, from Middle Dutch clocke, from Old Dutch *clocca, from Proto-West Germanic *klokkā, from Medieval Latin clocca, from Old Irish cloc, from Proto-Celtic *klokkos (“bell”), ultimately of onomatopoeic origin. In Early Modern Dutch, too, klokke still referred primarily to a bell
From Middle Dutch clove, from Proto-West Germanic *klubō, from Proto-Germanic *klubô, related to *kleubaną (“to split, cleave”). Cognate with German Klobe, Kloben, Cimbrian khlóop.
From Middle Dutch cluse, from Old Dutch *klūsa, from Proto-West Germanic *klūsā.
From Middle Dutch cluven, from Old Dutch *klūvon, from Proto-West Germanic *klūbōn. Originally a weak verb, it became strong by analogy with other verbs.

Thieves' slang, presumably related to Rotwelsch knök, kneks (“guilder”); in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries there was a small German coin called Knack(e), Knacker. Of uncertain origin: * The word seems to be related to the regular word for "bone" in Germanic dialects, e.g. Middle Dutch knook
From Middle Dutch cnāpe, from Old Dutch cnapo, from Proto-West Germanic *knappō.
From Middle Dutch cnagen, from Old Dutch *gnagan, *knagan, from Proto-West Germanic *gnagan, from Proto-Germanic *gnaganą.
From Middle Dutch knaken, probably ultimately related to Proto-West Germanic *knokōn (“to knock, beat on”).
From Middle Dutch cnecht, from Old Dutch cneht, from Proto-West Germanic *kneht.
From Middle Dutch cnēden, from Old Dutch *knedan, from Proto-West Germanic *knedan, from Proto-Germanic *knudaną.
From Middle Dutch cnuesen, from Old Dutch *cnusen, from Proto-West Germanic *knussjan.
From Middle Dutch cnie, from Old Dutch *cnio, from Proto-West Germanic *kneu, from Proto-Germanic *knewą, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵónu.
From Middle Dutch knipen, from Old Dutch *knīpen, from Proto-West Germanic *knīpan, from Proto-Germanic *knīpaną. Likely related to nijpen.

parole.significato: garlic (Allium sativum: the plant or its bulb, used in cooking)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch knofloick, knuuflooch, a dissimilated variant of earlier Middle Dutch cloffloc (literally “clove-leek”), from Old Dutch *kloflōk, from Proto-West Germanic *klobulauk (literally “clove-leek”), equivalent to klieven + look. Compare German Knoblauch, West Frisian knyflok and English c

From Middle Dutch cnokel, from Old Dutch *knukil, from Proto-West Germanic *knukil, from Proto-Germanic *knukilaz, a diminutive of *knukô (“bone”) (whence knook). Thus, it is synchronically equivalent to knook (“bone”) + -el (diminutive suffix). Compare English knuckle, German Knöchel, Knochen, Dani
From Middle Dutch cnōke, from Old Dutch *knoko, from Proto-West Germanic *knokō, from Proto-Germanic *knukô.

parole.significato: cow; a female of certain mammals, in particular bovines
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch coe, from Old Dutch cuo, from Proto-West Germanic *kō (“cow”), from Proto-Germanic *kōz (“cow”).
From Middle Dutch coel, from Old Dutch *kuol, from Proto-West Germanic *kōl(ī), from Proto-Germanic *kōlaz.

From Middle Dutch coelen, a merger of two Old Dutch verbs: * *cuolen (“make cooler”), from Proto-West Germanic *kōlijan, from Proto-Germanic *kōlijaną. * *cuolon (“become cooler”), from Proto-West Germanic *kōlēn. Equivalent to koel + -en.
From Middle Dutch coene, from Old Dutch *cuoni, from Proto-West Germanic *kōnī, from Proto-Germanic *kōniz, the root of which also yielded the Dutch verb kunnen.
Compound of koe (“cow”) + warm (“warm”); possibly inherited from a Proto-West Germanic *kūwarm, considering Old English cūwearm and German kuhwarm.
From Middle Dutch cof (“barn, stable”), related to koof (“curved”), from Old Dutch *kovo, from Proto-West Germanic *kobō, from Proto-Germanic *kubô (“hut, shed”). Also see kuif.
From Middle Dutch cōken, from Old Dutch *kokon, from Proto-West Germanic *kokōn.
From Middle Dutch colve, from Proto-West Germanic *kolbō, from Proto-Germanic *kulbaz (“round object”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“to form into a ball”).
From Middle Dutch colc, from Old Dutch *kolk, from Proto-West Germanic *kolk (“hollow, pit, gully”), from Proto-Germanic *kulukaz, an extension of *kelǭ (“throat”).
From Middle Dutch cōmen, from Old Dutch cuman, from Proto-West Germanic *kweman, from Proto-Germanic *kwemaną, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷem-.
From Middle Dutch conden, from Old Dutch cunden, from Proto-West Germanic *kunþijan, from Proto-Germanic *kunþijaną. By surface analysis, kond + -en.
From Middle Dutch cōninc, from Old Dutch cuninc, from Proto-West Germanic *kuning, from Proto-Germanic *kuningaz. Cognate to English king.

From Middle Dutch koninkrike, from Old Dutch *kuningrīki, from Proto-West Germanic *kuningarīkī, from Proto-Germanic *kuningarīkiją. Equivalent to koning + rijk. Compare German Königreich, Danish kongerige.
From Middle Dutch conte (“vagina”, also generally “sex organ”), from Old Dutch *kunta (“vagina”), from Proto-West Germanic *kuntā, from Proto-Germanic *kuntǭ. Compare English cunt.

From Middle Dutch cole, from Old Dutch *kol, *kolo, from Proto-West Germanic *kol, from Proto-Germanic *kulą, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷol-, from *ǵwelH- (“to burn, shine”). May originate from a neuter plurale tantum that was reanalysed as a feminine singular; compare Old Norse kol. Cognate with W

From Middle Dutch coon, from Old Dutch *koun, from Proto-West Germanic *kaun (“jaw, cheek”), from Proto-Germanic *kauną (“jaw, jawbone, cheek”), from Proto-Indo-European *gew- (“to bend, curve”). Cognate with West Frisian koan (“cheek”), Old Norse kaun (“sore, abscess”).
From Middle Dutch côopman, from Old Dutch kōpman, from Proto-West Germanic *kaupamann, equivalent to koop (“buy, trade”) + man.

From Middle Dutch coopmanscap, copenschap, possibly inherited from Proto-West Germanic [Term?]; compare Middle High German koufmanschaft (German Kaufmannschaft), Middle Low German kōpmanschop, English chapmanship, Old Frisian kapenskip (West Frisian keapmanskip). By surface analysis, koopman (“merch
From Middle Dutch côpen, from Old Dutch cōpon, from Proto-West Germanic *kaupōn, from Proto-Germanic *kaupōną, from Latin caupō.
From Middle Dutch copren, from Old Dutch *kuprīn, from Proto-West Germanic *kupprīn, equivalent to koper + -en.

From Middle Dutch koren, corn, from Old Dutch korn, coren, from Proto-West Germanic *korn, from Proto-Germanic *kurną, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵr̥h₂nóm. Compare Low German Koorn, German Korn, English corn, Danish korn. Doublet of graan.
From Middle Dutch corf, from Old Dutch *korf, from Proto-West Germanic *korb.
Inherited from Middle Dutch cort, from Old Dutch curt, from Proto-West Germanic *kurt, an early borrowing from Latin curtus.

From Middle Dutch cot, from Old Dutch *kot, from Proto-West Germanic *kot, from Proto-Germanic *kutą (“shed”). Cognate with English cot (“pen, coop”), the feminine stem variant Middle Dutch cote (Old Dutch kota) corresponds to German Kate (“hut”).
From older koude, from Middle Dutch coude, alteration (based on the adjective) of kelde, from Old Dutch *keldi, from Proto-West Germanic *kaldī. Cognate with German Kälte and English cold (noun).
From Middle Dutch cout, from Old Dutch calt, from Proto-West Germanic *kald, from Proto-Germanic *kaldaz, from Proto-Indo-European *gel-.

parole.significato: one of certain related birds of the genus Corvus or of the family Corvidae
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch crâye, from Old Dutch *krāia, from Proto-West Germanic *krāā, from Proto-Germanic *krēǭ.

parole.significato: to crow, make to sound of roosters and certain other birds
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch crâyen, from Old Dutch crāien, from Proto-West Germanic *krāan (“to crow, shout”).

From Middle Dutch crāne, from Old Dutch *crano, from Proto-West Germanic *kranō, from Proto-Germanic *kranô. The senses “tap” and “crane” as a machine are both based on resemblance with the bird's neck.
From Middle Dutch cracht, from Old Dutch craft, from Proto-West Germanic *kraftu, from Proto-Germanic *kraftuz.

From Middle Dutch crāken, from Old Dutch *krakon, from Proto-West Germanic *krakōn. The sense "to support a sports team or sportsperson" is a semantic loan from Sranan Tongo kraka (“to support (with a wedge)”).

parole.significato: staple (U-shaped metal fastener to bind materials together, for example to attach fence wire to posts)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch cramme, from Middle Dutch crimmen (“to catch, grab (with claws)”), from Proto-West Germanic *krimman.
From Middle Dutch cranc, from Old Dutch *cranc, from Proto-West Germanic *krank. Related to krenken (“to hurt”).

parole.significato: lobster, crayfish, used of certain members of the Pleocyemata
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch crevet, creeft, from Old Dutch *krevit, from Proto-West Germanic *krabit, from Proto-Germanic *krabitaz. Akin to German Krebs and Swedish kräfta.

parole.significato: a small inlet or gully of the sea, a creek (UK meaning)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch creke, from Old Dutch krika, from Proto-West Germanic *krikō, from Proto-Germanic *krikô.

From Middle Dutch crōke, perhaps related to Proto-West Germanic *krōk (“bend, hook”). Cognate with English crook, Middle Low German kroke, krake (“fold, wrinkle”), Danish krog (“crook, hook”), Swedish krok (“crook, hook”), Icelandic krókur (“hook”).
From Middle Dutch croken, from Old Dutch *krōkon, from Proto-West Germanic *krōkōn, equivalent to kreuk (“wrinkle”) + -en.
