From Middle Dutch malve, maluwe, from Old Dutch *malwa, from Proto-West Germanic *malwā, from Latin malva. Doublet of mauve.

parole.significato: man, human male, either adult or age-irrespective
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch man, from Old Dutch man, from Proto-West Germanic *mann, from Proto-Germanic *mann-.

parole.significato: basket (receptacle, traditionally made of wicker, now also frequently of plastic)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch mande, from Old Dutch *manda, from Proto-West Germanic *mandu.
From Middle Dutch mâre, from Old Dutch māri, from Proto-West Germanic *mārī (“story”).

parole.significato: a nocturnal monster or spirit that torments its victims while they are sleeping
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch māre (“incubus”), from Old Dutch *mara, from Proto-West Germanic *marā, from Proto-Germanic *marǭ.
From Middle Dutch maren, from Old Dutch *māren, from Proto-West Germanic *mārijan, from Proto-Germanic *mērijaną. Cognate with Old High German māren. Related to mare.

parole.significato: mast (pole on a ship, to which sails can be rigged)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch mast, from Old Dutch *mast, from Proto-West Germanic *mast, from Proto-Germanic *mastaz.
From Old Dutch mithi, stressed variant of mit (from which met), from Proto-West Germanic *midi, from Proto-Germanic *midi.
From Middle Dutch mēde, from Old Dutch *medu, *medo, from Proto-West Germanic *medu, from Proto-Germanic *meduz. Cognate of English mead.
From Middle Dutch mēle, Old Dutch *melo, Proto-West Germanic *melu, from Proto-Germanic *melwą.
From Middle Dutch mēre, from Old Dutch meri, from Proto-West Germanic *mari, from Proto-Germanic *mari, from Proto-Indo-European *móri.

parole.significato: grassland or meadow near water; marshy pasture
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch mersch, from Old Dutch *mersk, from Proto-West Germanic *marisk. Doublet of moeras.

parole.significato: tit, bird of the family Paridae
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch mêse, from Old Dutch *mēsa, from Proto-West Germanic *maisā, from Proto-Germanic *maisǭ (“chickadee, titmouse”).
From Middle Dutch meest, from Old Dutch *mēsto, from Proto-West Germanic *maist, from Proto-Germanic *maistaz. Cognates include German meist and English most.

parole.significato: a seagull, seabird of the family Laridae
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch mêwe, from Old Dutch *mēo, from Proto-West Germanic *maiwī, from Proto-Germanic *maiwaz.
Ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *meldā, from Proto-Germanic *meldǭ. Cognate to German Melde.

parole.significato: to report, to communicate; let know
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch melden, from Old Dutch *meldon (attested in maltho (“I declare”)), from Proto-West Germanic *melþōn.

parole.significato: milk (nutritious liquid produced by a lactating mammalian mother)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle Dutch melc, from Old Dutch miloc, from Proto-West Germanic *meluk, from Proto-Germanic *meluks, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂melǵ-.
From Middle Dutch melken, from Old Dutch *melkan, from Proto-West Germanic *melkan, from Proto-Germanic *melkaną, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂melǵ-.

parole.significato: to think; to have an opinion or assumption
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch mênen, from Old Dutch mēnen, from Proto-West Germanic *mainijan, from Proto-Germanic *mainijaną.
From Middle Dutch mengen, from Old Dutch *mengen, from Proto-West Germanic *mangijan.
From Middle Dutch menich, from Old Dutch *manag, *menig, from Proto-West Germanic *manag, from Proto-Germanic *managaz.

parole.significato: human, any member of the species Homo sapiens
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch mensche, from Old Dutch mennisko, a substantivised form of the adjective *mennisk (“human, humanlike”), from Proto-West Germanic *mannisk, from Proto-Germanic *manniskaz.
From Middle Dutch meren, from Old Dutch *mēron, from Proto-West Germanic *mairōn. Cognate with English moor.

From Middle Dutch march, from Old Dutch marg, *merg, from Proto-West Germanic *maʀg, from Proto-Germanic *mazgą, from Proto-Indo-European *mosgʰos. Cognate with Limburgish mérg, West Flemish mark, Zealandic merk, Old Saxon marg, Middle Low German marg, Plautdietsch Moakj, Old Frisian *march, West Fr
From Middle Dutch marc, merc, from Old Dutch marc, from Proto-West Germanic *mark, from Proto-Germanic *marką (“mark, sign”), cognate with English mark, German Mark.
From Middle Dutch merken, from Old Dutch merken, from Proto-West Germanic *markijan, from Proto-Germanic *markijaną.
From Middle Dutch mets, mes, contraction of *metses, from Old Dutch *metisas, *metsas, from Proto-West Germanic *matisahs (“food knife”).
From Middle Dutch messinc, from Proto-West Germanic *massing.

From Middle Dutch mest, from Old Dutch *mist, from Proto-West Germanic *mistu, from Proto-Germanic *mihstuz. Probably derived from *mīganą (“to urinate”) + *-þuz. Cognate with Old Saxon mist, Old High German mist, German Mist, Gothic 𐌼𐌰𐌹𐌷𐍃𐍄𐌿𐍃 (maihstus). More distantly related to Middle Dutch mes, m
From Middle Dutch mēten, from Old Dutch metan, from Proto-West Germanic *metan, from Proto-Germanic *metaną.
From Middle Dutch moesie, messie, muesie, diminutive of *meuse, *mose (whence West Flemish meuze), from Old Dutch *musi, from Proto-West Germanic *musi. Related to Gutnish mausa.
From Middle Dutch midden, from Old Dutch *middi, from Proto-West Germanic *midi, from Proto-Germanic *midjaz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *medʰyo-.
From Middle Dutch middewinter, from Old Dutch [Term?], from Proto-West Germanic *midiwintru. Equivalent to mid- + winter.
From Middle Dutch middesomer, from Old Dutch [Term?], from Proto-West Germanic *midisumar, from Proto-Germanic *midjasumaraz (“midsummer”). Equivalent to mid- + zomer.

From Middle Dutch meerrâdic. The second element of the compound derives from Proto-West Germanic *rādik (“radish”). The first element is of uncertain origin and is often held to be equivalent to meer (“more”) in a sense corresponding to Latin maior, with the original meaning then being "greater radi
From Middle Dutch mîden, from Old Dutch mīthan, from Proto-West Germanic *mīþan, from Proto-Germanic *mīþaną.
From Middle Dutch mijn, from Old Dutch mīn, from Proto-West Germanic *mīn, from Proto-Germanic *mīnaz.
From Middle Dutch min, minne, from Old Dutch minna, from Proto-West Germanic [Term?]; compare Old Frisian minne, Old Saxon minnia, Old High German minna (German Minne).
From Middle Dutch minnen, from Old Dutch minnon, from Proto-West Germanic *minnjōn, from Proto-Germanic *minjōną. Equivalent to min + -en.
From Middle Dutch mis, misse, from Old Dutch *missa, from Proto-West Germanic *missu (“failure, lack, mistake”).
From Middle Dutch misdadich, from Old Dutch *misdādig, from Proto-West Germanic *missadādīg, equivalent to misdaad + -ig.

parole.significato: medlar; any tree of the genus Mespilus, now Crataegus sect. Mespilus
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle Dutch mispele, mespele, from Old Dutch *mespila, from Proto-West Germanic *mespilā, from Late Latin mespila.
From Middle Dutch mistel, from Old Dutch *mistil, from Proto-West Germanic *mistil, from Proto-Germanic *mistilaz.

From moede with loss of -d-, from Middle Dutch moede (“tired, loath”), from Old Dutch muothi (“tired”), from Proto-West Germanic *mōþī, from Proto-Germanic *mōþaz. Cognate to German müde and Old English mēþe.
From Middle Dutch moet, from Old Dutch *muot, from Proto-West Germanic *mōd, from Proto-Germanic *mōdaz.
From Middle Dutch moeder, from Old Dutch muoder, from Proto-West Germanic *mōder, from Proto-Germanic *mōdēr, from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂tēr.
Inherited from Middle Dutch moeyen, inherited from Old Dutch *muoien, inherited from Proto-West Germanic *mōjan, inherited from Proto-Germanic *mōjaną.

From Middle Dutch moer (“morass”), from Old Dutch *mōr, from Proto-West Germanic *mōr, from Proto-Germanic *mōraz. Related to meer (“lake”). Cognate with English moor, Old English mōr (“moor, marsh”).
From Middle Dutch moerbeye, from Old Dutch *mōrberi, from Proto-West Germanic *mōrubaʀi.
From Middle Dutch moes, from Old Dutch muos, from Proto-West Germanic *mōs, from Proto-Germanic *mōsą.

parole.significato: to be necessary, to be required
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch moeten, from Old Dutch muotan, from Proto-West Germanic *mōtan, from Proto-Germanic *mōtaną. Cognate with English must, German müssen (“must”), and English mote (“may, might”). Unrelated to -moeten in ontmoeten.
From Middle Dutch mogen, from Old Dutch mugan, from Proto-West Germanic *magan, from Proto-Germanic *maganą, from Proto-Indo-European *magʰ-, *megʰ-.

parole.significato: mud fever (infection of a horse’s lower limb)
parole.testo: 17th century, a variant of muik, from Middle Dutch muke, muyke, from Proto-West Germanic *mūk-, *mukk-, perhaps from Proto-Germanic *mūkaz, from Proto-Indo-European *mewg- (“slimy, slippery”). Cognate with German Mauke, which see.

parole.significato: a mole, any insectivore of the family Talpidae
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch mol, from Old Dutch mol, mul, from Proto-West Germanic *mol, from Proto-Germanic *mulaz.
From Middle Dutch mont, from Old Dutch munt, from Proto-West Germanic *munþ, from Proto-Germanic *munþaz.
From Middle Dutch montvol, from Old Dutch *mundfoll, from Proto-West Germanic *munþafull, equivalent to mond + -vol. Compare English mouthful, German Mundvoll.
From Middle Dutch monic, from Old Dutch *monik, from Proto-West Germanic *munik. Compare German Mönch, English monk, West Frisian muonts.

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; Unknown; Possibly; perhaps; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch mooy, moy, from Old Dutch mōi (“beautiful, trim, neat”, attested in nicknames), further origin uncertain; possibly from Proto-West Germanic *mauwī (“clean, washed”), perhaps from Proto-Germanic *mawjaz, *maujaz, from Proto-Indo-European *mewH- (“to wet, wash”). Further etymology un

parole.significato: murder, a type of killing legally in a more severe degree than homicide
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch mort, from Old Dutch morth, from Proto-West Germanic *morþ, from Proto-Germanic *murþą, from Proto-Indo-European *mer- (“to die”).

From Middle Dutch morgen, from Old Dutch morgan, from Proto-West Germanic *morgin, *murgin, from Proto-Germanic *murganaz, from Proto-Indo-European *mr̥Hko (“to blink, twinkle”). Cognates Compare Low German Morgen, German Morgen, West Frisian moarn, English morn, morrow, Danish morgen, Swedish morgo

parole.significato: moss (small seedless plant(s) growing on surfaces)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch mos, from Old Dutch *mos, from Proto-West Germanic *mos, from Proto-Germanic *musą.

parole.significato: butterfly-like insect: moth (usually nocturnal insect of the order Lepidoptera)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch motte, from Proto-West Germanic *mottō, *moþþō, perhaps related to *muggju (“mosquito, midge”), or *maþō (“worm”). Cognate to English moth, German Motte.

From Middle Dutch malt, mout, from Old Dutch malt, from Proto-West Germanic *malt, from Proto-Germanic *maltą. Cognate with Limburgish maajt, Old Saxon malt, Middle Low German malt, German Low German Molt, Old Frisian malt, Saterland Frisian Moalt, Old English mealt, Middle English malt, English mal

parole.significato: a mosquito, a gnat, any fly of the suborder Nematocera except sometimes the larger tropical species (which are commonly…
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch mugge, from Old Dutch *mugga, from Proto-West Germanic *muggju, from Proto-Germanic *mugjō (“midge”). Compare Low German mügge, German Mücke, West Frisian mich, English midge, Danish myg.

parole.significato: a mule, an equine crossbreed between a stallion (horse) and a she-ass (donkey)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch muul, from Old Dutch *mūl, from Proto-West Germanic *mūl, from Latin mūlus.
From Middle Dutch muus, from Old Dutch *mūs, from Proto-West Germanic *mūs. The computing sense is a semantic loan from English mouse.

parole.significato: mousetrap (a device (contraption) for capturing or killing mice)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch muyseval, from Old Dutch *mūsfalla, from Proto-West Germanic *mūsfallā. Equivalent to muis (“mouse”) + -en- + val (“trap”).
From Middle Dutch munte, from Old Dutch munita, from late Proto-West Germanic *munit (“coin”).
From Middle Dutch mente, minte, from late Proto-West Germanic *mintā (“mint”), from Latin menta. Doublet of mint.

parole.significato: any of various small plants of the Caryophyllaceae family, particularly of genus Stellaria (chickweed) but also includi…
parole.testo: From Proto-West Germanic *meur-, of unknown origin, possibly a substrate word given the limited geographical distribution.
From Middle Dutch na, from Old Dutch *nāh, *nā, from Proto-West Germanic *nāhw, from Proto-Germanic *nēhw. Cognate to German nach and nahe.
From Middle Dutch na, from Old Dutch *nāh, *nā, from Proto-West Germanic *nāhw, from Proto-Germanic *nēhwaz.

parole.significato: a needle, a pin (for sewing, injections, tattooing etc.)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch naelde, from Old Dutch nālda, from a metathesis of earlier *nādla, from Proto-West Germanic *nāþlu, from Proto-Germanic *nēþlō. Compare the Old High German alternative form nālda, whence Luxembourgish Nol. Also cognate with German Nadel, English needle.

From Middle Dutch name, from Old Dutch namo, from Proto-West Germanic *namō, from Proto-Germanic *namô, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁nómn̥. Compare German Name, West Frisian namme, English name, Danish navn.

parole.significato: to, towards in time, space, consequence, purpose etc.
parole.testo: From earlier naer, from Middle Dutch nâer, from Old Dutch *nār, from Proto-West Germanic *nāhuriʀ(ō), from Proto-Germanic *nēhwiz. Originally the comparative of na, which is in Modern Dutch nader. Compare also English near, Swedish nära and när, and Danish & Norwegian nær and når.

From Middle Dutch naer, nare (“tight, sad”), from Old Dutch *naro (“narrow”), from Proto-West Germanic *naru, from Proto-Germanic *narwaz (“narrow, tight, constricted”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ner- (“turn, bend, twist, constrict”). Cognate with Low German naar (“ghastly, dismal”), Wes
Inherited from Middle Dutch nacht, from Old Dutch naht, from Proto-West Germanic *naht, from Proto-Germanic *nahts, from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts.
Inherited from Middle Dutch nachtegale, from Old Dutch *nahtagala, from Proto-West Germanic *nahtigalā.
From Middle Dutch nagaen, from Old Dutch nāgān, from Proto-West Germanic *nāhwagān. Equivalent to na (“after”) + gaan (“to go”). Cognate with German nachgehen.

parole.significato: a nail (on the fingers or toes)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch nāgel, from Old Dutch *nagal, from Proto-West Germanic *nagl, from Proto-Germanic *naglaz.

parole.significato: to nail, to fasten with nails
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch nāgelen, from Old Dutch *nagalen, from Proto-West Germanic *naglijan, from Proto-Germanic *naglijaną. Equivalent to nagel + -en.

parole.significato: to fulfill (one's promise), to carry out (an obligation)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch nacomen, from Old Dutch nākuman, from Proto-West Germanic *nāhwakweman. Equivalent to na + komen.

parole.significato: to check or verify information that one received earlier
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle Dutch nâlôpen, nâerlôpen, from Old Dutch *nālōpan, from Proto-West Germanic *nāhwahlaupan. Equivalent to na (“after”) + lopen (“to walk”). Cognate with German nachlaufen.
From Middle Dutch nat, from Old Dutch nat, from Proto-West Germanic *nat, from Proto-Germanic *nataz.

parole.significato: to succeed, to come after, to follow (an example)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch navolgen, from Old Dutch *nāfolgon, from Proto-West Germanic *nāhwafolgēn. Equivalent to na + volgen. Cognate with German nachfolgen.

From Middle Dutch nēder, from Old Dutch *nithar, from Proto-West Germanic *niþer, from Proto-Germanic *niþer, from Proto-Indo-European *niter. Cognates include German nieder, English nether and Luxembourgish nidder.
From Middle Dutch nēve, from Old Dutch *nefo, nevo, from Proto-West Germanic *nefō, from Proto-Germanic *nefô, from Proto-Indo-European *népōts. Doublet of niffo.

parole.significato: no; stressed or formal form of nee
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch neen, from Old Dutch nēn (“none, not one”), from Proto-West Germanic *nain, from Proto-Germanic *nainaz, from Proto-Germanic *ne + *ainaz. Cognate with English none, German nein.

From Middle Dutch nēgen, from Old Dutch nigun, from Proto-West Germanic *neun, from Proto-Germanic *newun, reflecting earlier *newunt, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥, with -t added through influence of "ten".
From Middle Dutch nēgende, from Old Dutch *nigundo, from Proto-West Germanic *neundō, from Proto-Germanic *newundô.

parole.significato: to tend, incline (to show a tendency)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch neigen, from Old Dutch neigen, from Proto-West Germanic *hnaigijan, from Proto-Germanic *hnaigijaną, the causative of nijgen. The weak verb adopted most intransitive uses from strong nijgen in modern Dutch, the latter being restricted to “bowing as a sign of respect”. Compare howev
From Middle Dutch nacke, necke, from Old Dutch *nakko, from Proto-West Germanic *hnakkō.

parole.significato: to take, to take hold of, to grasp or grab
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch nēmen, from Old Dutch neman, from Proto-West Germanic *neman, from Proto-Germanic *nemaną, from Proto-Indo-European *nem-. Compare English nim.

parole.significato: a nest (place to hatch young, especially bird structure)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch nest, from Old Dutch nest, from Proto-West Germanic *nest, from Proto-Germanic *nestą. Cognate with English, German Nest etc.
From Middle Dutch nastel, nestele, nestel, from Old Dutch nastila, *nestila, from Proto-West Germanic *nastilu.
From Middle Dutch netele, from Old Dutch *netila, from Proto-West Germanic *natilā.

From Middle Dutch netel (“malicious, angry”), from Old Dutch *nitul, from Proto-West Germanic *hnitul, from Proto-Germanic *hnitulaz + -ig. Often superficially interpreted as deriving from netel (“nettle”), which may however be completely unrelated etymologically.

Inherited from Middle Dutch *noken, from Old Dutch *nuken, from Proto-West Germanic *hnukēn, from Proto-Germanic *hnukāną (“to bend; flex; clump together”), with a special sense development in North Germanic, Old Dutch, and Old Saxon of "push, thrust, bump", from Proto-Indo-European *knewg- (“to pre
From Middle Dutch nose, nuese, from Old Dutch *nosa, from Proto-West Germanic *nosu.

parole.significato: female cousin; daughter of someone's uncle or aunt
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch nichte, from Old Dutch *nift, from Proto-West Germanic *nifti, from Proto-Germanic *niftiz, from Proto-Indo-European *néptih₂.

parole.significato: not, no, don't: used to express negation.
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch niwet, niet, from Old Dutch *niowiht, niewiht, from Proto-West Germanic *naiwwiht, essentially nio (“never”) + wiht (“thing, creature”). The former in turn derives from Proto-Germanic *ne (“not”) + *aiw- (“ever”) + *wihtą (“thing”). It was originally a pronoun meaning "not a thing"
From Middle Dutch niewe, from Old Dutch niuwi, from Proto-West Germanic *niwi, from Proto-Germanic *niwjaz, from Proto-Indo-European *néwyos.

From Middle Dutch niesen, from Old Dutch *niesan, from Proto-West Germanic *hneusan, from Proto-Germanic *hneusaną. Because of the onomatopoeic character of the word, variant forms with different initial consonants also exist(ed), such as fniezen (from Proto-Germanic *fneusaną) and English sneeze.
From Middle Dutch nijt, from Old Dutch nīth, from Proto-West Germanic *nīþ, from Proto-Germanic *nīþą. Cognate with German Neid.

parole.significato: to envy, to be jealous of
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch niden, from Old Dutch nīthen, from Proto-West Germanic *nīþijan, from Proto-Germanic *nīþijaną. Equivalent to nijd + -en.
From Middle Dutch nigen, from Old Dutch *nīgan, from Proto-West Germanic *hnīgan, from Proto-Germanic *hnīganą, *hnīwaną. Cognate with Old English hnigan, Old Norse hníga (Swedish niga).
From Middle Dutch nipen, from Old Dutch *nīpen, from Proto-West Germanic *hnīpan, from Proto-Germanic *hnīpaną. Likely related to knijpen.

From Middle Dutch nochdan, from Old Dutch *nohthan, from Proto-West Germanic *nohþan, from Proto-Germanic *nuhþan. Compare Gothic 𐌽𐌰𐌿𐌷𐌸𐌰𐌽 (nauhþan, “still, yet”), Old High German noh danne (“yet”), Old Saxon nohthan (“yet”), and the similarly formed German dennoch (“anyhow”).

From Middle Dutch noch, from Old Dutch noh (“until now, still”), from Proto-West Germanic *noh, from Proto-Germanic *nuh (“still”, literally “now too”), from Proto-Indo-European *nu (“now”) + *-kʷe- (“and, also”).

parole.significato: emergency, crisis, distress (often used in compounds)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch nôot, from Old Dutch *nōd, from Proto-West Germanic *naudi, from Proto-Germanic *naudiz.
From Middle Dutch nort, from Old Dutch *nord, from Proto-West Germanic *norþr, from Proto-Germanic *nurþrą. Compare German Nord, West Frisian noard, English north, Danish nord.
From Middle Dutch nōte, from Old Dutch *nutu, from Proto-West Germanic *hnut, from Proto-Germanic *hnuts.
From Middle Dutch nou, a variant of nu, from Old Dutch nu, from Proto-West Germanic *nū, from Proto-Germanic *nu.

parole.significato: a knot or knurl in a tree or wood; gnarl
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch *oest (attested only with proclitic n as noest), from Old Dutch *uost, *ōst, from Proto-West Germanic *ōst.
From Middle Dutch offer, offere, from Old Dutch *offar, from Proto-West Germanic *offr. By surface analysis, deverbal from offeren (“to sacrifice”).
From Middle Dutch offeren, from Old Dutch offeron, from Proto-West Germanic *offrōn, from Latin offerō. Doublet of offreren.
From Middle Dutch and Old Dutch ôgen, from Proto-West Germanic *augijan. Equivalent to oog + -en.
From Middle Dutch ombe, omme, from Old Dutch umbi, umbe, from Proto-West Germanic *umbi.
From Middle Dutch on-, from Old Dutch un-, from Proto-West Germanic *un-, from Proto-Germanic *un-, from Proto-Indo-European *n̥-.
From Middle Dutch onde, from Old Dutch *unthia, from Proto-West Germanic *unþi, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *unþī. Cognate to German Unde.
From Middle Dutch onder, from Old Dutch under, from Proto-West Germanic *undar, from Proto-Germanic *under. Cognate with Old Saxon undar, German unter, English under.
From Middle Dutch ondervangen, ondervaen, from Old Dutch underfān, from Proto-West Germanic *undarfą̄han. Equivalent to onder- + vangen. Cognate to German unterfangen.
From Middle Dutch *ônen, from Old Dutch *ōnon, from Proto-West Germanic *aunōn, from Proto-Germanic *aunōną.
From Middle Dutch ongehoorsam, from Old Dutch *ungihōrsam, from Proto-West Germanic *ungahauʀisam. Equivalent to on- + gehoorzaam.
From Middle Dutch ongehoorsamheit, from Old Dutch *ungihōrsamhēd, from Proto-West Germanic *ungahauʀisamahaidu. Equivalent to ongehoorzaam + -heid.

From Middle Dutch ongehiere, from Old Dutch *ungihiuri, from Proto-West Germanic *ungahiurī (see also *unhiurī). The unprefixed form of this word still existed in Middle Dutch as ghehure, meaning "pleasant". Compare German ungeheuer. Possibly related to eunjer (“wizard”).
From Middle Dutch onlust, from Old Dutch *unlust, from Proto-West Germanic *unlustu, from Proto-Germanic *unlustuz. By surface analysis, on- + lust.

parole.significato: powerlessness, the state of lacking power
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch onmacht, from Old Dutch *unmaht, from Proto-West Germanic [Term?], from Proto-Germanic *unmahtiz. By surface analysis, on- + macht.
From Middle Dutch onmachtich, from Old Dutch unmahtig, from Proto-West Germanic [Term?], from Proto-Germanic *unmahtīgaz. By surface analysis, onmacht + -ig or on- + machtig.
From Middle Dutch onreine, from Old Dutch unreini, from Proto-West Germanic *unhrainī, from Proto-Germanic *unhrainiz. Equivalent to on- + rein.
From Middle Dutch onscerp, onscarp, from Old Dutch *unskarp, from Proto-West Germanic *unskarp, equivalent to on- + scherp.

parole.significato: un-, de-; forms verbs meaning to negate, remove or separate.
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch ont-, from Old Dutch ant-, from Proto-West Germanic *anda-, from Proto-Germanic *andi-, *anda-, *and-.
From Middle Dutch ontbēren, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *beran, from Proto-Germanic *beraną (“to bear”). Equivalent to ont- + beren, see also baren.

From Middle Dutch entfarmen, ontfarmen, from Old Dutch *intfarmon, with two prefixes ont- and af attached to Proto-West Germanic *armēn, from Proto-Germanic *armāną (“to pity”). The word erbarmen derives from the same source, via Old High German and with a different prefix. Related to arm (“poor”).

parole.significato: to pay for, to suffer for, cop it, get some stick for
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch *ontgelden, from Old Dutch antgeldan, from Proto-West Germanic *andageldan. By surface analysis, ont- + gelden.

From Middle Dutch ontmoeten, untmuten, entmuten, from ont- + moeten. The latter verb is from Old Dutch *muoten, from Proto-West Germanic *mōtijan, from Proto-Germanic *mōtijaną (“to meet”) and is unrelated to modern Dutch moeten (“to have to, must”). The unprefixed form is cognate to Low German möte
From Middle Dutch ontrouwe, from Old Dutch *untriuwi, from Proto-West Germanic *untriuwī, from Proto-Germanic *untriwwiz. Equivalent to on- + trouw.
From Middle Dutch ontrouwe, from Old Dutch *untriuwa, from Proto-West Germanic *untreuwu; compare German Untreue, Old English untrēow. Equivalent to on- + trouw.

From Middle Dutch onvrēde, from Old Dutch *unfrithu, from Proto-West Germanic *unfriþu, from Proto-Germanic *unfriþuz. By surface analysis, on- + vrede. Compare to English fray ("conflict, quarrel, heated argument,") which derives by aphesis from affray—an Old French loan—ultimately equivalent to a

From Middle Dutch onvri; from Old Dutch [Term?], from Proto-West Germanic *unfrī; cognates include Middle High German unfrī (German unfrei), Middle Low German unvrī, Middle English unfre (English unfree). By surface analysis, on- + vrij.
Inherited from Middle Dutch ovet, from Old Dutch ovit, from Proto-West Germanic *obaet, from Proto-Germanic *ubetą or *ubatją.
From Middle Dutch ôge, from Old Dutch ōga, from Proto-West Germanic *augā (“eye”), Proto-Germanic *augô, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ekʷ- (“eye; to see”).

parole.significato: apple of someone's eye (someone or something dear)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch ogeappel, from Old Dutch *ougappul, from Proto-West Germanic *augapl. Equivalent to oog + appel. Related to German Augapfel (“eyeball”).

From oog (“eye”) + taal (“hair”); this meaning of taal is long-obsolete in modern Dutch and derives from Proto-West Germanic *tagl (“hair, tail”). It is thus cognate with English tail, and etymologically distinct from the common word taal meaning "language".

From Middle Dutch ooi, ou, from Old Dutch *ōi, from Proto-West Germanic *awi, from Proto-Germanic *awiz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ówis. Compare German Aue, West Frisian ei, English ewe. Unrelated to ooibos (“riparian forest”).
From Middle Dutch ôoc, from Old Dutch ōk, from Proto-West Germanic *auk, from Proto-Germanic *auk. Compare German auch.
From Middle Dutch oom, from Old Dutch *ōm, from Proto-West Germanic *auhaim (“maternal uncle”).

From Middle Dutch ore, from Old Dutch ōra, from Proto-West Germanic *auʀā, from the voiced Verner alternant of Proto-Germanic *ausô, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ows-. Compare German Ohr, West Frisian ear, English ear, Danish øre.

parole.significato: A prefix with a variety of meanings, but originally meaning "out" or "original".
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch or-, oor-, from Old Dutch ur-, or-, from Proto-West Germanic *uʀ-, from Proto-Germanic *uz-. Related to oer-.
From Middle Dutch ort, oort, from Old Dutch ort, from Proto-West Germanic *oʀd, from Proto-Germanic *uzdaz.

From Middle Dutch orloven (first attested 1201), which could have been a new formation based on the elements or- + loven (“to praise”) and influenced by oorlof (“permission”). Otherwise, if inherited, from Old Dutch *irlouven, from Proto-West Germanic *uʀlaubijan, from Proto-Germanic *uzlaubijaną (“
From Middle Dutch oost, from Old Dutch ōst, from Proto-West Germanic *austr, from Proto-Germanic *austrą. Compare German Ost, English and West Frisian east, Norwegian aust. Doublet of Dutch oosten.
From Middle Dutch oost, from Old Dutch ōst, from Proto-West Germanic *austr, from Proto-Germanic *austrą. Doublet of Dutch oost.
From Middle Dutch ōpen, from Old Dutch opan, from Proto-West Germanic *opan, from Proto-Germanic *upanaz.
From Middle Dutch ōpenen, from Old Dutch opanon, from Proto-West Germanic *opanōn, from Proto-Germanic *upanōną. Equivalent to open + -en.
From Middle Dutch oprecht, from Old Dutch [Term?], from Proto-West Germanic [Term?]; compare English upright, German aufrecht, West Frisian oprjocht. By surface analysis, op + recht.
From Middle Dutch otter, from Old Dutch *ottar, from Proto-West Germanic *otr.

parole.significato: old (having existed for a relatively long period of time)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch out, from Old Dutch alt, from Proto-West Germanic *ald, from Proto-Germanic *aldaz, from Proto-Indo-European *altós, *h₂eltós, from *h₂el- (“grow, nourish”). Compare German alt, West Frisian âld, Low German old, olt, oll, English old.
From Middle Dutch ouder, from Old Dutch aldar, from Proto-West Germanic *aldr, from Proto-Germanic *aldrą.
From Middle Dutch ōven, from Old Dutch *ovan, from Proto-West Germanic *ofn, from Proto-Germanic *ufnaz.

From Middle Dutch ōver, from Old Dutch *ovar, from Proto-West Germanic *obar, from Proto-Germanic *uber, from Proto-Indo-European *upér, from *upo. Compare German ober, über, Low German over, över, English over.
From Middle Dutch pert, pāert, from Old Dutch *pered, *perid, from Proto-West Germanic *parafred, from Late Latin paraverēdus. Compare German Pferd. Doublet of palefroot.

parole.significato: lease (in particular of land and immovable goods)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch pacht, Old Dutch *paht, from Proto-West Germanic [Term?], from Latin pactum. Cognates include Old High German pfāht, Old Frisian pacht; the effects of the Germanic spirant law in these words and the effects of the High German consonant shift in the High German cognate in particular
From Middle Dutch pat, from Old Dutch path, from Proto-West Germanic *paþ, from Proto-Germanic *paþaz (“path”). Cognate with English path, West Frisian paad and German Pfad.

parole.significato: toad (an amphibian of the order Anura similar to a frog with shorter legs and more ragged skin)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch padde, pedde, from Old Dutch *padda, from Proto-West Germanic *paddā, from Proto-Germanic *paddǭ (“toad”). Cognates Cognate with Old English padde (compare English paddock), Old Norse padda (Swedish padda, Danish/Norwegian padde).
From Middle Dutch pac, from Old Dutch *pakko, from Proto-West Germanic *pakkō, from Proto-Germanic *pakkô.
From Middle Dutch panne, from Old Dutch *panna, from Proto-West Germanic *pannā, from Proto-Germanic *pannǭ (“pan”).

parole.significato: A peacock, a fowl of the genus Pavo.
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch pau, pauwe, from Old Dutch *pauwo, from Proto-Germanic *pāwô, from Latin pāvō, likely from Ancient Greek ταώς (taṓs), of uncertain further origin.
From Middle Dutch pēgel, from Old Dutch *pegil, from Proto-West Germanic *pagil. Doublet of peil.
From Middle Dutch peyl, a Hollandic variant of peghel, from Old Dutch pegil, from Proto-West Germanic *pagil. Doublet of pegel (“icicle”).

parole.significato: pitch (sticky substance used as an adhesive and sealant)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle Dutch pec, from Old Dutch pek, from Proto-West Germanic *pik, from Latin pīx. Cognate with German Pech (from which Dutch pech), English pitch.
From Middle Dutch poluwe, from Old Dutch *puluwī, from Proto-West Germanic *pulwī, from Latin pulvīnus.

parole.significato: pepper (Piper nigrum or the spice obtained from its berries)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch peper, from Old Dutch *pipar, *pepar, from Proto-West Germanic *pipar, from Latin piper, from Ancient Greek πέπερι (péperi), from an Indo-Aryan language.
From Middle Dutch perseke, from Old Dutch *persika, from Proto-West Germanic *persik, ultimately borrowed from Late Latin persicum, persica.
From Middle Dutch pijl, pile, from Old Dutch pīl, from Proto-West Germanic *pīl (“missile, arrow”), from Latin pīlum (“javelin, spear”).
From Middle Dutch pine, from Old Dutch *pīna, from Proto-West Germanic *pīnā.
From Middle Dutch pijn, from Proto-West Germanic *pīnā.
From Middle Dutch pîpe, from Old Dutch *pīpa, from Proto-West Germanic *pīpā and Vulgar Latin *pipa, both from Latin pipō.

parole.significato: to fellate, to blow, to suck (the object usually indicates the receiving person, but sometimes the member or item under…
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch pipen (“to play a wind instrument, to pipe”), from Old Dutch *pīpan, from Proto-West Germanic *pīpan. Perhaps equivalent to pijp + -en.
From Middle Dutch picke, from Old Dutch *pīk, from Proto-West Germanic *pīk (“pickaxe, sharp point”).

parole.significato: to peck (as with a bird's beak), hammer
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch picken, from Old Dutch *pikken, from Proto-West Germanic *pikkōn. Cognate with English prick; see there for more details.

From Middle Dutch pinne, from Old Dutch *pinna, from Proto-West Germanic *pinnā, of obscure origin. Cognate with English pin, Low German pin, pinne (“pin, point, nail, peg”), German Pinn, Pinne (“pin, tack, peg”), Bavarian Pfonzer, Pfunzer (“sharpened point”), Danish pind (“pin, pointed stick”), Nor

From Middle Dutch plien, later plēgen, originally a class 4 strong verb. Presumably from Old Dutch *plian, from Proto-West Germanic *plehan (“to vouch for”). However, the form plegan already occurs in Old Dutch with -g-, and likewise for Old Saxon plegan and Old High German pflegan, so it is not cer

From Middle Dutch plecke, from Old Dutch *plekka (“mark, spot, place”), from Proto-West Germanic *plakkju, from Proto-Germanic *plakjō (“spot, stain”). Cognate with Middle Low German plecke (“spot, mark”), English pleck (“spot, place”). More at English pleck.
From Middle Dutch pletten, from Old Dutch *pletten, from Proto-West Germanic *plattjan. Equivalent to plat (“flat”) + -en (“deadjectival”) and shows the effect of historical umlaut.
From Middle Dutch plicht, from Old Dutch *pliht, from Proto-West Germanic *plihti. Equivalent to plegen (“to commit”) + -t (“verbal noun”).

parole.significato: to pluck (i.e. to pull something sharply or to pull something out)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch plucken, from Old Dutch *plukkon, from Proto-West Germanic *plukkōn, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *plukkōną, *plukkijaną; see there for more.

parole.significato: a standing body of water; pool, puddle
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch poel, from Old Dutch *puol, from Proto-West Germanic *pōl, from Proto-Germanic *pōlaz.

parole.significato: unit of mass, often broadly similar to 500 grams
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch pont, pond, from Old Dutch punt, from Proto-West Germanic *pund, from Proto-Germanic *pundą (“pound, weight”), borrowed from Latin pondō.

parole.significato: to set, plant, place a young plant or large seed individually in soil or other substrate where it can grow; sow
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch pōten, from Old Dutch *poton, from Proto-West Germanic *putōn, from Proto-Germanic *putōną.
From Middle Dutch prangen, from Old Dutch *prangan, from Proto-West Germanic *prangan, from Proto-Germanic *pranganą. Cognate with Gothic 𐌰𐌽𐌰𐍀𐍂𐌰𐌲𐌲𐌰𐌽 (anapraggan).

From Middle Dutch *prettig (attested only in form pertich (“smart, cunning, swift, lively, pert”) > Dutch pertig (“ill-tempered, disturbed, quirky”), West Flemish pertig (“cute, nice, pretty, graceful”)), from Old Dutch *prettig, *prattig, from Proto-West Germanic *prattīg, from Proto-Germanic *prat

parole.significato: a plum tree, one of certain trees of the genus Prunus, especially Prunus domestica
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch prume, from Old Dutch *prūma. A variant of *plūma, from Proto-West Germanic *plūmā, from Latin prūnum, from Ancient Greek προῦμνον (proûmnon).
From Middle Dutch put, from Old Dutch *putti, from Proto-West Germanic *puti (“a well”), borrowed from Latin puteus.

parole.significato: spar (horizontal beam or pole of a ship's mastwork)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch ra, from Old Dutch *rā, from Proto-West Germanic *rahu, from Proto-Germanic *rahō. Cognate with German Rah, Old Norse rá.
From Middle Dutch râet, from Old Dutch rāt, from Proto-West Germanic *rād, from Proto-Germanic *rēdaz.
From Middle Dutch raetsel, from Old Dutch *rādisli, from Proto-West Germanic *rādislī. Equivalent to raden + -sel.

From Middle Dutch rāve, formed by rebracketing from the older singular form rāven which was reinterpreted as a plural; the singular raven (plural ravens or ravenen) persisted in some dialects until at least the eighteenth century, well beyond the Middle Dutch period. The Middle Dutch furthermore des
From Middle Dutch rāke, from Old Dutch *raka, from Proto-West Germanic [Term?], from Proto-Germanic *rakō; compare riek.

parole.significato: wheel (a circular device facilitating movement or transportation)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch rat, from Old Dutch *rath, from Proto-West Germanic *raþ, from Proto-Germanic *raþą, from Proto-Indo-European *Hret-.
From Middle Dutch rat, from Old Dutch *rath, *rad, from Proto-West Germanic *hraþ, *hrad, from Proto-Germanic *hradaz, *hraþaz, from Proto-Indo-European *kret-.
From Middle Dutch râden, from Old Dutch rādan, from Proto-West Germanic *rādan, from Proto-Germanic *rēdaną.
From Middle Dutch rāken, from Old Dutch *racon, from Proto-West Germanic *rakōn.
From Middle Dutch ranc, from Old Dutch *ranc, from Proto-West Germanic *rank, from Proto-Germanic *rankaz.

From Middle Dutch ranc, ranke, from Old Dutch *ranca, from Proto-West Germanic [Term?], probably ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *hrinkwaną (“to curl, bend”). Cognate with Old High German hranca (German Ranke).

From Middle Dutch ratele, a compound of râte (“honeycomb”) and -ele. The suffix is ultimately from Proto-Germanic *-ilaz (agent/instrumental/diminutive suffix), and râte (now raat) is ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *hrātu (“honeycomb”), which is probably inherited from Proto-Germanic *hrētō-.
From Middle Dutch rou, raeu, also roo, from Old Dutch *rao, *rō, from Proto-West Germanic *hrau, from Proto-Germanic *hrawaz, from Proto-Indo-European *krewh₂-.
From Middle Dutch râsen, from Old Dutch *rāson, from Proto-West Germanic *rāsōn, from Proto-Germanic *rēsōną.
From Middle Dutch recht, from Old Dutch reht, from Proto-West Germanic *rehta, from Proto-Germanic *rehtą, a substantive derivation of the adjective.

From Middle Dutch redden, from Old Dutch *redden, from Proto-West Germanic *hraddjan, from Proto-Germanic *hradjaną. Equivalent to rad (“quick”) + -en (“deadjectival”) and shows the effect of historical umlaut.
From Middle Dutch ree, from Old Dutch rēa, from Proto-West Germanic *raihō, from Proto-Germanic *raihô.

parole.significato: line drawn on the ground, furrow
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch rīven, from Proto-West Germanic *rīfan.

parole.significato: a strip, resulting from ripping, cutting etc.
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch rep, reep, from Old Dutch reip, rēp, from Proto-West Germanic *raip, from Proto-Germanic *raipaz (“rope, cord, band, ringlet”), from Proto-Indo-European *roypnós (“strap, band, rope”). Cognates Cognate with Low German Reep, German Reif (“ring, hoop”), West Frisian reap, English rop
From Middle Dutch rēgen, from Old Dutch regan, from Proto-West Germanic *regn, from Proto-Germanic *regną.
From Middle Dutch regenboge, from Old Dutch *reganbogo, from Proto-West Germanic *regnabogō, from Proto-Germanic *regnabugô (“rainbow”), equivalent to regen (“rain”) + boog (“bow”).
From Middle Dutch rēgenen, from Old Dutch *reganon, from Proto-West Germanic *regnōn, from Proto-Germanic *regnōną. Equivalent to regen + -en.

First attested 1563. From Middle Dutch *regenworm, from Old Dutch *reganwurm, from Proto-West Germanic *regnawurmi (see there for cognates). By surface analysis, regen (“rain”) + worm (“worm”), so called because of the animal's habit of surfacing after rainfall.

parole.significato: to reach, to extend out, to stretch
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch reiken, from Old Dutch *reiken, from Proto-West Germanic *raikijan, from Proto-Germanic *raikijaną.
From Middle Dutch reine, from Old Dutch reini, from Proto-West Germanic *hrainī, from Proto-Germanic *hrainiz.

From Middle Dutch rêse, reise, from Old Dutch *rēsa, from Proto-West Germanic *raisu. Distantly related to English rise and raise. The form with -ei- is expected only in south-eastern dialects; several sources suspect that it was reinforced by Middle High German reise, modern German Reise.
From Middle Dutch reisen, from Old Dutch *reison, from Proto-West Germanic *raisōn.
From Middle Dutch recken, from Old Dutch *rekken, from Proto-West Germanic *rakkjan, from Proto-Germanic *rakjaną (“to stretch, to straighten”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃roǵéyeti.

From Middle Dutch remmen, from Old Dutch *remmen, from Proto-West Germanic *hrammjan, from Proto-Germanic *hramjaną. Historically derived from raam (“window, framework”) + -en (“denominative”) affected by umlaut. However, most speakers won't perceive this assocation and would rather derive the verb

parole.significato: to bring up, to mention (often used with van or over)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch reppen (“to set in motion, to touch”), from Old Dutch *reppen, from Proto-West Germanic *hrappijan, from Proto-Germanic *hrappijaną.
From Middle Dutch ruese, rose, rese, from Old Dutch *riso, *risi, from Proto-West Germanic *risi, from Proto-Germanic *risiz (“giant”). Cognate to German Riese (“giant”) and Old Norse risi (“giant”).

From Middle Dutch richten, from Old Dutch rihten, from Proto-West Germanic *rihtijan, from Proto-Germanic *rihtijaną (“to right”), derived from *rehtaz (“right, straight”). Equivalent to recht (“right, straight”) + -en (“deadjectival”) and shows the effect of historical i-mutation.
From Middle Dutch riec, from Old Dutch *reko, from Proto-West Germanic *rekō, from Proto-Germanic *rekô (“rake”). Compare raak (“rake”).
From Middle Dutch rieken, from Old Dutch riecan, from Proto-West Germanic *reukan, from Proto-Germanic *reukaną. Doublet of ruiken. Cognate to English reek.
From Middle Dutch rieme, from Old Dutch *riemo, *riomo, from Proto-West Germanic *reumō.
From Middle Dutch rieme, from Old Dutch *riemo, from Proto-West Germanic *rēmō, borrowed from Latin rēmus.
From Middle Dutch riet, from Old Dutch riet, ried, *riod, from Proto-West Germanic *hreud (“reed”).

parole.significato: corpse, dead animal body of esp. a human, particularly when already significantly decomposed
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch rijf, from Old Dutch ref (“belly; womb”), from Proto-West Germanic *hrif, from Proto-Germanic *hrefaz (“body; torso; belly”), from Proto-Indo-European *krep- (“body”).
From Middle Dutch rië, from Old Dutch *rīa, from Proto-West Germanic *rīhu, *rīgu. Cognate with German Reihe.
From Middle Dutch riden, from Old Dutch rīdan, from Proto-West Germanic *rīdan, from Proto-Germanic *rīdaną, from Proto-Indo-European *reydʰ-.

parole.significato: to pierce, to impale, to spit
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch rien, rigen, from Old Dutch *rīan, from Proto-West Germanic *rīhan, from Proto-Germanic *rīhaną.

From Middle Dutch rike, rijc, from Old Dutch *rīki, from Proto-West Germanic *rīkī, from Proto-Germanic *rīkijaz (“mighty”), from *rīks, from Proto-Celtic *rīxs (“king”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃rḗǵs (“king”).

parole.significato: a realm, kingdom ruled by a monarch
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch rike, from Old Dutch rīki, from Proto-West Germanic *rīkī, from Proto-Germanic *rīkiją (“realm”), from Proto-Celtic *rīgyom (“kingdom”), from *rīxs (“king”) (compare Irish rí), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃rḗǵs (“king”).

parole.significato: to rhyme (to have a rhyme with another word)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle Dutch rīmen which is a merger of: * Old Dutch *rīman, from Proto-West Germanic *rīman, from Proto-Germanic *rīmaną (“to count”), a strong verb. * Old Dutch *rīmen, from Proto-West Germanic *rīmijan, a weak verb. Analysable as rijm + -en. In Middle Dutch the verb could still be
From Middle Dutch ripe, from Old Dutch rīpi, from Proto-West Germanic *rīpī, from Proto-Germanic *rīpiz.

From Middle Dutch ripe, from Old Dutch *rīpo, from Proto-West Germanic *hrīpō. Cognate with Old Saxon hrīpo, Old High German hrīfo (German Reif). Likely related with (and possibly from the oblique stem of) Proto-Germanic *hrīmô, whence Dutch rijm, English rime.
From Middle Dutch ripen, from Old Dutch *rīpon, from Proto-West Germanic *rīpēn. By surface analysis, rijp (“ripe”) + -en.
From Middle Dutch rijs, from Old Dutch rīs, from Proto-West Germanic *hrīs, from Proto-Germanic *hrīsą. Cognate with German Reis “twig”, Old Norse hrís, Dansish, Norwegian and Swedish ris.
From Middle Dutch riten, from Old Dutch *rītan, from Proto-West Germanic *hrītan, from Proto-Germanic *hrītaną.

From Middle Dutch riven, from Old Dutch *rīvan, from Proto-West Germanic *hrīban, from Proto-Germanic *hrībaną, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kréybʰeti, from the root *(s)kreybʰ-. Doublet of schrijven.

From Middle Dutch risen, from Old Dutch *rīsan, from Proto-West Germanic *rīsan, from Proto-Germanic *rīsaną, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rey-. Compare Low German risen, dialectal German reisen, West Frisian rize, English rise, Icelandic rísa.
From Middle Dutch rinc, from Old Dutch rinc, from Proto-West Germanic *hring, from Proto-Germanic *hringaz.
Uncertain; compare English rabbit, as well as English rub, referring to the fur. Or, from Proto-West Germanic *reufan (“to tear”), hinted by the animals' digging of tunnels.
From Middle Dutch roef, from Old Dutch *ruof, from Proto-West Germanic *hrōf, from Proto-Germanic *hrōfą.
From Middle Dutch roec, from Old Dutch *ruok, from Proto-West Germanic *hrōk, from Proto-Germanic *hrōkaz.

parole.significato: to pay attention to, to heed
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch roeken, from Old Dutch ruoken, from Proto-West Germanic *rōkijan, from Proto-Germanic *rōkijaną.
From Middle Dutch roemen, from Old Dutch ruomen, from Proto-West Germanic *hrōmijan.
From Middle Dutch roepen, from Old Dutch ruopan, from Proto-West Germanic *hrōpan, from Proto-Germanic *hrōpaną.

From a contraction of earlier roeder, from Middle Dutch roeder, from Old Dutch *ruother, from Proto-West Germanic *rōþr, from Proto-Germanic *rōþrą. Cognate with West Frisian roer, German Ruder, English rudder.
From Middle Dutch roeren, from Old Dutch ruoren, from Proto-West Germanic *hrōʀijan, from Proto-Germanic *hrōzijaną.
From Middle Dutch roest (“rust”), from Old Dutch *rōst, from Proto-West Germanic *rust, from Proto-Germanic *rustaz. The vowel oe is due to an irregular sound development. See English rust.

From Middle Dutch rogge, from Old Dutch *roggo, from Proto-West Germanic *roggō, from Proto-Germanic *ruggô. Cognate with Limburgish rogke, West Flemish rogge, Old Saxon roggo, Middle Low German rogge, Low German Rogg, Plautdietsch Rogg, Old High German rocko, Middle High German rocke, German Rocken
From Middle Dutch roc, from Old Dutch rok, from Proto-West Germanic *(h)rokk, from Proto-Germanic *rukkaz.
Plural and case form of older rokke, from Middle Dutch rocke, from Old Dutch *rocko, from Proto-West Germanic *rokkō, from Proto-Germanic *rukkô.
From Middle Dutch rôot, from Old Dutch rōt, from Proto-West Germanic *raud, from Proto-Germanic *raudaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rowdʰós, from the root *h₁rewdʰ-.
From Middle Dutch roof, from Old Dutch *rōf, *rouf, from Proto-West Germanic *raub, from Proto-Germanic *raubaz. More at robe.
From Middle Dutch rôme, from Old Dutch *rōm, from Proto-West Germanic *raum, from Proto-Germanic *raumaz, from Proto-Indo-European *réwgʰmn̥ (“cream”).
From Middle Dutch rôosten, from Old Dutch *rōsten, from Proto-West Germanic *raustijan.
From Middle Dutch ros, from Old Dutch ros, hors, from Proto-West Germanic *hross, from Proto-Germanic *hrussą (“horse”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱers- (“to run”). Doublet of kar.

parole.significato: to rot, to go bad, to decay
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch rotten, reformed from earlier roten, from Old Dutch *roton, from Proto-West Germanic *rotēn, from Proto-Germanic *rutāną. By surface analysis, rot + -en.
From Middle Dutch rouwe, ruwe, from Old Dutch *reuwa, from Proto-West Germanic *hreuwu. The noun rouw belongs to the verb rouwen.
From Middle Dutch rôven, from Old Dutch *rōvon, from Proto-West Germanic *raubōn, from Proto-Germanic *raubōną.

parole.significato: to smell (i.e. to perceive a smell)

parole.significato: sheep (a woolly ruminant animal of the genus Ovis)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch schâep, from Old Dutch skāp, scāp, from Proto-West Germanic *skāp, from Proto-Germanic *skēpą.
From Middle Dutch scare, schere, from Old Dutch *skāri, originally a plural form, from Proto-West Germanic *skeran.

parole.significato: a shaft, a pole-shaped object or part of one, e.g. a handle

From Middle Dutch schaduwe, from Old Dutch scado, from Proto-West Germanic *skadu. Cognate with German Schatten.
From Middle Dutch schākel, from Old Dutch *skakul, from Proto-West Germanic *skakul, from Proto-Germanic *skakulaz.

From Middle Dutch schap, from Old Dutch *skap, from Proto-West Germanic *skap, from Proto-Germanic *skapą.

From Middle Dutch schenden, from Old Dutch *skenden, from Proto-West Germanic *skandijan. Equivalent to schande (“shame, disgrace”) + -en (“denominative”) and shows the effect of historical umlaut.

From Middle Dutch schinen, from Old Dutch skīnan, from Proto-West Germanic *skīnan, from Proto-Germanic *skīnaną.

From Middle Dutch schilt, from Old Dutch skilt, from Proto-West Germanic *skeldu (“shield”), from Proto-Germanic *skelduz (“shield”).

From Middle Dutch sniden, from Old Dutch snīthan, from Proto-West Germanic *snīþan, from Proto-Germanic *snīþaną, from Proto-Indo-European *sneyt- (“to cut”).

parole.testo: From Middle Dutch specht, from Old Dutch *speht, from Proto-West Germanic *spiht, from Proto-Germanic *spihtaz, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)peyk-.
From Middle Dutch spēre, from Old Dutch *speru, from Proto-West Germanic *speru, from Proto-Germanic *speru.

From Middle Dutch spec, from Old Dutch spek, from Proto-West Germanic *spik, from Proto-Germanic *spiką. Cognate with West Flemish spek, Zealandic spek, Old Saxon spek, Middle Low German spek, German Low German Speck, Old Frisian spek, North Frisian speek, Saterland Frisian Späk, West Frisian spek,
From Middle Dutch spel, from Old Dutch *spil, from Proto-West Germanic *spil.

From Middle Dutch spenen, spanen, from Old Dutch *spennen, *spanōn, from Proto-West Germanic *spanōn, *spannjan, from Proto-Germanic *spanōną, *spanjaną (“to wean”), from Proto-Germanic *spanō, *spenô (“teat, nipple”); equivalent to speen + -en. Cognate with Middle Low German spenen, spānen, spōnen
From Middle Dutch sperware, from Old Dutch *sparwaro, *sparwari, from Proto-West Germanic *sparwarī. Cognate with German Sperber.

parole.significato: mirror (reflective surface that shows an image of what is in front of it)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch spiegel, from Old Dutch spēgal, from Proto-West Germanic *spēgl.
From Middle Dutch spiker, from Old Dutch spīkere, from Proto-West Germanic *spīkr, from Proto-Germanic *spīkraz (“spike”), from Proto-Indo-European *spey- (“to be pointed; sharp point, stick”).
From Middle Dutch spīker, from Old Dutch *spīkāri, from Proto-West Germanic *spīkārī, from Late Latin spīcārium. Compare German Speicher, Old Saxon spīkari.

parole.significato: to spin: make yarn by twisting and winding fibres together
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch spinnen, from Old Dutch *spinnan, from Proto-West Germanic *spinnan, from Proto-Germanic *spinnaną.

From Middle Dutch spliten, from Old Dutch *splītan, from Proto-West Germanic *splītan, from Proto-Germanic *splītaną. Compare German spleißen, West Frisian and Danish splitte, English split (borrowed from Middle Dutch).
From Middle Dutch spoet, from Old Dutch *spuot, from Proto-West Germanic *spōdi. The "emergency department" sense is a clipping of spoedafdeling.
From Middle Dutch spoelen, from Old Dutch *spuolen, from Proto-West Germanic *spōlijan.
From Middle Dutch spore, from Old Dutch *spora, variant of *sporo, from Proto-West Germanic *spurō, from Proto-Germanic *spurô, from Proto-Indo-European *sperH- (“to kick”).
From Middle Dutch spouden, from Old Dutch *spaldan, from Proto-West Germanic *spaldan.

parole.significato: speech (act, manner or faculty of speaking)
parole.testo: From earlier sprake, from Middle Dutch sprâke, from Old Dutch sprāca, from Proto-West Germanic *sprākkijā, *sprāku; the word thus ultimately represents an ablauted derivation, with lengthened vowel (vṛddhi), from the same root as spreken.
From Middle Dutch sprēken, from Old Dutch sprecan, from Proto-West Germanic *sprekan, from Proto-Germanic *sprekaną.

From Middle Dutch sproke, from Old Dutch *spruki, from Proto-West Germanic *spruki, from the verb *sprekan (“to speak”). See spreken. Cognate with German Low German Spröök, German Spruch. Doublet of sproke.

parole.significato: long, narrow shoot from a plant; blade (of grass or corn), sprig
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch spriet, from Old Dutch *spriet, from Proto-West Germanic *spreut.

parole.significato: grasshopper, locust (insect of the suborder Caelifera or infraorder Acrididea)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch sprinchane, from Old Dutch sprinco (“grasshopper”) + hano (“cock, rooster”). The extension is believed to be due to association with the rooster’s twitching movements. Old Dutch sprinco continues Proto-West Germanic *sprinkō (cognate with Middle High German höusprinke), derived fro
From Middle Dutch sprong, from Old Dutch sprunc, from Proto-West Germanic *sprung; cognate with German Sprung. An ablauted (zero-grade) verbal noun of springen (“to jump, leap”).

Variant of spel, from Middle Dutch spel, spul, from Old Dutch *spel, from Proto-West Germanic *spil (“play, movement, performance”). The sense shifted from "play/performance" to "the equipment or props used for a performance" (as retained in kermisspul), and eventually generalized to mean "stuff, go
From Middle Dutch spuwen, from Old Dutch *spīwan, *spiuwan, from Proto-West Germanic *spīwan, from Proto-Germanic *spīwaną, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ptyēw- (“to spit, vomit”).
From Middle Dutch stâen, from Old Dutch stān, from Proto-West Germanic *stān, from Proto-Germanic *stāną.
From Middle Dutch stert, stāert, from Old Dutch *stert, from Proto-West Germanic *stert, from Proto-Germanic *stertaz.

From Middle Dutch stat, from Old Dutch stat, stedi (whence stede, stee), from Proto-West Germanic *stadi, from Proto-Germanic *stadiz, from Proto-Indo-European *stéh₂tis. The plural has preserved the old Germanic umlaut in a morphological function, a rarity in Dutch. Several derived terms have umlau
From Middle Dutch staf, from Old Dutch *staf, from Proto-West Germanic *stab, from Proto-Germanic *stabaz. More at staaf.

parole.significato: a stable, a place to keep hoofed animals
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch stal, from Old Dutch *stal, from Proto-West Germanic *stall, from Proto-Germanic *stallaz.

From Middle Dutch stalen, stalin, stalijn, from Old Dutch *stālīn, from Proto-West Germanic *stahlīn, equivalent to staal + -en (“suffix forming adjectives relating to substances”). Cognate with English steelen.
From Middle Dutch stam, from Old Dutch *stam, from Proto-West Germanic *stamni, from Proto-Germanic *stamniz.
From Middle Dutch stāmelen, from Old Dutch *stamalon, from Proto-West Germanic *stamlōn.
From Middle Dutch stampen, from Old Dutch *stampon, from Proto-West Germanic *stampōn, from Proto-Germanic *stampōną.
From Middle Dutch stant, from Old Dutch *stand, from Proto-West Germanic *stand, related to the verb *stān (“to stand”) (whence staan).
From Middle Dutch stanghe, from Old Dutch *stanga, from Proto-West Germanic *stangu, from Proto-Germanic *stangō.
From Middle Dutch stapel, from Old Dutch stapal, from Proto-West Germanic *stapul, from Proto-Germanic *stapulaz. Doublet of etappe.

From Middle Dutch stappen (preterite stiep and stappede), also steppen. Probably from a merger of Old Dutch *steppan and *stappon, respectively from Proto-West Germanic *stappjan (whence English step) and *stappōn (whence German stapfen). By surface analysis, stap + -en. The sense to go out (ca. 197
From Middle Dutch star, from Old Dutch *star, from Proto-West Germanic *star, from Proto-Germanic *staraz.
From Middle Dutch stāren, from Old Dutch *staron, from Proto-West Germanic *starēn.

parole.significato: a prick (insect bite), a stab, a thrust
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch stēke, from Old Dutch *stiki, from Proto-West Germanic *stiki.

From Middle Dutch stēle, from Old Dutch *stelo, from Proto-West Germanic *stelō, *stalu, from Proto-Germanic *staluz, *steluz (“post, trunk, stump, stem, tail”), from Proto-Indo-European *stel- (“to put, place”). Cognate with dialectal English steal (“stem, stalk”), Scots steel, stiel (“stalk”).

From Middle Dutch stêen, from Old Dutch stēn, from Proto-West Germanic *stain, from Proto-Germanic *stainaz. Doublet of -stein, a toponymic element indicating a castle borrowed in Middle Dutch from Middle High German.

parole.significato: a jetty; a small, often wooden landing for boats or small ships
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch steiger, steger, from Old Dutch *steiger, from Proto-West Germanic *staigri, from Proto-Germanic *staigriz.
From Middle Dutch steil, *stegel, from Old Dutch *steigil, *steigal, from Proto-West Germanic *staigil (“steep”).
From Middle Dutch stēken, from Old Dutch *stecan, from Proto-West Germanic *stekan, from Proto-Germanic *stikaną, originally a class 1 strong verb.
Inherited from Middle Dutch stelen, from Old Dutch *stelan, from Proto-West Germanic *stelan, from Proto-Germanic *stelaną.
From Middle Dutch stellen, from Old Dutch *stellen, from Proto-West Germanic *stalljan.

parole.significato: voice, sound made by the mouth using airflow
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch stemme, from Old Dutch *stemma, from Proto-West Germanic *stebnu, from Proto-Germanic *stebnō, *stamnijō. Under influence of Latin vox (“voice, word”), it acquired the now obsolete sense of “word”.
From Middle Dutch sterre, sterne, from Old Dutch sterro, sterno, from Proto-West Germanic *sternō, from Proto-Germanic *sternô, *sternǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂stḗr.
From Middle Dutch starc, sterc, from Old Dutch starc, from Proto-West Germanic *stark, from Proto-Germanic *starkaz.
From Middle Dutch sterken, from Old Dutch *sterken, from Proto-West Germanic *starkijan.
From Middle Dutch stercte, sterkede, from Old Dutch *sterkitha, from Proto-West Germanic *starkiþu. By surface analysis, sterk + -te.

parole.significato: to support, keep up, back up, assist
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch stōnen, from Old Dutch *stonōn, *stunōn, from Proto-West Germanic *stunōn (“to sound, crash, bang, strike, knock”), from Proto-Germanic *stunōną (“to make a loud sound, thunder, crash, rumble, groan”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tenh₂- (“to thunder”).

parole.significato: a sturgeon, fish of the genus Acipenser
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch store, from Old Dutch sturo, from Proto-West Germanic *sturjō, from Proto-Germanic *sturjô (“sturgeon”). Cognates include Old High German sturio and Old English styria and more remotely Russian осётр (osjótr, “sturgeon”), Lithuanian eršketras.

parole.significato: step-; a prefix indicating the individual being referred to is related through the marriage of a parent
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch stief-, stiep-, from Old Dutch *stiop-, from Proto-West Germanic *steupa-, from Proto-Germanic *steupa- (“bereft, pushed out”). Cognate with German stief-, English step-. The form with -f- arose through assimilation before the word vader (“father”); the generalization of this form
From Middle Dutch stijf, from Old Dutch *stīf, from Proto-West Germanic *stīf, from Proto-Germanic *stīfaz.

parole.significato: to climb, to go up, to rise
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch stigen, from Old Dutch stīgan, from Proto-West Germanic *stīgan, from Proto-Germanic *stīganą.
From Middle Dutch sticken, from Old Dutch *sticcon, from Proto-West Germanic *stikkōn, from Proto-Germanic *stikkōną.
From Middle Dutch sticken, from Old Dutch *sticken, from Proto-West Germanic *stikkjan, from Proto-Germanic *stikjaną.
From Middle Dutch stille, from Old Dutch stilli, from Proto-West Germanic *stillī.
From Middle Dutch stinken, from Old Dutch stincan, from Proto-West Germanic *stinkwan, from Proto-Germanic *stinkwaną.
From Middle Dutch stubbe, from Old Dutch *stubbo, from Proto-West Germanic *stubbō, from Proto-Germanic *stubbô.

parole.significato: a chair, a piece of furniture used for sitting, normally portable and having four legs
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch stoel, from Old Dutch stuol, from Proto-West Germanic *stōl, from Proto-Germanic *stōlaz, from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂-.

From Middle Dutch stoep, stoope, from Old Dutch *stōpa, from Proto-West Germanic *stōpā, related to the verb *stappjan (“to tread, step”). Cognate to German Low German Stuuf, German Stufe, Old English stōpel (“footprint”).
From Middle Dutch stof, from Old Dutch *stof, from Proto-West Germanic *stob, from Proto-Germanic *stubą (“dust”).
From Middle Dutch stōken, from Old Dutch *stokon, from Proto-West Germanic *stokōn, from Proto-Germanic *stukōną.

parole.significato: mute, unable to speak, as medical condition or species-determined
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch stom, from Old Dutch stum, from Proto-West Germanic *stumm, from Proto-Germanic *stummaz. Cognate with German stumm, Old Saxon stum.

From Middle Dutch stonde, from Old Dutch stunda (“time, while”), from Proto-West Germanic *stundu, from Proto-Germanic *stundō (“time, while”). More at English stound, German Stunde, Low German Stünn.
From Middle Dutch stōve, from Old Dutch *stova, from Proto-West Germanic *stubu.
From Middle Dutch *stôom, from Old Dutch *stōm, from Proto-West Germanic *staum, from Proto-Germanic *staumaz.
From Middle Dutch stôot, from Old Dutch *stōt, from Proto-West Germanic *stauti, from Proto-Germanic *stautiz. Equivalent to a deverbal from stoten.
From Middle Dutch stoppen, from Old Dutch *stoppon, from Proto-West Germanic *stoppōn. Doublet of stofferen.
From Middle Dutch stôren, from Old Dutch *stōren, from Proto-West Germanic *staurijan.
Inherited from Middle Dutch storke, from Old Dutch *stork, from Proto-West Germanic *stork, from Proto-Germanic *sturkaz.

parole.significato: storm; a wind scale for very strong wind, stronger than a gale, less than a hurricane
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch storm, from Old Dutch *storm, from Proto-West Germanic *sturm, from Proto-Germanic *sturmaz.
From Middle Dutch sterten, from Old Dutch *sturten, from Proto-West Germanic *sturtijan. Doublet with starten, which came from English start.
From Middle Dutch stôten, from Old Dutch stōtan, from Proto-West Germanic *stautan, from Proto-Germanic *stautaną.
From Middle Dutch stoven, from Old Dutch *stōven, from Proto-West Germanic *staubijan. By surface analysis, stoof + -en.

parole.significato: ray (a beam of light or radiation)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch strâel, strâle, from Old Dutch strāla, from Proto-West Germanic *strālu.

From Middle Dutch strâte, from Old Dutch strāta, from Proto-West Germanic *strātu (“street”), from Latin strāta, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sterh₃- (“to stretch out, extend, spread”). The geographical sense “strait” is a phono-semantic matching of Middle English streit, from Old French est

From Middle Dutch strēke, strēec, from Old Dutch *striki, from Proto-West Germanic *striki, from Proto-Germanic *strikiz. In Middle Dutch there may have been a merger of the above noun with a descendant of related Proto-West Germanic *straik. Compare the German distinction between Strich and Streich

parole.significato: to stretch, to extend, to reach
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch strecken, from Old Dutch *strecken, from Proto-West Germanic *strakkjan. Equivalent to strak (“straight, tight, tense”) + -en (“deadjectival”) and shows the effect of historical umlaut.
From Middle Dutch strêlen, an eastern form (with umlaut on long vowel) from Old Dutch *strālen, from Proto-West Germanic *strālijan. Cognate with Luxembourgish stréilen, archaic German strählen.
From Middle Dutch stremmen, from Old Dutch *stremmen, from Proto-West Germanic *strammjan. Equivalent to stram (“tight, stiff”) + -en (“deadjectival”) and shows the effect of historical umlaut.

parole.significato: to hit hard, like the elements
parole.testo: Ultimately related to Proto-West Germanic *strālu (“arrow”).

From Middle Dutch strijt, from Old Dutch *strīt, from Proto-West Germanic *strīd, from Proto-Germanic *strīdaz. Cognate to Old Saxon strīd, Old High German strīt, German Streit, Old Frisian strīd, Old Norse stríð.

parole.significato: to fight, to wage battle or war
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch striden, from Old Dutch strīdan, from Proto-West Germanic *strīdan, from Proto-Germanic *strīdaną.
From Middle Dutch striken, from Old Dutch *strīcan, from Proto-West Germanic *strīkan, from Proto-Germanic *strīkaną, from Proto-Indo-European *streyg-.
From Middle Dutch strô, from Old Dutch *strō, from Proto-West Germanic *strau, from Proto-Germanic *strawą.
From Middle Dutch stroet, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *strōd.

parole.significato: to match, fit together, be in agreement
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch strôken, from Old Dutch *strōken, from Proto-West Germanic *straukijan, from Proto-Germanic *straukijaną, the causative of *streukaną.

From Middle Dutch stront (“shit, dreck, manure”), from Old Dutch *strunt (“excrement, turd, shit”), from Proto-West Germanic *strunt (“dirt, filth”). Compare French étron (“turd, crap”), Italian stronzo (“turd, crap”). Cognate with English strunt.
From Middle Dutch strôyen, from Old Dutch *strōien, from Proto-West Germanic *strauwjan, from Proto-Germanic *strawjaną.

parole.significato: a flow, current or flush, as of moving water or other liquid
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch strôom, from Old Dutch *strōm, from Proto-West Germanic *straum, from Proto-Germanic *straumaz, from Proto-Indo-European *srew- (“to flow”). Cognate with German Strom and English stream.
From Middle Dutch stuven, from Old Dutch *stūvan, from Proto-West Germanic *steuban.

parole.significato: a piece, part, share (of a whole)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch stucke, stuc, from Old Dutch *stukki, from Proto-West Germanic *stukkī, from Proto-Germanic *stukkiją. Cognate with German Stück, dialectal English steck and borrowed shtick. Doublet of stuc.
From Middle Dutch sturen, from Old Dutch stiuren, from Proto-West Germanic *stiurijan, from Proto-Germanic *stiurijaną.
From Middle Dutch stouwe, from Old Dutch *stōa, *stuoa, from Proto-West Germanic *stōu.
From suffen, from Middle Dutch suffen, from Old Dutch *suffen, from Proto-West Germanic *suffjan, from Proto-Germanic *sufjaną (“to doze off”).
From Middle Dutch taey, from Old Dutch *tāi, from earlier *tāhi, from Proto-West Germanic *tą̄h(ī), from Proto-Germanic *tanhuz. Cognate with German zäh, English tough.

parole.significato: language (form of communication consisting of vocabulary and grammar)
parole.testo: From earlier tale, from Middle Dutch tāle, from Old Dutch tala, from Proto-West Germanic *talu, from Proto-Germanic *talō. Compare Danish tale.
From Middle Dutch tac (“pointy object, forked object”), from Old Dutch *takko, from Proto-West Germanic *takkō (“twig, branch, shoot”). Unrelated to the prefix takke-, as in takkewijf.
From Middle Dutch tāken, from Old Dutch *takan, from Proto-West Germanic *takan (“to take; grasp, touch”), from Proto-Germanic *takaną (“to touch, grasp; take”).
From Middle Dutch tal, from Old Dutch *tal, from Proto-West Germanic *tal, from Proto-Germanic *talą.
From Middle Dutch tālen, from Old Dutch *talon, from Proto-West Germanic *talōn, from Proto-Germanic *talōną. Cognate with English tale.
From Middle Dutch tam, from Old Dutch *tam, from Proto-West Germanic *tam.
From Middle Dutch tant, from Old Dutch tant, from Proto-West Germanic *tanþ, from Proto-Germanic *tanþs, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃dónts.
From Middle Dutch tanghe, from Old Dutch tanga, from Proto-West Germanic *tangu, from Proto-Germanic *tangō.
From Middle Dutch tappe (“closing pin, stopper”), from Old Dutch *tappo, from Proto-West Germanic *tappō, from Proto-Germanic *tappô.

From Middle Dutch tarwe, from Old Dutch *tarwa, from Proto-West Germanic *taru, from Proto-Germanic *tarwō, from Proto-Indo-European *der(H)- (“to tear, crack”). Cognate with Limburgish terve, West Flemish terwe, Zealandic tèrve, Old Saxon tarwa, Middle Low German tarwe, German Low German Tarwe, Old

parole.significato: a bitch, a female dog: a female dog or other canine
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch teve, from Old Dutch *tiva, from Proto-West Germanic *tibā, perhaps from the root of Old Norse tík (“bitch”). Cognate to Old English tife and probably German Zibbe.
From Middle Dutch teke, from Old Dutch *tika, from Proto-West Germanic *tīkō (“tick”).
From Middle Dutch teelt, from Old Dutch [Term?], from Proto-West Germanic [Term?]. By surface analysis, telen + -te. Cognate with Old English tilþ (English tilth), Old Frisian tilath.

From Middle Dutch têe, from Old Dutch *tēa, from Proto-West Germanic *taihā, from Proto-Germanic *taihwǭ. The modern form was originally a plural (retained in van top tot teen), which was reanalysed as a singular. Compare schoen where the same has happened, or raaf and ui which went the opposite way
From Middle Dutch tene, teene, from Old Dutch *tein, *tēn, from Proto-West Germanic *tain, from Proto-Germanic *tainaz.

From Middle Dutch tree, from Old Dutch *trio, *treo, from Proto-West Germanic *treu, from Proto-Germanic *trewą (“tree, wood”), from pre-Germanic *dréwom, thematic e-grade derivative of Proto-Indo-European *dóru (“tree”). Cognate with English tree, Danish træ.
From Middle Dutch tigele, tegel, from Old Dutch tegela, from Proto-West Germanic *tigulā, from Proto-Germanic *tigulǭ, from Latin tegula. Compare German Ziegel, English tile.
From Middle Dutch tegen, tjegen, from te jegen, the latter from Old Dutch gegin, from Proto-West Germanic *gagin, from Proto-Germanic *gagin. See also jegens.
From Middle Dutch têken, from Old Dutch tēkan, from Proto-West Germanic *taikn, from Proto-Germanic *taikną. Cognate with German Zeichen, English token and Danish tegn.

parole.significato: to cultivate, to grow plants, notably crops
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch tēlen, from Old Dutch tilon, from Proto-West Germanic *tilōn, from Proto-Germanic *tilōną.
From Middle Dutch telch, from Old Dutch *telg, from Proto-West Germanic *telguʀ, from Proto-Germanic *telguz.

From Middle Dutch tellen, from Old Dutch tellen, from Proto-West Germanic *talljan, from Proto-Germanic *taljaną. Equivalent to tal (“number”) + -en (“denominative”) or taal (“language”) + -en (“denominative”) and shows the effect of historical umlaut.
From Middle Dutch temmen, from Old Dutch *temmen, from Proto-West Germanic *tammjan. Equivalent to tam (“tame”) + -en (“deadjectival”) and shows the effect of historical umlaut.

parole.significato: to eat or drink what is necessary to survive
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch tēren (“to destroy, to use (up)”), from Old Dutch *teren, from Proto-West Germanic *tarjan, from Proto-Germanic *tarjaną, related to *teraną (“to tear, rip apart”). Cognate with German zehren. Also related with English tear (“to rip”).
From Middle Dutch tergen, from Old Dutch *tergen, from Proto-West Germanic *targijan, from Proto-Germanic *targijaną. Cognate with German Low German targen, English tarry.
From Middle Dutch toghe, tueghe, from Old Dutch *tugi, from Proto-West Germanic *tugi, from Proto-Germanic *tugiz. Compare German Zug.
From Middle Dutch tigele, from Old Dutch tegela, from Proto-West Germanic *tigulā, from Proto-Germanic *tigulǭ, from Latin tēgula. More at tegel.
From Middle Dutch tien, from Old Dutch tēn, *tien, from Proto-West Germanic *tehun, from Proto-Germanic *tehun, from Proto-Indo-European *déḱm̥.

From Middle Dutch tieren, from Proto-West Germanic *tiari- (“neat, splendid”), from Proto-Germanic *diH-or-i-. The ultimate origin is uncertain, but cognate with Old Norse tærr (“clear (water)”), which could be related to tár (“tear”) << Proto-Germanic *tahrą. Cognate with German zieren, and also si

Inherited from Middle Dutch tijt, from Old Dutch tīt, from Proto-West Germanic *tīdi, from Proto-Germanic *tīdiz, from Proto-Indo-European *déh₂itis, from *deh₂y- + *-tis. In the 19th and 20th centuries, Dutch tijd was exclusively masculine, but prior to that it was alternatively feminine. This vari
From Middle Dutch tidinge, tydinge, from Proto-West Germanic *tīdungō (“message”), from the verb *tīdōjan (“to happen”), from Proto-Germanic *tīdiz (“time, interval”).
From Middle Dutch tiën, from Old Dutch *tīan, from Proto-West Germanic *tīhan, from Proto-Germanic *tīhaną, from Proto-Indo-European *deyḱ- (“to show”).
From Middle Dutch tien, from Old Dutch tian, from Proto-West Germanic *teuhan, from Proto-Germanic *teuhaną, from Proto-Indo-European *dewk- (“to pull”).
From Middle Dutch timmer, from Old Dutch *timmer, from Proto-West Germanic *timr, from Proto-Germanic *timrą, from Proto-Indo-European *dem- (“build, house”).

parole.significato: to perform carpentry, to build, to construct
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch timmeren, from Old Dutch timbren, from Proto-West Germanic *timrijan, from Proto-Germanic *timrijaną.

parole.significato: come on!, go on! (used when trying to coax someone into doing something)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch toe, from Old Dutch *tuo, from Proto-West Germanic *tō, from Proto-Germanic *tō.
From Middle Dutch toe-, from Old Dutch *tō-, from Proto-West Germanic *twiʀ-, from Proto-Germanic *twiz-.
From Middle Dutch toelaten, from Old Dutch *tuolātan, from Proto-West Germanic *tōlātan. Equivalent to toe + laten. Cognate with German zulassen.

parole.significato: then, subsequently (at a time in the past)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch doe, doen (with -n from dan), from Old Dutch thuo, from Proto-West Germanic *þō. Cognate with Luxembourgish dunn and similar forms (do, du, dun) in German dialects.
From Middle Dutch tocken, tucken, from Old Dutch *tokkon, *tukkon, from Proto-West Germanic *tukkōn, from Proto-Germanic *tukkōną.
From Middle Dutch tômen, from Old Dutch *tōmen, from Proto-West Germanic *taumijan, from Proto-Germanic *taumijaną. Equivalent to toom (“briddle”) + -en.
From Middle Dutch tunder, from Old Dutch *tundar, from Proto-West Germanic *tundr, from Proto-Germanic *tundrą.

From Middle Dutch tonge, from Old Dutch tunga, from Proto-West Germanic *tungā, from Proto-Germanic *tungǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *dn̥ǵʰwéh₂s. The sense "Solea solea" likely refers to these flat fish' resemblance to a tongue.
From Middle Dutch toom, from Old Dutch *tōm, from Proto-West Germanic *taum, from Proto-Germanic *taumaz. Doublet of team.
From Middle Dutch top, topp, from Old Dutch *topp, *top, from Proto-West Germanic *topp, from Proto-Germanic *tuppaz.

parole.significato: to unpick; to loosen a stitch
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch ternen, from earlier trennen by liquid metathesis (compare Kerstmis (“Christmas”) and vorst (“frost”)), from Old Dutch *trennen, from Proto-West Germanic *trannijan, from Proto-Germanic *trannijaną.
From Middle Dutch tôver, from Old Dutch *tōver, from Proto-West Germanic *taubr, from Proto-Germanic *taubrą.

From Middle Dutch tôveren, from Old Dutch *tōvaron, from Proto-West Germanic *taubrōn, from Proto-Germanic *taubrōną. Equivalent to tover (“magic”) + -en. Cognates include German Low German tovern, tövern and German zaubern.
From Middle Dutch trā, trāde, from Old Dutch *trada, from Proto-West Germanic *tradu, from Proto-Germanic *tradō (“spoor, track”). More at English trade.
From Middle Dutch trâge, from Old Dutch *trāgi, from Proto-West Germanic *trāgī, from Proto-Germanic *trēgiz. Cognate with German träge and träg.
From Middle Dutch trâen, from Old Dutch trān, from Proto-West Germanic *trahnu (“tear”). Cognate with German Träne (“tear”) and Tran (“fish oil”).
From Middle Dutch trachten, from Old Dutch *trahton, from Proto-West Germanic *trahtōn, from Latin tractō. Doublet of trakteren.
From Middle Dutch trappe, from Old Dutch *trappa, from Proto-West Germanic *trappā.
From Middle Dutch trēden, from Old Dutch tredan, from Proto-West Germanic *tredan, from Proto-Germanic *trudaną. Cognate with English tread.
From Middle Dutch trecken, from Old Dutch *trecken, from Proto-West Germanic *trakkjan, from Proto-Germanic *trakjaną (“to drag”).

From Middle Dutch troch, from Old Dutch *trog, from Proto-West Germanic *trog, from Proto-Germanic *trugą, *trugaz (compare West Frisian trôch, English trough, German Trog, Swedish tråg), from Proto-Indo-European *dru-kó- (compare Middle Irish drochta (“wooden basin”), Old Armenian տարգալ (targal, “
From Middle Dutch trouwe, from Old Dutch triuwa, from Proto-West Germanic *treuwu, from Proto-Germanic *trewwō.
From Middle Dutch trouwe, from Old Dutch *triuwi, from Proto-West Germanic *triuwī, from Proto-Germanic *triwwiz.

From Middle Dutch tuyg (“tools, apparatus, utensil, ornament”), from Old Dutch *tiug, from Proto-West Germanic *teug, from Proto-Germanic *tiugiją, *teugą (“stuff, matter, device”), from *teuhaną (“to lead, bring, pull”), from Proto-Indo-European *dewk- (“to pull, lead”). Cognate with German Zeug (“
From Middle Dutch tuun, from Old Dutch tūn, from Proto-West Germanic *tūn, from Proto-Germanic *tūną, from Proto-Celtic *dūnom.
From Middle Dutch torf, from Old Dutch *torf, from Proto-West Germanic *turb, from Proto-Germanic *turbz (“turf, lawn”), from Proto-Indo-European *derbʰ- (“tuft, grass”).
From Middle Dutch twêe, from Old Dutch twē, neuter form of twēne, from Proto-West Germanic *twai-, from Proto-Germanic *twai, from Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ with plural suffix *-i.
From Middle Dutch twivel, twifel, from Old Dutch twīval, from Proto-West Germanic *twīfl, from Proto-Germanic *twīflaz, equivalent to an old derivation of Dutch twee (“two”).

Originally the dative and accusative form of jij/gij, from Middle Dutch u, from Old Dutch iu, from Proto-West Germanic *iwwiz, from Proto-Germanic *iwwiz, West Germanic variant of *izwiz, dative/accusative of *jūz, from Proto-Indo-European *yúHs. Doublet of jou. The use as a nominative form is linke

parole.significato: owl, bird of the order Strigiformes
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch ule, from Old Dutch *ūwila, *ūwala, *ūla, from Proto-West Germanic *uwwulā (“owl”).

parole.significato: out, from the inside to the outside
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch uut, ute, from Old Dutch ūt, from Proto-West Germanic *ūt, from Proto-Germanic *ūt. Compare West Frisian út, English out, German aus, Danish ud, Norwegian ut.

parole.significato: to go out (to go to public places for leisure)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch ûtegâen, from Old Dutch ūtgān, from Proto-West Germanic *ūtgān. Equivalent to uit + gaan.

parole.significato: your; second-person singular and plural possessive determiner
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch uwe, from Old Dutch *iuwa, from Proto-West Germanic *iuwar, from Proto-Germanic *izweraz. Doublet of jouw.

parole.significato: heifer (cow approximately 2 years old that has not calved)
