parole.testo: From Middle Dutch veerse, verse, from Proto-West Germanic *farsijā, derived from Proto-Germanic *farzaz (“bull, ox”), whence Dutch var. Cognate with Middle Low German verse, German Färse.
From Middle Dutch vāert, from Old Dutch farth, fard, from Proto-West Germanic *fardi, from Proto-Germanic *fardiz. Equivalent to varen (“to travel by boat”) + -t (“verbal noun”).
From Middle Dutch vaerwech, from Old Dutch *faraweg, from Proto-West Germanic *faraweg, equivalent to varen + weg (“road, way”). Cognate with English fareway, German Fahrweg.
From Middle Dutch vadem, from Old Dutch *fatham, from Proto-West Germanic *faþm, from Proto-Germanic *faþmaz.
From Middle Dutch vāder, from Old Dutch fadar, from Proto-West Germanic *fader, from Proto-Germanic *fadēr, from Proto-Indo-European *ph₂tḗr.
From Middle Dutch vâgen, from Old Dutch *fāgon, from Proto-West Germanic *fāgōn, from Proto-Germanic *fēgōną. Closely related to modern Dutch vegen, which shows a different ablaut vowel.

parole.significato: a compartment (e.g. a shelf, a section)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch vac, from Old Dutch *fak, from Proto-West Germanic *fak, from Proto-Germanic *faką. In some of the contemporary senses probably influenced by cognate German Fach.

parole.significato: a fall (act or event of falling)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch val, from Old Dutch *fal, from Proto-West Germanic *fall, from Proto-Germanic *fallaz. Equivalent to a deverbal from vallen (“to fall”).

parole.significato: a falcon, bird of the family Falconidae, in particular of the genus Falco
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch valke, from Old Dutch *falco, from Proto-West Germanic *falkō, from Proto-Germanic *falkô.
From Middle Dutch vallen, from Old Dutch fallan, from Proto-West Germanic *fallan, from Proto-Germanic *fallaną.

From Middle Dutch van, from Old Dutch fan (“from”), from Proto-West Germanic *fanā, from Proto-Germanic *fanē, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂poneh₁ (“from”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂epo, *h₂pó (“off, of”). Cognate with Old Saxon fana, fan (“from”), Old Frisian fan, fon (“from”), Old High German fo
Inherited from Middle Dutch van dane (literally “from thence”); the second element is from Old Dutch *thanana, from Proto-West Germanic *þananā.
From Middle Dutch vangen, from Old Dutch fangan. Back-formation from the past-tense forms of Middle Dutch vâen, from Old Dutch fān, from Proto-West Germanic *fą̄han, from Proto-Germanic *fanhaną.

parole.significato: to sail, to go by boat, to navigate
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch vāren (“to go, travel”), from Old Dutch faran, from Proto-West Germanic *faran, from Proto-Germanic *faraną. The restriction to “travel by water” comes (expectably) from the western dialects; the more general sense survives in the east, but is no longer part of standard Dutch.
From Middle Dutch varen, from Old Dutch *farn, from Proto-West Germanic *farn.
From Middle Dutch vast, from Old Dutch fast, from Proto-West Germanic *fastī, from Proto-Germanic *fastuz.
From Middle Dutch vasten, from Old Dutch *faston, from Proto-West Germanic *fastēn, from Proto-Germanic *fastāną.
From Middle Dutch vat, from Old Dutch *fat, from Proto-West Germanic *fat, from Proto-Germanic *fatą.

From earlier vaten, from Middle Dutch vāten, from Old Dutch *faton, from Proto-West Germanic *fatōn, from Proto-Germanic *fatōną. By surface analysis, vat (“vat, keg, vessel”) + -en. The short vowel, which appears from the 15th century, is usually explained through influence of the underlying noun v
From Middle Dutch vechten, from Old Dutch fehtan, from Proto-West Germanic *fehtan, from Proto-Germanic *fehtaną, from Proto-Indo-European *peḱ-. Cognate with English fight and German fechten.

From Middle Dutch vêe, from Old Dutch fē, from Proto-West Germanic *fehu, from Proto-Germanic *fehu, from Proto-Indo-European *peḱu- (“livestock”). Cognate with German Vieh, Low German Veeh, English fee.

From Middle Dutch veghe, veyghe, veych (“doomed to die; near death”), from Old Dutch *fēgi, from Proto-West Germanic *faigī, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *faigijaz (“fey, doomed to die”), from Proto-Indo-European *peyḱ-, *pAig- (“ill-meaning, bad”). Cognate with English fey.
From Middle Dutch vēne, from Old Dutch *feni, from Proto-West Germanic *fani, from Proto-Germanic *fanją. Doublet of ven.

A contraction of veder, from Middle Dutch vedere, from Old Dutch fethara, from Proto-West Germanic *feþru, from Proto-Germanic *feþrō, from Proto-Indo-European *péth₂r̥ ~ pth₂én- (“feather, wing”), from *peth₂- (“to fly”). The sense "spring" is derived from the ability of feathers to resume their sh
From Middle Dutch vere f, from Old Dutch *feri (in toponyms), from Proto-West Germanic [Term?], from Proto-Germanic *farjǭ. Cognate with German Fähre.
From Middle Dutch vēgen, from Old Dutch *fegon, from Proto-West Germanic *fegōn. Closely related to modern Dutch vagen, which shows a different ablaut vowel.
From Middle Dutch veilich, from Proto-West Germanic *failī (“true, familiar, good”). Note the conflation of the stem with *faliz (“venal”) in cognates Dutch veil (“venal”) and German feil (“venal”).

From Middle Dutch vel, from Old Dutch *fel, from Proto-West Germanic *fell, from Proto-Germanic *fellą, from Proto-Indo-European *pello-, *pelno-, whence Latin pellis, Greek πέλλα; cognate with German Fell.
From Middle Dutch velt, from Old Dutch felt, from Proto-West Germanic *felþu, from Proto-Germanic *felþuz, from Proto-Indo-European *pelh₂-.
From Middle Dutch vellen, from Old Dutch *fellen, from Proto-West Germanic *fallijan, from Proto-Germanic *fallijaną. A causative verb to vallen (“to fall”).

From Middle Dutch vent (“hero; man”). Unknown earlier origin. Compare West Frisian feint (“servant; fellow; boyfriend”), Low German Fent (“young fellow”), Saterland Frisian Wäänt (“boy, lad”). * Possibly from Proto-West Germanic *fanþijō (“walker, walking”), from Proto-Indo-European *pent- (“to go,

From earlier verre, from Middle Dutch verre, Old Dutch ferro, from Proto-West Germanic *ferrō, from Proto-Germanic *ferrai, from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“to go over”). Originally solely an adverb, adjectival usages represent a secondary development visible in many Germanic languages. The now-obso

parole.significato: to do or to become what the stem (following this prefix) refers to
parole.testo: The result of a merger of two Middle Dutch prefixes: * Middle Dutch er-, an unstressed variant of ur-, or- (modern oor-), from Old Dutch ur-, ir-, from Proto-West Germanic *uʀ-, from Proto-Germanic *uz-. * Middle Dutch ver-, from Old Dutch fir-, far-, itself from a mixture of Proto-Germanic *firi-,
From Middle Dutch verbannen, from Old Dutch *firbannan, from Proto-West Germanic *frabannan. Equivalent to ver- + bannen. Compare German verbannen and English forban.
From Middle Dutch verbieden, from Old Dutch *farbiodan, from Proto-West Germanic *furibeudan, from Proto-Germanic *furibeudaną. Equivalent to ver- + bieden.

From Middle Dutch verbinden, from Old Dutch *farbindan, from Proto-West Germanic *frabindan. Equivalent to ver- + binden. Cognate with German verbinden and Old English forbindan (whence Middle English forbinden).

parole.significato: to spoil, to ruin, to corrupt
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch verderven, from Old Dutch fardervan, from Proto-West Germanic *fraderban. Unrelated to derven, but related to bederven.
From Middle Dutch varwe, verwe, from Old Dutch *farwa, from Proto-West Germanic *faru, from Proto-Germanic *farwō.
From Middle Dutch vergetel, from Old Dutch *fargetal, from Proto-West Germanic *fragetul, an adjective based on the verb *fragetan (whence vergeten). Obsolete since the 17th century.
From Middle Dutch vergēten, from Old Dutch fargetan, from Proto-West Germanic *fragetan.
From Middle Dutch verquisten, from Old Dutch [Term?], from Proto-West Germanic *frakwistijan, from Proto-Germanic *frakwistijaną. Equivalent to ver- + kwisten.
From Middle Dutch verlâten, from Old Dutch farlātan, from Proto-West Germanic *fralātan, from Proto-Germanic *fralētaną. Equivalent to ver- + laten.

From Middle Dutch verleiden, verlêden, from Old Dutch *farleiden, *farlēden, from Proto-West Germanic *fralaidijan. Equivalent to ver- + leiden. Cognate with Old Saxon farlēdian, English forlead, German verleiten.

parole.significato: to shift the body's position while lying
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch verliggen, from Old Dutch *farliggen, from Proto-West Germanic *fraliggjan, equivalent to ver- + liggen. Cognate with English forlie, German verliegen.
From Middle Dutch verraden, from Old Dutch farrādan, from Proto-West Germanic *frarādan. Equivalent to ver- + raden. Cognate to German verraten.

From Middle Dutch verrukken, from Old Dutch *firrukken, from Proto-West Germanic *frarukkijan. Equivalent to ver- + rukken. Cognate with German Low German verrücken, German verrücken, Saterland Frisian ferrukje, ferrukke.

From Middle Dutch versch, from Old Dutch *fersk, *frisk, from Proto-West Germanic *frisk, from Proto-Germanic *friskaz, from Proto-Indo-European *preysk-. Doublet of fris. Cognate with German frisch, West Frisian farsk, English fresh, Danish fersk, Norwegian Bokmål fersk, Swedish färsk.
From Middle Dutch verslinden, from Old Dutch *farslindan, from Proto-West Germanic *fraslindan, from Proto-Germanic *fraslindaną.
Inherited from Middle Dutch verspilden, from Old Dutch [Term?], from Proto-West Germanic *fraspilþijan. Equivalent to ver- + spillen.

parole.significato: to trample, to destroy by trampling
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch vertrēden, from Old Dutch *fartredan, from Proto-West Germanic *fratredan, from Proto-Germanic *fratrudaną. Equivalent to ver- + treden (“to tread”).
From Middle Dutch verwâten, a strong perfect participle from Old Dutch farwātan, from Proto-West Germanic *frahwātan.
From Middle Dutch verwerken, from Old Dutch farwirken. By surface analysis, ver- + werken (“to work”).
From Middle Dutch verwonden, from Old Dutch *farwundon, from Proto-West Germanic *frawundōn. By surface analysis, ver- + wonden. Cognate with English forwound, German verwunden, Old Saxon farwundon.
From Middle Dutch versāken, from Old Dutch farsacan, from Proto-West Germanic *frasakan (“to forsake, renounce”). Compare English forsake, Norwegian forsake, Danish forsage and Swedish försaka.
From Middle Dutch versieden, from Old Dutch *farsiethan, from Proto-West Germanic *fraseuþan, equivalent ver- + zieden (“to boil”).

From Middle Dutch versûmen, from Old Dutch *farsūmen, from Proto-West Germanic *frasūmijan, from *sūmijan. By surface analysis, ver- + zuimen, a verb which became obsolete in the early modern period. Compare German versäumen, Danish forsømme.
From Middle Dutch vet, from Old Dutch fētit, fet, from Proto-West Germanic *faitid, originally a past participle.
From Middle Dutch vete, from Old Dutch *faitha, from Proto-West Germanic *faihiþu.

parole.significato: a fibre (Commonwealth); fiber (US) (single piece/strand of fabric or other material)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch *vesele (from which veselen), from vese + -ele. Equivalent to vees + -el. Ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *fasō (“fiber”), see Old High German faso.
From Middle Dutch vier, from Old Dutch *fiuwar, *viuwar, *vier, from Proto-West Germanic *feuwar, from Proto-Germanic *fedwōr, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwṓr, the neuter form of *kʷetwóres.
From Middle Dutch vierde, from Old Dutch *fiortho, from Proto-West Germanic *feurþō, from Proto-Germanic *fedurþô.
From Middle Dutch viant, from Old Dutch fīand, from Proto-West Germanic *fijand, from Proto-Germanic *fijandz. Compare English fiend.
From Middle Dutch vijf, from Old Dutch fīf, vīf, from Proto-West Germanic *fimf, from Proto-Germanic *fimf, from *pémpe, variant of Proto-Indo-European *pénkʷe.
From Middle Dutch vile, from Old Dutch *fīla, from Proto-West Germanic *fį̄hlu, from Proto-Germanic *finhlō.
From Middle Dutch villen, from Old Dutch fillen, from Proto-West Germanic *fillijan. Equivalent to vel (“skin”) + -en (“denominative”) and shows the effect of historical i-mutation.
From Middle Dutch vilt, from Old Dutch *filt, from Proto-West Germanic *felt.
From Middle Dutch vinden, from Old Dutch findan, from Proto-West Germanic *finþan, from Proto-Germanic *finþaną, from Proto-Indo-European *pent- (“to go, pass; path, bridge”).
From Middle Dutch vinger, from Old Dutch fingar, from Proto-West Germanic *fingr, from Proto-Germanic *fingraz.

parole.significato: to fish, to try to catch fish
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch visschen, from Old Dutch *fiscon, from Proto-West Germanic *fiskōn. Equivalent to vis + -en.

parole.significato: a sweet custard-based or cornflour-based dessert
parole.testo: From earlier vlade, from Middle Dutch vlāde, from Old Dutch *flatho, *flatha, from Proto-West Germanic *flaþō. Doublet of vlaai.

parole.significato: a type of fruit pie traditionally made and consumed in the Limburg province of the Netherlands
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch vlaeye, vlaaye, southeastern variant of vlāde, from Old Dutch *flado, from Proto-West Germanic *flaþō. Doublet of vla.
From Middle Dutch vlac, from Old Dutch *flak, from Proto-West Germanic *flak, from Proto-Germanic *flakaz.
From Middle Dutch vlêesch, from Old Dutch flēsc, from Proto-West Germanic *flaiski.

parole.significato: a flail, threshing tool (or by extension equivalent machinery)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch vlegel, vleil, from Old Dutch *flegil, from Proto-West Germanic *flagil, likely from Latin flagellum (“whipping flail”).

parole.significato: to flatter, coax, sweet-talk, wheedle (praise excessively and disingenuously)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch vleien, from Old Dutch *fleien, from Proto-West Germanic *flaihijan.

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; perhaps; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch vleck, vlecke (also vlacke), from Old Dutch flec (attested as a byname) and *flekko, from Proto-West Germanic *flekkō, from Proto-Germanic *flekka- (“spot, mark, blemish”), of uncertain origin. Perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂g-, *pleh₂k- (“to beat, strike”).

From Middle Dutch vlerc, vleric, vlederic, from Old Dutch fetherak, from Proto-West Germanic *feþruk, *fiþrik (“wing”), from *feþru (“feather”). The -l- visible from Middle Dutch onward likely arose through the influence of words such as vlueghel/vloghel (“wing”), vliegen (“to fly”), vleder (“wing”)
From Middle Dutch vloge (“flight”) (the genitive of which yields modern fluks), from Old Dutch *flugi, from Proto-West Germanic [Term?], from Proto-Germanic *flugiz.
From Middle Dutch vliegen, from Old Dutch fliegan, from Proto-West Germanic *fleugan, from Proto-Germanic *fleuganą, from Proto-Indo-European *plewk-.
From Middle Dutch vlieder, from Old Dutch fliethar, from Proto-West Germanic *fleuþr.

parole.significato: body of moving water; stream, river, creek
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch vliet, from Old Dutch fliet, from Proto-West Germanic *fleut, from Proto-Germanic *fleutą (“stream, river”). Cognate with English fleet (“an arm of the sea; a run of water”).
From Middle Dutch vlieten, from Old Dutch flietan, from Proto-West Germanic *fleutan, from Proto-Germanic *fleutaną.

From Middle Dutch vliën (“to arrange, to organize, to give something its place”), from Proto-West Germanic *flīhan, of unknown ultimate origin; possibly related to the root of *flaihijan (“to be sly, to flatter”), though the semantic gap is wide.
From Middle Dutch vlijt, from Old Dutch *flīt, from Proto-West Germanic *flīt, from Proto-Germanic *flītaz, for which compare Proto-West Germanic *flītan (“to strive”).

parole.significato: a flea, insect of the order Siphonaptera
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch vlô, from Old Dutch *flō, from Proto-West Germanic *flauh, from Proto-Germanic *flauhaz, from Proto-Indo-European *plówkos, a variant of *plus- (“flea”).
From Middle Dutch vloet, from Old Dutch fluot, from Proto-West Germanic *flōdu, from Proto-Germanic *flōduz. Equivalent to vloeien (“to flow”) + -d (“verbal noun”).

parole.significato: to flow (to move as a fluid)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle Dutch vloeyen, inherited from Old Dutch *fluoien, inherited from Proto-West Germanic *flōan, inherited from Proto-Germanic *flōaną.

parole.significato: wooden walkway over a creek, a duckboard
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch vlonder, from Old Dutch *flonder, from Proto-West Germanic *flonþr. Has also occasionally been seen as a by-form of vonder, but this is controversial. This latter hypothesis has most recently been advocated for by De Vaan, who argues that it is very unlikely that the two words do n

parole.significato: flight (the act of flying, an instance thereof)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch vlucht, from Old Dutch *fluht, from Proto-West Germanic *fluhti, derived from *fleugan (“to fly”), whence Dutch vliegen.
From Middle Dutch vlucht, from Old Dutch *fluht, from Proto-West Germanic *fluhti, derived from *fleuhan (“to flee”), whence Dutch vlieden.

From Middle Dutch vlugge, from Old Dutch *fluggi, from Proto-West Germanic *flugi, from Proto-Germanic *flugjaz, related to *fleuganą (“to fly”), whence Dutch vliegen. Cognate with Ripuarian flögg (“fast”), Middle Low German vlügge, German flügge (both “full-fledged”). Compare also German flugs (“qu

From Middle Dutch vucht, vocht. Substantivized form of an identical adjective, from Old Dutch *fuhti (“humid, wet, damp; marsh-like”), from Proto-West Germanic *fų̄ht, from Proto-Germanic *funhtijaz (“humid, wet, damp”). In Middle Dutch the word gradually shifted from being an adjective to being a n
From Middle Dutch vochten, from Old Dutch fūhten, *fūhton from Proto-West Germanic *fų̄htijan, *fų̄htēn.
From Middle Dutch voeden, from Old Dutch *fuoden, from Proto-West Germanic *fōdijan, from Proto-Germanic *fōdijaną, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂-.
From Middle Dutch voegen, from Old Dutch fuogen, from Proto-West Germanic *fōgijan, from Proto-Germanic *fōgijaną. Cognate with German fügen, German Low German fögen.

parole.significato: to feel, to have sensation of
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch voelen, from Old Dutch *fuolen, from Proto-West Germanic *fōlijan (“to feel”).

parole.significato: fodder, grub, animal food, feed, (for humans) inferior food
parole.testo: Contraction of voeder, from Middle Dutch voeder, from Old Dutch *fuoder, from Proto-West Germanic *fōdr.
Contraction of voeder, from Middle Dutch voeder, from Old Dutch *fuothar, from Proto-West Germanic *fōþr.
From Middle Dutch voeren, from Old Dutch fuoren, from Proto-West Germanic *fōrijan, from Proto-Germanic *fōrijaną, causative of *faraną (modern varen).
A contraction of voederen, from Middle Dutch voederen, from voeder (“lining”), from Proto-West Germanic *fōdr (“sheath”).
From Middle Dutch voet, from Old Dutch fuot, from Proto-West Germanic *fōt, from Proto-Germanic *fōts, from Proto-Indo-European *pṓds.

parole.significato: bird, any member of the class Aves
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch vōgel.
From Middle Dutch vol, from Old Dutch fol, ful, full, from Proto-West Germanic *full, from Proto-Germanic *fullaz, from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₁nós.

parole.significato: to complete what the stem refers to
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch vol, from Old Dutch fol, ful, from Proto-West Germanic *full, from Proto-Germanic *fullaz, from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₁nós.

From Middle Dutch voldoen, from Old Dutch *folduon, from Proto-West Germanic *fulladōn, equivalent to vol- + doen. Cognate with Old English fuldōn (whence English fulldo), Middle High German voltuon, volletuon.
From Middle Dutch volgen, from Old Dutch folgon, from Proto-West Germanic *folgēn, from Proto-Germanic *fulgāną.
From Middle Dutch volc, from Old Dutch folc, from Proto-West Germanic *folk, from Proto-Germanic *fulką.

parole.significato: synonym of vondst (“a find; the act of finding”)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch vont, from Old Dutch *fund, from Proto-West Germanic *fund, from Proto-Germanic *fundaz (compare *fundiz), an ablaut variant of *finþaną, the verb underlying modern Dutch vinden. Cognate with German Fund.

parole.significato: narrow bridge or beam over water
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch vondere, from Old Dutch *fundra, *fundera, from Proto-West Germanic *fundru. Perhaps related to vlonder (see there for more).
From Middle Dutch vonken, from Old Dutch *funkon, from Proto-West Germanic *funkōn (“to spark, sparkle”).

From Middle Dutch vore, vor, voor, from Old Dutch fora, fore, from Proto-West Germanic *forē, from Proto-Germanic *furai. There were originally two distinct Germanic forms, *furai and *furi, which functionally merged in most Germanic languages, including Dutch. The form derived from the former becam
From Middle Dutch vore, from Old Dutch *furh, from Proto-West Germanic *furh, from Proto-Germanic *furhs.

parole.significato: denotes primarily that something is before or in front of another thing or higher in a hierarchy
parole.testo: Ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *forē-. Cognate with English fore-.
From Middle Dutch vort, vōort, from Old Dutch *furt, from Proto-West Germanic *furdu, from Proto-Germanic *furduz, from Proto-Indo-European *pértus. Doublet of fjord.
From Middle Dutch vortbringen, from Old Dutch forthbringan, from Proto-West Germanic *forþbringan, equivalent to voort + brengen. Analogous to English forthbring and bring forth.
From Middle Dutch vorke, from Old Dutch furka, from Proto-West Germanic *furkō, from Latin furca. Doublet of fork.

parole.significato: the generic term for prince, monarch, ruler
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch vorste, from Old Dutch furista, fursta, from the substantivised weak inflection of Proto-West Germanic *furist, from Proto-Germanic *furistaz (“first”).
From Middle Dutch vorst, a metathetic form of Old Dutch *frost, from Proto-West Germanic *frost, from Proto-Germanic *frustaz. Equivalent to vriezen (“to freeze”) + -t (“verbal noun”).

parole.significato: copse, grove, woodland (a coppiced land smaller than a forest)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch vorst, voerst, from Old Dutch furost, from Proto-West Germanic *furhisti.

From Middle Dutch vorst, vorste, from Proto-West Germanic *fursti, from Proto-Germanic *furstiz, variant of *firstiz. Most closely related to Middle Low German vorst, Middle High German forst. Through the i-form also cognate with Middle Dutch verst, verste, French faîte, German First, Old English fi

parole.significato: fox, carnivore of the tribe Vulpini
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle Dutch vos, from Old Dutch fus, vus, from Proto-West Germanic *fuhs, from Proto-Germanic *fuhsaz.
From Middle Dutch vouden, from Old Dutch *faldan, from Proto-West Germanic *falþan, from Proto-Germanic *falþaną.
From Middle Dutch vrage, from Old Dutch *frāga, from Proto-West Germanic *frāgu, from Proto-Germanic *frēgō, from Proto-Indo-European *preḱ-.

From Middle Dutch vraet, from Old Dutch [Term?], from Proto-West Germanic [Term?], from Proto-Germanic *fraētaz, deverbal from *fraetaną, whence vreten. This word is thus effectively a verbal noun to vreten. Cognate with German Fraß.
From Middle Dutch vrâgen, from Old Dutch frāgon, from Proto-West Germanic *frāgēn. See *fregnan (“to ask”).
From Middle Dutch vrēde, from Old Dutch fritho, from Proto-West Germanic *friþu.

From Middle Dutch vremt, vreemt, from Old Dutch fremithi, from Proto-West Germanic *framiþī, from Proto-Germanic *framaþiz (“foreign, not one's own”), from Proto-Indo-European *perəm-, *prom- (“forth, forward”), from *per- (“to go over”). Cognate with German fremd.

From Middle Dutch vrec, vrek (“miserly; miser”), from Old Dutch *frek, from Proto-West Germanic *frek, from Proto-Germanic *frekaz. Originally an adjective, but substantivised in early Middle Dutch at the latest. Cognate to German frech (Old High German freh), Old English frec.

parole.significato: to eat savagely, stuff, hog, wolf (down), gobble
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch vrēten, from Old Dutch *fretan, from Proto-West Germanic *fraetan, from Proto-Germanic *fraetaną. Corresponds to ver- + eten and thus represents a doublet of vereten.
From Middle Dutch vrient, from Old Dutch friunt, from Proto-West Germanic *friund, from Proto-Germanic *frijōndz. Related to the verb vrijen (“to make love; to be in a relationship”).
From Middle Dutch vriendeloos, from Old Dutch [Term?], from Proto-West Germanic [Term?]; compare Old High German friuntlōs, Old English frēondlēas. By surface analysis, vriend + -e- + -loos.
Derived Middle Dutch vrientschap, from Old Dutch friundscap, from Proto-West Germanic *friundskapi. Equivalent to vriend + -schap.
From Middle Dutch vriesen, from Old Dutch *friesan, from Proto-West Germanic *freusan, from Proto-Germanic *freusaną, from Proto-Indo-European *prews-.

From Middle Dutch vri, from Old Dutch frī, from Proto-West Germanic *frī, from Proto-Germanic *frijaz, from Proto-Indo-European *priHós, a derivation from *preyH- (“to be fond of”). Related to vrijen (“to make love”), vrijdag (“Friday”), vriend (“friend”), and vrede (“peace”).

From Middle Dutch vrīdach, vriendach, from Old Dutch *frīadag, from Proto-West Germanic *Frījā dag, calque of Latin dies Veneris. Compare Low German Freedag, German Freitag, West Frisian freed, English Friday, Danish fredag.
From Middle Dutch vrijdom, from Old Dutch *frīduom (“freedom”), from Proto-West Germanic *frijadōm (“freedom”). From vrij + -dom.

parole.significato: to make love, to have sex
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch vrien, from Old Dutch *frīon, from Proto-West Germanic *frijōn (“to love”).
From Middle Dutch vroech, extended form of vroe, from Old Dutch fruo, from Proto-West Germanic *frō(ī) (“early”).

From Middle Dutch vrouwe, from Old Dutch frouwa, vrouwa, from Proto-West Germanic *frauwjā, from Proto-Germanic *frawjǭ. Vrouw replaced wijf as a neutral descriptor for a woman in the Early Modern period (see there for more), whereas vrouw mostly referred to well-off or aristocratic women in Middle

parole.significato: fruit (often edible, seed-bearing part of a plant)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch vrucht, from Old Dutch fruht, from Proto-West Germanic *fruhti (“fruit”). Doublet of fruit.
From Middle Dutch vruchten, from Old Dutch *furhten, forhten, from Proto-West Germanic *furhtijan, from Proto-Germanic *furhtijaną.

From Middle Dutch vuul, from Old Dutch *fūl. The adjective is from Proto-West Germanic *fūl, from Proto-Germanic *fūlaz, the noun from Proto-Germanic *fūlą. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pū-, *pew-. Akin to English foul, German faul, Danish and Swedish ful.
From Middle Dutch vuust, from Old Dutch *fūst, from Proto-West Germanic *fūsti.

From Middle Dutch vullen, from Old Dutch *fullen, from Proto-West Germanic *fullijan, from Proto-Germanic *fullijaną. Equivalent to vol (“full”) + -en (“deadjectival”) and shows the effect of historical umlaut.

From Middle Dutch vuur, from Old Dutch fuir, from Proto-West Germanic *fuir, from Proto-Germanic *fōr, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *péh₂wr̥. The adjectival slang sense is a calque of the slang sense of English fire.
From Middle Dutch wâge, from Old Dutch wāga, from Proto-West Germanic *wāgu, from Proto-Germanic *wēgō.

From Middle Dutch wāge f, alternative form of rare waech m, from Old Dutch *wāg, from Proto-West Germanic *wāg, from Proto-Germanic *wēgaz. The feminine may be a mere variant (if old from Old Dutch *wāga, from Proto-West Germanic *wāgu, from Proto-Germanic *wēgō), or it may be due to a merger with a
From Middle Dutch wâyen, from Old Dutch *wāien, from Proto-West Germanic *wāan, from Proto-Germanic *wēaną, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂weh₁-.

parole.significato: a Walloon person, a person from Wallonia
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch Wale, from Old Dutch *Wala, *Wale, from Proto-West Germanic *walh, from Proto-Germanic *walhaz (“foreigner”).
From Middle Dutch walsch, waalsch, from Old Dutch *walisc, from Proto-West Germanic *walhisk, from Proto-Germanic *walhiskaz. Cognate with German welsch, English Welsh, Danish vælsk.
From Middle Dutch wâen, from Old Dutch wān, from Proto-West Germanic *wāni, from Proto-Germanic *wēniz.
From Middle Dutch wâer, from Old Dutch *wār, from Proto-West Germanic *wār, from Proto-Germanic *wēraz.

parole.significato: a holm, holme, an area surrounded by rivers or a riverine floodplain
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch wāert, wēert, wert, from Old Dutch *werith, from Proto-West Germanic *wariþ, from Proto-Germanic *wariþa-, *waruþa-.

By surface analysis, waard (“value”, pedicative adjective) + -e (abstract noun suffix). From Middle Dutch werde which still has the expected i-mutation (compare kou, hulde), from Proto-West Germanic *werþī f. In Middle Dutch the forms warde, waerde arose under influence of the adjective. Cognate wit
From Middle Dutch waerhede, from Old Dutch wārheit, wārheid, wārheide, from Proto-West Germanic *wārahaidu. Equivalent to waar + -heid.
From Middle Dutch wāse, wāze, waes (“mud, mire”), from Proto-West Germanic *waisā, from Proto-Germanic *waisǭ.
From Middle Dutch wachtele, from Old Dutch [Term?], from Proto-West Germanic *wahtilu or *hwahtlā.
From Middle Dutch wachten, from Old Dutch *wahton, from Proto-West Germanic *wahtwēn. Equivalent to wacht (“watch, vigil”) + -en.
From Middle Dutch wāgen, from Old Dutch wagan, from Proto-West Germanic *wagn, from Proto-Germanic *wagnaz, from Proto-Indo-European *weǵʰ-. Doublet of wagon.
From Middle Dutch wāgen, from Old Dutch *wagon, from Proto-West Germanic *wagōn, from Proto-Germanic *wagōną.
From Middle Dutch waken, from Old Dutch wacon, from Proto-West Germanic *wakēn, from Proto-Germanic *wakāną (“to be awake”).
From Middle Dutch wacker, from Old Dutch *wakkar, from Proto-West Germanic *wakr. Cognate with German wacker (“stalwart”), dialectal English waker (“vigilant”, see there).

From Middle Dutch wal (“whale”), from Old Dutch *wal, from Proto-West Germanic *hwal, from Proto-Germanic *hwalaz (“whale”). Cognate with English whale. Possibly to avoid confusion with wal (“wall; shore”), the derived compound word walvis (“whale; lit. whale-fish”) gained currency over wal (“whale”

parole.significato: to cause to become nauseated, to disgust
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch walgen, from Old Dutch *walgon, from Proto-West Germanic *walgōn, from Proto-Germanic *walgōną (“to roll”).
From Middle Dutch wan, wanne, Old Dutch *wanna, from Proto-West Germanic *wannu, from Latin vannus.

parole.significato: to stroll, be on a walk (‘to go for a walk’ = ‘gaan wandelen’)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch wandelen, from Old Dutch *wandilon, from Proto-West Germanic *wandalōn.

parole.significato: to misbelieve (believe falsely or incorrectly) oneself to be something, to delude oneself into thinking to be something
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch wânen, from Old Dutch wānen, from Proto-West Germanic *wānijan, from Proto-Germanic *wēnijaną.
From Middle Dutch wange, from Old Dutch *wanga, from Proto-West Germanic *wangā, from Proto-Germanic *wangô (“cheek”), from Proto-Indo-European *wenǵ- (“neck, cheek”).
From Old Dutch *wankal, from Proto-West Germanic *wankul.

From Middle Dutch wanneer, wan eer, from Old Dutch *wan ēr. The former part is found as Middle Dutch wan, from Old Dutch *wan, from Proto-West Germanic *hwan, from Proto-Germanic *hwan. The latter part is identical with modern eer (“before”). Cognate with Low German wannehr, Luxembourgish wéini, obs
From Middle Dutch wannen, from Old Dutch *wannon, from Proto-West Germanic *wannōn, ultimately from Latin vannus (“winnowing basket”).
From Middle Dutch wâpen, from Old Dutch wāpan, from Proto-West Germanic *wāpn, from Proto-Germanic *wēpną.
Inherited from Middle Dutch werre, warre (“confusion, disarray, conflict”), from Old Dutch *werra, from Proto-West Germanic *werʀu (“confusion; quarrel”).

Unknown. The only cognate found is West Frisian waarje. Perhaps related to Old High German wadalōn (“to roam, wander”); if so, related to Proto-West Germanic *wāan (“to blow (of wind)”); compare modern German Wallfahrt (“pilgrimage”). Or, related to Old English wāþ (“wandering, hunt”), from Proto-We
From Middle Dutch waren, from Old Dutch *waron, from Proto-West Germanic *warōn, from Proto-Germanic *warōną.
From Middle Dutch wasschen, from Old Dutch wascan, from Proto-West Germanic *waskan, from Proto-Germanic *waskaną, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wed- (“water, wet”).

parole.significato: what: e.g. (1) asking for a subject complement; (2) asking for a sentence object
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch wat, from Old Dutch wat, from Proto-West Germanic *hwat, from Proto-Germanic *hwat, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷód, *kʷod, compare West Frisian wat, English what, German was, Danish hvad.
From Middle Dutch wāter, from Old Dutch watar, from Proto-West Germanic *watar, from Proto-Germanic *watōr, from Proto-Indo-European *wódr̥.
From Middle Dutch waterhoen, from Old Dutch *watarhuon, from Proto-West Germanic *watarhōn, equivalent to water + hoen. Cognate with German Wasserhuhn (“coot”).
From Middle Dutch waterich, from Old Dutch *watarig, from Proto-West Germanic *watarīg. Equivalent to water + -ig.

parole.significato: a plant of species Isatis tinctoria (woad or dyer's woad)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch wede, from Old Dutch *wēd, from Proto-West Germanic *waiʀd, from Proto-Germanic *waizdaz. Doublet of wouw.
From Middle Dutch wederich, from Old Dutch *witherig, from Proto-West Germanic *wiþrīg.
From Middle Dutch weduwe, Old Dutch widowa, from Proto-West Germanic *widuwā, from Proto-Germanic *widuwǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁widʰéwh₂ (“widow”). Compare German Witwe, English widow.
From Old Dutch *wē, from Proto-West Germanic *wai, from Proto-Germanic *wai. Compare Old English wā (English woe), Old High German wē (German weh), Old Norse vei.
From Middle Dutch wēke, from Old Dutch *wica, from Proto-West Germanic *wikā, from Proto-Germanic *wikǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *weyg- (“to bend, wind, turn, yield”).
From Middle Dutch wêec, from Old Dutch *wēc, from Proto-West Germanic *waikw, from Proto-Germanic *waikwaz.

Contracted form of weder (“again”), from Middle Dutch wēder, from Old Dutch wither, from Proto-West Germanic *wiþr, from Proto-Germanic *wiþrą (“against”), from Proto-Indo-European *wit(e)rom (“more apart”), from *wí (“separation”).
Contracted form of weder (“weather”), from Middle Dutch wēder, from Old Dutch *wedar, from Proto-West Germanic *wedr, from Proto-Germanic *wedrą, from Proto-Indo-European *wedʰrom.
From Middle Dutch wēre, from Old Dutch weri, from Proto-West Germanic *warī.
From Middle Dutch wēder, from Old Dutch withar (“wether, ram”), from Proto-West Germanic *weþru, from Proto-Germanic *weþruz (“wether”), from Proto-Indo-European *wet- (“year”).

From Middle Dutch wêer, wier, warre, from Old Dutch *warr, probably from Proto-West Germanic *warʀ, from Proto-Germanic *warzaz, but this leaves the vowel ê in Middle Dutch unexplained. Related to wrat, Old English wearr (whence English war), and Latin verrūca.
From older weder, from Middle Dutch wēder, from Old Dutch *wether, from Proto-West Germanic *hwaþar, from Proto-Germanic *hwaþeraz.
From Middle Dutch wēer, from Old Dutch *wer-, from Proto-West Germanic *wer, from Proto-Germanic *weraz.
From Middle Dutch wermoed, from Old Dutch *wermuoda, from Proto-West Germanic *warjamōdā. Doublet of vermout.
From Middle Dutch weerspreken, wederpreken, from Old Dutch *witharsprekan, from Proto-West Germanic *wiþrasprekan, equivalent to weer- + spreken.
From Middle Dutch wēerwolf, from Old Dutch *werwulf, from Proto-West Germanic *werawulf. Equivalent to weer (“man, were”) + wolf (“wolf”).

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Possibly; Probably; modello unc/uncertain
parole.significato: an orphan, person or animal having survived both parents
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch wêse, from Old Dutch wēso, from Proto-West Germanic *waisō, of uncertain origin, with no solid cognates outside of Germanic; possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁widʰéwh₂ (“widow”). Cognate with German Waise, Middle Low German wêse, probably Old English *wāsa (in wuduwās
From Middle Dutch wech, from Old Dutch weh, weg, from Proto-West Germanic *weg, from Proto-Germanic *wegaz, from Proto-Indo-European *weǵʰ-.

parole.significato: to weigh (to determine the weight or be of a specified weight)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch wēgen, from Old Dutch *wegan, from Proto-West Germanic *wegan, from Proto-Germanic *weganą, from Proto-Indo-European *wéǵʰeti.

parole.significato: a product obtained from milk; whey
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch wei, from Old Dutch *wei, from Proto-West Germanic *hwaij (“whey”).
From Middle Dutch weide, from Old Dutch weitha, from Proto-West Germanic *waiþu, from Proto-Germanic *waiþijō, *waiþō. Cognate with German Weide.

parole.significato: to refuse, to deny (not to allow)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch weigeren, from Old Dutch *weigaron, *wēgaron, from Proto-West Germanic *waigrōn (“to be stubborn”).

From Middle Dutch weit, weet, from Old Dutch *weit, *wēt, from Proto-West Germanic *hwaitī, from Proto-Germanic *hwaitijaz, from *hwītaz (“white”). Cognate with Low German Weten, West Frisian weet, German Weizen, English wheat.
From Middle Dutch wêken, from Old Dutch *wēken, from Proto-West Germanic *waikwijan, from Proto-Germanic *waikwijaną.
From Middle Dutch wecken, from Old Dutch wecken, from Proto-West Germanic *wakkjan, from Proto-Germanic *wakjaną.
From Middle Dutch *welle, from Old Dutch *wella, from Proto-West Germanic *wallijā, from Proto-Germanic *wallijǭ.
From Middle Dutch welich, from Old Dutch *welag, from Proto-West Germanic *welag. Equivalent to wel + -ig.

From Middle Dutch welken, from Old Dutch *wilken, from Proto-West Germanic *wilkijan; according to Kluge, ultimately related to Proto-West Germanic *wolkn (“cloud”). Akin to German welken, English welk.

parole.significato: to soak, to soften by putting into water
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch wellen, Old Dutch *wellen, from Proto-West Germanic *wallijan.
From Middle Dutch wellustich, waellustich, wallustich, from Old Dutch *walalustig, from Proto-West Germanic *walalustig, equivalent to wel- + lustig.
From Middle Dutch wenden, from Old Dutch wenden, from Proto-West Germanic *wandijan, from Proto-Germanic *wandijaną. Historically a causative verb to winden (“to wind”).

parole.significato: to get used (to), to become accustomed
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch wennen, from Old Dutch *wennen, from Proto-West Germanic *wannjan.

From Middle Dutch wensch, next to eastern wonsch, from Old Dutch *wunsk, from Proto-West Germanic *wunsk, from Proto-Germanic *wunskaz. Cognate with German Wunsch, English wish, West Frisian winsk, Danish ønske.

From Middle Dutch werelt, from Old Dutch werilt, werolt, from Proto-West Germanic *weraldi, from Proto-Germanic *weraldiz, from Proto-Germanic *weraz (“man”) + *aldiz (“time, age, old”), hence "age of man". Cognate to West Frisian wrâld, English world, German Welt, Swedish värld.

From Middle Dutch wereltwijs, from Old Dutch [Term?], from Proto-West Germanic [Term?]; compare Old High German weraltwīs, Old English weoroldwīs (English worldwise). By surface analysis, wereld (“world”) + wijs (“wise”).

parole.significato: to hold back, to keep out
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch wēren, from Old Dutch werien, from Proto-West Germanic *warjan, from Proto-Germanic *warjaną.

From Middle Dutch werf, warf, from Old Dutch *warf, from Proto-West Germanic [Term?]. Cognate with Old Saxon hwarba, Old High German -warf, Old Frisian hwarf, hwerf. Related to werven in its original meaning of "to turn" (compare the frequentative verb wervelen and the noun wervel, and see *hwerban)
From Middle Dutch werc, from Old Dutch *werk, from Proto-West Germanic *werk, from Proto-Germanic *werką, from Proto-Indo-European *wérǵom.
From Middle Dutch werken, from Old Dutch wirken, from Proto-West Germanic *wirkijan, from Proto-Germanic *wirkijaną (“to work, make”), from Proto-Indo-European *werǵ- (“to work, act”).
From Middle Dutch werpen, from Old Dutch werpan, from Proto-West Germanic *werpan, from Proto-Germanic *werpaną. Cognate with German werfen.
From Middle Dutch wers (“worse”), from Old Dutch *wirs, from Proto-West Germanic *wirsiʀō, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *wirsizô. Cognate with English worse.

parole.significato: to recruit, notably for enlistment or civil employment
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch werven, from Old Dutch *wervan, from Proto-West Germanic *hwerban, from Proto-Germanic *hwerbaną.

parole.significato: wasp (various insects of the order Hymenoptera, especially of the superfamily Vespoidea)
parole.testo: From earlier Modern Dutch wespe, from Middle Dutch wespe, from Old Dutch *wespa, with metathesis from Proto-West Germanic *wapsu, from Proto-Germanic *wepsō-, from Proto-Indo-European *wóbʰseh₂ (“wasp”), from *webʰ- (“weave”). Cognate with German Wespe, Low German Wösp, English wasp.
From Middle Dutch west, from Old Dutch west, from Proto-West Germanic *westr, from Proto-Germanic *westrą. Compare German West, English and West Frisian west, Danish vest.
From Middle Dutch wet, wette, wit, weet, from Old Dutch witat, witut (“rule, law”), from Proto-West Germanic *witōþ, from Proto-Germanic *witōþą (“law”).

parole.significato: to know (knowledge), to be aware of something
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch wēten, from Old Dutch witan, from Proto-West Germanic *witan, from Proto-Germanic *witaną, from Proto-Indo-European *wóyde (“know”), a root perfect from the root *weyd-. The past tense forms is also composed of the regular past tense marker -te.

parole.significato: to whet, hone or rub on with something for the purpose of sharpening an object (typically a blade)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch wetten, from Old Dutch *wetten, from Proto-West Germanic *hwattjan, from Proto-Germanic *hwatjaną.
From Middle Dutch wēven, from Old Dutch wevan, from Proto-West Germanic *weban, from Proto-Germanic *webaną, from Proto-Indo-European *webʰ-.

From Middle Dutch wever, from Old Dutch [Term?], from Proto-West Germanic *webārī; cognates include Old High German weberi (German Weber), Old English *wæfre (in compounds; modern English weaver). By surface analysis, weven + -er.

parole.significato: A weasel; any mustelid of genus Mustela.
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch wēsel, from Old Dutch *wisula, *wisala, from Proto-West Germanic *wisulā, from Proto-Germanic *wisulǭ.

From Middle Dutch wēsen, from Old Dutch wesan, from Proto-West Germanic *wesan, from Proto-Germanic *wesaną. See zijn. The noun represents a substantivization of the verb and is attested as such since as early as c. 1100.

From Middle Dutch wicht, from Old Dutch *wiht, from Proto-West Germanic *wihti, from Proto-Germanic *wihtiz. The gender gradually shifted from feminine to neuter from the Middle Dutch phase onwards, influenced by gewicht.
From Middle Dutch wie, from Old Dutch wie, from Proto-West Germanic *hwaʀ, from Proto-Germanic *hwaz, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷos.
From Middle Dutch wied (“weed”), from Old Dutch *wiod, from Proto-West Germanic *weud. Doublet of wiet (“marijuana”), which came from English weed (“marijuana”).
From Middle Dutch wiege, possibly from an affective variant of Proto-West Germanic *wagā (“craddle”), from Proto-Germanic *wagǭ. Compare the Old High German variants wīga (later Wiege) and waga.

parole.significato: sail of a windmill or blade on a wind turbine
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch wieke, from Proto-West Germanic *weukā (“flax bundle, wick”), from Proto-Indo-European *weg- (“to weave”).
From Middle Dutch wiel, from Old Dutch *wiol, from Proto-West Germanic *hwehwl, from Proto-Germanic *hwehwlą, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷekʷlóm, *kʷékʷlos.

From older wiedewaal by assimilation of -d- to -l-, from Middle Dutch wedewale. The first part, wede- probably stems from Proto-West Germanic *widu (“wood, forest”), whereas -wale could be onomatopoeic.

From Middle Dutch wier (“seaweed”), possibly descended through Old Dutch from Proto-West Germanic *wair, related to *wīraz, or was borrowed from West Frisian. Cognate with dialectal English ware (“seaweed”), Old English wār (“seaweed”).
From Middle Dutch wegghe, from Old Dutch *weggi, from Proto-West Germanic *wagi, from Proto-Germanic *wagjaz.

parole.significato: we; first-person plural subjective personal pronoun
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch wi, from Old Dutch wī, from Proto-West Germanic *wiʀ, from Proto-Germanic *wīz, from Proto-Indo-European *wéy, plural of *éǵh₂. Compare Low German wi, West Frisian wy, German wir, English we, Danish vi.

From earlier wijen, from Middle Dutch wiën, from Old Dutch wīen, from Proto-West Germanic *wīhijan, from Proto-Germanic *wīhijaną. The -d- was inserted in the early modern period due to hypercorrection, the earlier and original form wijen being mistakenly identified as the result of deletion of inte

parole.significato: woman, potentially being as pejorative as bitch
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch wijf, from Old Dutch wīf, from Proto-West Germanic *wīb, from Proto-Germanic *wībą. While initially a neutral term for "woman", the word gradually acquired negative connotations in some dialects from the late 16th century onwards, developing over the centuries to the current situat

From Middle Dutch wijc, from Old Dutch *wīk, from Proto-West Germanic *wīk, from Latin vīcus (“hamlet, village, neighborhood”), from Proto-Indo-European *weyḱ- (“village, household”). Cognate with English wick, -wich, -wick, German Weich- in dated Weichbild (“municipal area”). Compare Gothic 𐍅𐌴𐌹𐌷𐍃 (

parole.significato: secondary canal in a turf extraction area
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch wijc (“canal”), from Old Dutch *wīk, *wīka (in placenames), from Proto-West Germanic *wīku, from Proto-Germanic *wīkō (“inlet, bay”). Related to wijken, wik, Old English wīc, Old Norse vík.
From Middle Dutch wiken, from Old Dutch *wīcan, from Proto-West Germanic *wīkwan, from Proto-Germanic *wīkwaną.
From Middle Dutch wile (“while”), Old Dutch *wīla, from Proto-West Germanic *hwīlu. Cognate with English while, Low German Wiel, German Weile.

parole.significato: wine (an alcoholic beverage produced by a certain fermentation procedure; unless otherwise specified or indicated by co…
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch wijn, from Old Dutch wīn, from Proto-West Germanic *wīn, from Latin vīnum.
From Middle Dutch witen, from Old Dutch wītan, from Proto-West Germanic *wītan, from Proto-Germanic *wītaną.
From Middle Dutch wisen, from Old Dutch wīsen, from Proto-West Germanic *wīsijan, from Proto-Germanic *wīsijaną.

parole.significato: vetch, leguminous plant of the genus Vicia
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch wicke, from Old Dutch *wikka, from Proto-West Germanic *wikkjā, from Latin vicia.
From Middle Dutch wille, from Old Dutch willo, from Proto-West Germanic *willjō, from Proto-Germanic *wiljô.
From Middle Dutch wilt, from Old Dutch wildi, from Proto-West Germanic *wilþī, from Proto-Germanic *wilþijaz.
From Middle Dutch wilge, from Old Dutch *wilga, from Proto-West Germanic *wilgijā.

From Middle Dutch willen, from Old Dutch willen, from Proto-West Germanic *willjan, from Proto-Germanic *wiljaną, from Proto-Indo-European *welh₁-. The variant past forms with ou go back to early Middle Dutch wolde(n), following the regular shift old, olt > oud, out.
From Middle Dutch wimpel, from Old Dutch *wimpil, from Proto-West Germanic *wimpil, from Proto-Germanic *wimpilaz.

From Middle Dutch wint, from Old Dutch wint, from Proto-West Germanic *wind, from Proto-Germanic *windaz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wéh₁n̥ts (“blowing”), present participle of *h₂weh₁- (“to blow”).

parole.significato: shop, store (establishment that sells goods to the public)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch winkel (“corner”), from Old Dutch winkel, from Proto-West Germanic *winkil, from Proto-Indo-European *weng- (“to bend, bow, arch, curve”). Cognate with German Winkel, Old English wincel. The meaning "shop" is derived from the meaning "corner in which merchandise is stalled".

parole.significato: to win, to triumph, to be victorious (in)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch winnen, from Old Dutch winnan, from Proto-West Germanic *winnan, from Proto-Germanic *winnaną, from Proto-Indo-European *wenh₁- (“to strive, desire, wish, love”).
From Middle Dutch wisperen, from Old Dutch *wisperon, from Proto-West Germanic *hwisprōn, from Proto-Germanic *hwisprōną.

From Middle Dutch wit, from Old Dutch *wit, from Proto-West Germanic *hwīt, from Proto-Germanic *hwittaz. The geminate is unexpected as the usual Proto-Germanic form is *hwītaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱweytos (“shine; bright”). The geminate is sometimes explained as being the result of Kluge's la

From Middle Dutch wit, from Old Dutch *witti, from Proto-West Germanic *witi, from Proto-Germanic *witją (“knowledge, reason”), from Proto-Indo-European *weyd- (“see, know”). Related to weten (“to know”), wis (“knowledge”) and wijs (“wise”). Cognate with English wit, German Witz.
From Middle Dutch woensdach, from Old Dutch *wuodenesdag, from Proto-West Germanic *Wōdanas dag (“day of Woden”), calque of Latin dies Mercurii. Equivalent to Woen (“Wodan”) + -s- + dag (“day”).
From Middle Dutch woeste, from Old Dutch wuosti, from Proto-West Germanic *wōstī.

parole.significato: desert (environmental area with very little precipitation)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch woestine, from Old Dutch wuostinna, from Proto-West Germanic *wōstini. Cognate with German Wüste, English waste.
From Middle Dutch wolle, from Old Dutch *wulla, from Proto-West Germanic *wullu, from Proto-Germanic *wullō.

parole.significato: wolf (Canis lupus; the largest wild member of the canine subfamily)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch wolf, from Old Dutch *wulf, from Proto-West Germanic *wulf, from Proto-Germanic *wulfaz, from Proto-Indo-European *wĺ̥kʷos.
From Middle Dutch wolke, from Old Dutch wulko, from Proto-West Germanic *wolkn.
From Middle Dutch wolvinne, from Old Dutch *wulfinna, from Proto-West Germanic *wulfini. Equivalent to wolf + -in.
From Middle Dutch wonden, from Middle Dutch *wundon, from Proto-West Germanic *wundōn, from Proto-Germanic *wundōną. By surface analysis, wond + -en.

From Middle Dutch wonder, wunder, from Old Dutch wunder, from Proto-West Germanic *wundr, from Proto-Germanic *wundrą, from Proto-Indo-European *wenh₁- (“to wish for, desire, strive for, win, love”). Compare Low German wunder, wunner, German Wunder, West Frisian wonder, wûnder, English wonder, Danis
From Middle Dutch wōnen, from Old Dutch wonon, from Proto-West Germanic *wunēn, from Proto-Germanic *wunāną, from Proto-Indo-European *wenh₁- (“to wish, love”).
From Middle Dutch wort, from Old Dutch wort, from Proto-West Germanic *word, from Proto-Germanic *wurdą, from Proto-Indo-European *wr̥dʰom. Doublet of verbum.

parole.significato: to become, to get, to grow, to turn
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch werden, from Old Dutch werthan, from Proto-West Germanic *werþan, from Proto-Germanic *werþaną, from Proto-Indo-European *wert-.

From Middle Dutch worst, from Old Dutch *wurst, *worst, from Proto-West Germanic *wursti. Cognate with Limburgish wósj, Zealandic woste, Old Saxon worst, Middle Low German worst, Plautdietsch Worscht, Old Frisian *wurst, West Frisian woarst, Old High German wurst, Middle High German wurst, German Wu
From Middle Dutch worte, from Old Dutch *wurta, from Proto-West Germanic *wurtiju.
From Middle Dutch wout, from Old Dutch walt, from Proto-West Germanic *walþu, from Proto-Germanic *walþuz.

parole.significato: a kite, certain bird of the family Accipitridae; especially of the genera Milvus, Harpagus and Haliastur
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch wouwe, wīwe, wīe, from Old Dutch [Term?], from Proto-West Germanic [Term?], from Proto-Germanic *wīwô, a derivate of Proto-Indo-European *weyh₁- (“to hunt, pursue”). Compare German Weihe, Low German Wieh, both “harrier”.
From Middle Dutch woude, wouwe; ultimately derived from a variant of Proto-West Germanic *waiʀd. Cognate with English weld. Doublet of wede.

From Middle Dutch wrāke, wraeck, from Old Dutch wrāka, wrāca, from Proto-West Germanic *wrāku, from Proto-Germanic *wrēkō (“persecution, revenge”), from Proto-Indo-European *wreg- (“to drive, press, urge”). Cognate with English wrack and wreak (“vengeance, revenge”), Low German Wraak (“revenge, veng

parole.significato: wreck, wreckage (remains of a vehicle, vessel, aircraft or other piece of machinery)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch wrac, from Old Dutch *wrac, from Proto-West Germanic *wrak (“floating debris”), from Proto-Germanic *wraką. Nominalisation of the adjective wrak (“derelict”).
From Middle Dutch wrac, from Old Dutch *wrac, from Proto-West Germanic *wrak, from Proto-Germanic *wrakaz.
From Middle Dutch wranc, from Old Dutch *wrang, from Proto-West Germanic *wrang, from Proto-Germanic *wrangaz.
From Middle Dutch wreet, from Old Dutch *wrēth, from Proto-West Germanic *wraiþ, from Proto-Germanic *wraiþaz. Cognate with English wrath.

parole.significato: to (take) revenge, to avenge, to take vengeance
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch wrēken, from Old Dutch *wrekan, from Proto-West Germanic *wrekan.
From Middle Dutch vrevelich, from Old Dutch *fravalī̌g, from Proto-West Germanic *frafalīg, equivalent to wrevel (“spite”) + -ig (“-y”).

From Middle Dutch writen, from Old Dutch *wrītan, from Proto-West Germanic *wrītan, from Proto-Germanic *wrītaną. This verb originally meant 'to scratch, carve'. In West Germanic languages, its meaning started to diversify following the different dialects. While Old English and Old Saxon kept the me
From Middle Dutch wriven, from Old Dutch *wrīvan, from Proto-West Germanic *wrīban.
From Middle Dutch wroeten, from Old Dutch *wruotan, from Proto-West Germanic *wrōtan, from Proto-Germanic *wrōtaną.
From Middle Dutch weiven (the original vocalism is still reflected in the frequentative weifelen), from Old Dutch *weiven, from Proto-West Germanic *waibijan, from Proto-Germanic *waibijaną.

parole.significato: true whelk (one of certain whelks (edible sea snails) of the genus Buccinum)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch wilc, variant of willoc, from Old Dutch *wiluk, *weluk, from Proto-West Germanic *weluk.

parole.significato: plant seed, either natural or for agri- or horticultural use
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch saet, from Old Dutch *sāt, from Proto-West Germanic *sād, from Proto-Germanic *sēdiz. Equivalent to zaaien (“to sow”) + -d (“verbal noun”). Compare Low German Saad, German Saat, West Frisian sied, English seed, Danish sæd.
From Middle Dutch sage, from Old Dutch *saga, from Proto-West Germanic *sagu, from Proto-Germanic *sagō, from Proto-Indo-European *sek- (“to cut”).
From Middle Dutch sâyen, from Old Dutch *sāien, from Proto-West Germanic *sāan (“to sow”).

parole.significato: a thing, matter (general term with for a concept other than animate beings)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch sāke, from Old Dutch *saka, from Proto-West Germanic *saku, from Proto-Germanic *sakō. Cognate with English sake, West Frisian saak (“cause; business”), Low German Saak, German Sache (“thing; matter; cause; legal cause”), Yiddish זאַך (zakh), Danish sag, Swedish and Norwegian sak,
From Middle Dutch sale, from Old Dutch sala, from Proto-West Germanic *sali, from Proto-Germanic *saliz.
From Middle Dutch saen, from Old Dutch *sān, from Proto-West Germanic *sān(ō).
From Middle Dutch sachte, from Old Dutch sāfti, from Proto-West Germanic *samftī.

parole.significato: sack or sack-like container, such as a bag, sachet, pouch
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch sac, from Old Dutch sac, from Proto-West Germanic *sakku, from Proto-Germanic *sakkuz, from Latin saccus.
From Middle Dutch salve, from Old Dutch salva, from Proto-West Germanic *salbu, from Proto-Germanic *salbō.
From Middle Dutch salich, from Old Dutch *sālig, from Proto-West Germanic *sālīg, from *sāli.
From Middle Dutch salven, from Old Dutch salvon, from Proto-West Germanic *salbōn, from Proto-Germanic *salbōną.
From Middle Dutch sant, from Old Dutch *sant, from Proto-West Germanic *samd, from Proto-Germanic *sandaz. Compare German Sand, Low German Sand, West Frisian sand, English sand, Danish sand.
From Middle Dutch sanc, from Old Dutch sang, from Proto-West Germanic *sangu, from Proto-Germanic *sangwaz. Doublet of song.

parole.significato: having had enough, having had it up to here, fed up
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch sat, from Old Dutch *sat, *sad, from Proto-West Germanic *sad, from Proto-Germanic *sadaz, from Proto-Indo-European *seh₂-. Compare German satt, English sad, Danish sat.

From Middle Dutch saterdach, from Old Dutch [Term?], from Proto-West Germanic *Sāturnas dag, calque of Latin dies Saturni. Compare Low German Saterdag, West Frisian saterdei, English Saturday. Saturn or Saturnus is the sixth planet of the solar system, and it was the name of the Roman god of fertili
From Middle Dutch sēdich, from Old Dutch *sidig, from Proto-West Germanic *sidīg, from Proto-Germanic *sidugaz. By surface analysis, zede + -ig.
From Middle Dutch sêe, from Old Dutch sēo, from Proto-West Germanic *saiwi, from Proto-Germanic *saiwiz.
From Middle Dutch seve, sef, from Old Dutch *sivi, *sif, from Proto-West Germanic *sibi.
From Middle Dutch sêel, from Old Dutch *sēl, from Proto-West Germanic *sail, from Proto-Germanic *sailą.
From Middle Dutch seep, sepe, from Old Dutch *sēpa, from Proto-West Germanic *saipā. Doublet of soap. Cognate with German Seife.
From Middle Dutch sēge, from Old Dutch *sigi, from Proto-West Germanic *sigʀ, from Proto-Germanic *segaz.
From Middle Dutch *segge, from Old Dutch *seggi, from Proto-West Germanic *sagi.

From Middle Dutch seggen, from Old Dutch seggen, from Proto-West Germanic *saggjan. The irregular past tense is a common Ingvaeonic development of the northern dialects, seen also in brein and zeil. (In an unrelated, later development the same also happened in Middle High German sagen.)

From Middle Dutch seiken, from Old Dutch *seiken, from Proto-West Germanic *saikijan, from Proto-Germanic *saikijaną. Cognate with archaic German seichen (“to piss”) and regional German sicken (“to piss”), sickig (“annoyed”).
From Middle Dutch seil, from Old Dutch *segil, from Proto-West Germanic *segl, from Proto-Germanic *seglą.

parole.significato: to sail (to ride in a sailboat)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch seilen, from Old Dutch *seglon, from Proto-West Germanic *seglōn. By surface analysis, zeil + -en.

From Middle Dutch seise, seisene, from Old Dutch *sagisna, *segisna, from Proto-West Germanic *sagisnu. Cognate with German Sense, more distantly related to English scythe (the Dutch cognate of which is zicht).
From Middle Dutch sēker, from Old Dutch *sikur, from Proto-West Germanic *sikur (“free, secure”), borrowed from Latin sēcūrus.
From Middle Dutch selden, from Old Dutch *seldan, from Proto-West Germanic *seldanā, from Proto-Germanic *seldanē.

From Middle Dutch senden, from Old Dutch senden, from Proto-West Germanic *sandijan, from Proto-Germanic *sandijaną. The original past tense was weak with Rückumlaut, thus sande or (through apocope) sant. Based on this latter form the verb then joined the strong class of Middle Dutch vinden, vant, g

From Middle Dutch singroene, sindegroen, from Old Dutch *singrōni, from Proto-West Germanic *singrōnijā. Possibly an early calque of Latin sempervīvum, itself a calque of Ancient Greek ἀείζωον (aeízōon). This word represents the sole inherited survival of the Germanic prefix *sin- in modern Dutch; z
From Middle Dutch sengen, from Old Dutch *sengen, from Proto-West Germanic *sangijan.

From Middle Dutch sarp, from Old Dutch *sarp, from Proto-West Germanic *sarp. Cognate with Old High German sarf. Further etymology uncertain, but the word has been related to ἅρπη (hárpē, “bird of prey, sickle, scimitar”), Proto-Slavic *sьrpъ (“sickle”), apparently deriving from a Proto-Indo-Europea
From Middle Dutch ses, from Old Dutch ses, from Proto-West Germanic *sehs, from Proto-Germanic *sehs, from Proto-Indo-European *swéḱs.
From Middle Dutch setten, from Old Dutch setten, from Proto-West Germanic *sattjan, from Proto-Germanic *satjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *sodéyeti. A causative verb to zitten (“to sit”).

From Middle Dutch soge, suege, from Old Dutch *soga, from Proto-West Germanic *sugu. The regular form in Middle Dutch was soge with a back vowel, with fronted suege occurring only in the western dialects. The original form is still found dialectally as zoog.

From Middle Dutch sēven, from Old Dutch sivun, sivon, from Proto-West Germanic *sebun, from Proto-Germanic *sebun, from earlier *sebunt, from Proto-Indo-European *septḿ̥, with -t added through influence of "nine" and "ten".
From Middle Dutch sêver, from Old Dutch *sēfar, from Proto-West Germanic *saifr.
From Middle Dutch sichte, from Old Dutch *siht, from Proto-West Germanic *sihti. Equivalent to zien (“to see”) + -t (“verbal noun”).
From Middle Dutch sieden, from Old Dutch *siethan, from Proto-West Germanic *seuþan, from Proto-Germanic *seuþaną.
From Middle Dutch siec, from Old Dutch siec, from Proto-West Germanic *seuk, from Proto-Germanic *seukaz. Cognate with English sick, German siech, Swedish sjuk. Doublet of sick.

From Middle Dutch siele, from Old Dutch *siola, contraction of an earlier *sēola (compare Old Saxon sēola), from Proto-West Germanic *saiwalu, from Proto-Germanic *saiwalō. The attested Old Dutch form sēla, with a different form of contraction, would have led to modern Dutch *zeel as in German Seele
From Middle Dutch siften, originally sichten, from Old Dutch *siften, from Proto-West Germanic *siftijan.
From Middle Dutch side, from Old Dutch sīda, from Proto-West Germanic *sīdā, from Proto-Germanic *sīdǭ.

parole.significato: to slump, to fall down, to drop
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch sigen (“to drop down, to slump”), from Old Dutch *sīgan, from Proto-West Germanic *sīgan, from Proto-Germanic *sīganą.
From Middle Dutch siën (“to filter, to seep”), from Old Dutch *sīan, from Proto-West Germanic *sīhwan, from Proto-Germanic *sīhwaną.

parole.significato: his; third-person singular masculine possessive determiner
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch sijn, from Old Dutch sīn (originally a reflexive form), from Proto-West Germanic *sīn, from Proto-Germanic *sīnaz, from Proto-Indo-European *seyno-. Cognate with German sein, Swedish sin. Ultimately a form of the Proto-Indo-European reflexive pronoun *swe. Compare Russian себя (seb
From Middle Dutch sin, from Old Dutch sin, from Proto-West Germanic *sinn.
From Middle Dutch sinken, from Old Dutch *sincan, from Proto-West Germanic *sinkwan, from Proto-Indo-European *sengʷ- (“to fall, sink”).
From Middle Dutch sinnen, from Old Dutch *sinnan, from Proto-West Germanic *sinnan, from Proto-Indo-European *sent-n-, a nasal suffix present from the root *sent- (“to feel”).
From Middle Dutch sitten, from Old Dutch sitten, from Proto-West Germanic *sittjan, from Proto-Germanic *sitjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *sed-.
From Middle Dutch sô, from Old Dutch sō, from Proto-West Germanic *swā, from a merger of Proto-Germanic *swa and *swē.
From Middle Dutch soeken, from Old Dutch suoken, from Proto-West Germanic *sōkijan, from Proto-Germanic *sōkijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *séh₂gyeti.
From Middle Dutch soete, from Old Dutch suoti, from Proto-West Germanic *swōtī, from Proto-Germanic *swōtuz, from Proto-Indo-European *sweh₂dus.
From Middle Dutch sôgen, from Old Dutch *sōgen, from Proto-West Germanic *saugijan, from Proto-Germanic *saugijaną. A causative verb to zuigen (“to suck”).
From Middle Dutch sômen, from Old Dutch *sōmen, from Proto-West Germanic *saumijan, from Proto-Germanic *saumijaną. Equivalent to zoom + -en.

From Middle Dutch somp, sump, from Old Dutch *sump, from Proto-West Germanic *sump, from Proto-Germanic *sumpaz. Cognates include Middle English sompe (“marsh, morass”), Middle Low German sump (“marsh, swamp”), German Sumpf (“swamp”).
From Middle Dutch sonne, from Old Dutch sunna, from Proto-West Germanic *sunnā, from Proto-Germanic *sunnǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *sh₂un-, *sóh₂wl̥.

From Middle Dutch sondach, sonnendach, from Old Dutch sunnadag (1151-1200; Reimbibel), from Proto-West Germanic *sunnōn dag (“day of the sun”), a calque of Latin dies Solis. By surface analysis, zon + dag. Compare Low German Sünndag, German Sonntag, West Frisian snein, English Sunday, Danish søndag.
From Proto-West Germanic *sunnig. By surface analysis, zon + -ig.
From Middle Dutch sôom, from Old Dutch *sōm, from Proto-West Germanic *saum, from Proto-Germanic *saumaz (“that which is sewn”).
From Middle Dutch sōne, from Old Dutch suno, from Proto-West Germanic *sunu, from Proto-Germanic *sunuz, from Proto-Indo-European *suHnús.

parole.significato: a heated and spiced alcohol beverage made of beer, rum and eggs that was sold and drunk during ice skating in early mod…
parole.testo: Diminutive from Middle Dutch sope, from Old Dutch *sopo, from Proto-West Germanic [Term?], from Proto-Germanic *supô. Doublet of soep, which via French ultimately derives from the same Germanic word of which zopie represents the directly inherited form (albeit with diminutive suffix).

From Middle Dutch sorge, sorghe, surghe, from Old Dutch sorga, from Proto-West Germanic *sorgu, from Proto-Germanic *surgō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *swergʰ- (“watch over, worry; be ill, suffer”). Compare German Sorge, West Frisian soarch, English sorrow, Danish sorg, Swedish sorg.
From Middle Dutch sorgen, from Old Dutch sorgon, from Proto-West Germanic *sorgēn, from Proto-Germanic *surgāną. By surface analysis, zorg + -en. Cognate with German sorgen.

From Middle Dutch sout, from Old Dutch *salt, from Proto-West Germanic *salt. The noun is from Proto-Germanic *saltą, the adjective from *saltaz. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *séh₂l-, *sḗh₂l. Compare German Salz, West Frisian sâlt, English salt, Danish salt.
From Middle Dutch soutsteen, from Old Dutch *saltstēn, from Proto-West Germanic *saltastain, equivalent to zout + steen. Cognate with English saltstone, German Salzstein.
From Middle Dutch sucht, socht, from Old Dutch *suft (“sigh, sip”), from Proto-West Germanic *sūftu.

From Middle Dutch suchte, from Old Dutch suhti, suhte (also sufte which is a hypercorrection), from Proto-West Germanic *suhti, from Proto-Germanic *suhtiz. Cognate to German Sucht and Old Norse sótt. Related to ziek.
From Middle Dutch suften, suchten, from Old Dutch *sufton, from Proto-West Germanic *sūftōn. Cognate with German seufzen.
From Middle Dutch suid, from Old Dutch *sūth, from Proto-West Germanic *sunþr, from Proto-Germanic *sunþrą. Compare West Frisian súd, German Süd, English south, Danish syd.
From Middle Dutch sugen, from Old Dutch sūgan, from Proto-West Germanic *sūgan, from Proto-Germanic *sūganą. The meaning "be bad" is a semantic loan from English suck.
From Middle Dutch suul, from Old Dutch sūl, from Proto-West Germanic *sūli, from Proto-Germanic *sūliz. Cognate with English sile.

parole.significato: dairy products (collective name for milk products)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch suvel, from Old Dutch *sūval (“food eaten with bread”), from Proto-West Germanic *sufl, from Proto-Germanic *suflą (“entremets, viands”), from Proto-Indo-European *sew-. Cognate with Old Saxon sūval, Middle Low German sûvel (“dairy products”), Old Frisian sūval, Saterland Frisian s

parole.significato: used to form the future tense of a verb, together with an infinitive; will, going to
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch solen, suelen, sollen, sullen, from Old Dutch sulan, from Proto-West Germanic *skulan, from Proto-Germanic *skulaną. Compare German sollen, English shall, Danish skulle.

From Middle Dutch suster, from Old Dutch swester, from Proto-Germanic *swestēr, from Proto-Indo-European *swésōr. The sense “nurse” from the fact that (before the Reformation and in Catholic areas until recently) the majority of nurses were nuns; already in Middle Dutch generalized to lay nurses.
From Middle Dutch suur, from Old Dutch *sūr, from Proto-West Germanic *sūr, from Proto-Germanic *sūraz. Cognate with Low German suur, West Frisian soer, German sauer, English sour, Danish sur.
From Middle Dutch swâer, from Old Dutch *swār, *swāri, from Proto-West Germanic *swār, from Proto-Germanic *swēraz, *swēriz.
From Middle Dutch swert, swaert, from Old Dutch swert, from Proto-West Germanic *swerd, from Proto-Germanic *swerdą, of uncertain origin; see there for more.

parole.significato: brother-in-law (brother of one's spouse or husband of one's sibling)
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch swager, from Old Dutch *swāgar, from Proto-West Germanic *swāgr, from Proto-Germanic *swēgraz.

parole.testo: From Middle Dutch swaluwe, from Old Dutch *swalwa, from Proto-West Germanic *swalwā, from Proto-Germanic *swalwǭ. Cognate with Danish and Norwegian svale, English swallow, German Schwalbe, Swedish svala. Doublet of schwalbe.
